teile.einleitung: A scooter is a ride-on toy with a footboard, two or three small wheels and a handlebar. You stand on it with one foot and push off the ground with the other. In Switzerland it is called a “Trottinett”, from the French word “trottinette”; in Germany people say “Tretroller” or “Roller”.
wichtigste: You move an ordinary scooter forward by pushing off with your foot.
The folding scooter with small wheels was invented by the Swiss Wim Ouboter.
An e-scooter has an electric motor and a rechargeable battery.
In Switzerland an e-scooter may go no faster than 20 km/h.
On an e-scooter you must ride on the cycle lane or the road, not on the pavement.
A helmet protects your head when you ride a scooter.

abschnitte.text: A scooter consists of a **footboard**, two or three wheels and a handlebar. You usually brake with your foot on a metal guard over the back wheel or with a hand brake. Many scooters can be folded up and are easy to carry. For small children there are models with three wheels that do not tip over so easily.

Simple wooden scooters existed as children's toys more than a hundred years ago. At the end of the 1990s, the Swiss **Wim Ouboter** in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich developed a light folding aluminium scooter with small wheels. He wanted to cover short distances faster. His company **Micro** made the scooter popular again all over the world.

An **e-scooter** has an electric motor and a rechargeable battery, so you no longer have to push off. In Switzerland it counts as a light moped and may go no faster than **20 km/h**. From 14 to 16 you need a category M driving licence for it; from 16 you no longer do. In many towns you can hire e-scooters using an app.

On an ordinary scooter you count as a pedestrian and may ride on the pavement, but you must be considerate towards others. E-scooters, on the other hand, belong on the **cycle lane** or the road. A **helmet** and lights at dusk make you safer. Only one person should ever stand on a scooter.

With **stunt scooters**, teenagers do jumps and tricks in skateparks. These scooters are built especially sturdily and cannot be folded. There are even competitions in which the best riders show off somersaults and spins. For children the scooter is also a popular way to get to school.

begriffe.erklaerung: The board you stand on when riding a scooter.
A scooter with an electric motor and a rechargeable battery.
A battery that can be charged again.
An especially sturdy scooter for tricks in a skatepark.

gewusst: Wim Ouboter invented his scooter because the way to his favourite sausage stand was too far to walk and too short to drive.
The word “trottinette” comes from the French “trottiner”, which means something like to trot along with little steps.

teile.einleitung: A web form is an area on a website into which you can enter data and send it off. You come across forms when logging in, shopping online or searching. They are built with special elements of the page language HTML.
wichtigste: A web form collects input from the visitors to a website.
It begins with the HTML element <form>.
The element <input> creates a one-line input field.
For longer text over several lines you use <textarea>.
The input type password hides the characters you type with dots.
With the type radio you can choose exactly one of several options.
The attribute required makes sure that a field has to be filled in.

abschnitte.text: A **web form** is like a paper form, only on the screen. It consists of input fields, drop-down lists, boxes and a button for sending. When you click send, the data is sent to a **server** and processed there. Examples are the login to a learning platform, a contact form or the search box of a search engine.

abschnitte.titel: How it is built in HTML
abschnitte.text: In **HTML** a form begins with the element <form> and ends with </form>. In between are the building blocks. The element <input> creates a one-line input field, and <textarea> a large field for longer texts. <select> creates a drop-down list, and a <button> sends the form.

With the <input> element, the attribute type decides what kind of field is created. The type **password** shows only dots instead of letters so that nobody can read along. The type **radio** creates round buttons, of which you can only choose exactly one. With checkbox you can tick several boxes, and types such as email or date help with particular kinds of input.

The element **<label>** connects a label text to an input field. If you click on the label, the cursor jumps straight into the matching field. This also helps people who browse with a screen reader. The attribute **required** means that a field must be filled in, otherwise the form cannot be sent.

Forms should only be sent over an encrypted connection with https. Only enter personal details on websites that you trust. Fraudsters sometimes build fake forms to steal passwords; this is called **phishing**. In Switzerland, the Data Protection Act regulates what companies may do with the data that is entered.

begriffe.erklaerung: The language with which websites are built.
A building block of a website, written in angle brackets.
An extra detail in an element, for example type or required.
A computer on the internet that receives and processes data.
Fraud using fake pages to get hold of passwords.

gewusst: The dots in the password field only protect against people looking over your shoulder, not against attackers on the network.
Many browsers can fill in forms automatically with saved names and addresses.
The little picture puzzle at the end of some forms is called a CAPTCHA and is meant to keep computer programs out.

teile.einleitung: An ambulance brings ill and injured people to hospital quickly and safely. It is like a small mobile emergency room in which help can be given on the way. In Switzerland you call it on the emergency number 144.
wichtigste: In Switzerland you dial the emergency number 144 for an ambulance.
Specially trained paramedics work in the ambulance.
With blue lights and a siren it may drive faster in an emergency and demand right of way.
The word on the front is often written back to front so that it can be read correctly in a rear-view mirror.
On board there is a stretcher, oxygen, a defibrillator and many medicines.
Other cars must make way for an ambulance with blue lights.
In serious emergencies in the mountains, Rega helps with its helicopter.

abschnitte.text: An ambulance is a specially equipped vehicle for the **emergency medical service**. It goes to accidents, to people with sudden pain or breathing difficulties and to many other emergencies. In Switzerland the vehicles are usually yellow, white or orange and covered with highly visible stripes. Many carry the Star of Life symbol, a blue star with a staff and a snake.

In a medical emergency in Switzerland you dial **144**. At the emergency call centre a specialist asks: where is the emergency, what has happened and how many people are affected. You should stay calm, speak clearly and only hang up when the call centre tells you to. The specialist often also explains on the phone how you can help until the ambulance arrives. Other important numbers are 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 1414 for Rega.

In the back of the ambulance the patient lies on a **stretcher** that can be rolled out. There is oxygen, dressings, splints for broken bones and many medicines. A **defibrillator** can use an electric shock to get a heart beating in the right rhythm again. Monitors check the pulse, blood pressure and oxygen in the blood. In this way treatment begins even before the hospital is reached.

Usually two people are on duty, often a qualified paramedic and an ambulance technician. In Switzerland, training to become a paramedic takes three years at a college of higher education. In very serious emergencies an **emergency doctor** joins them as well. The teams work around the clock, including at night and on public holidays.

abschnitte.titel: Blue lights and right of way
abschnitte.text: In an emergency the ambulance switches on its **blue lights** and the two-tone horn, which goes “nee-naw”. Other vehicles must then not get in its way and must make room. So that drivers in front can read it correctly, the word on the front (in German-speaking Switzerland “Ambulanz”) is often written in **mirror writing**. In a traffic jam on the motorway, cars form an emergency corridor so that the ambulance can get through. Pedestrians and cyclists should also pay attention and wait.

More than 200 years ago, the French military doctor Dominique-Jean Larrey had wounded soldiers treated quickly using light horse-drawn carts. These carts were called flying ambulances. Later there were motor ambulances, which at first were used mainly for transport. Today an ambulance is a real **emergency room** on wheels.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organisation that brings help quickly in emergencies.
A device that can use an electric shock to get a faltering heart back into rhythm.
A clear lane in a traffic jam that cars form for rescue vehicles.
Writing that is back to front and looks correct in a mirror.

gewusst: The word ambulance comes from the Latin word ambulare, which means to walk or to move about.
Children can call 144 too; the call is free and even works without credit on the mobile phone.
Switzerland has a separate number for poisoning: 145, run by Tox Info Suisse.

teile.einleitung: Two-factor authentication, 2FA for short, is a method in which you log in with two different kinds of proof. As well as your password, you need for example a code from an app on your mobile phone. Even if someone steals your password, they still cannot get into your account.
wichtigste: With 2FA you log in with two different kinds of proof.
The factors come from the areas of knowledge, possession and biometrics.
A password belongs to knowledge, a fingerprint to biometrics.
A password plus a code from an app on your mobile phone is a real two-factor combination.
Codes from an authenticator app are usually valid for about 30 seconds.
Recovery codes help if you lose your mobile phone.
A code you did not ask for suggests that someone knows your password.

abschnitte.text: With **two-factor authentication** you have to show two different kinds of proof to prove who you are. It is like a bank card: you need the card and the PIN code. A thief with only one of the two parts gets nowhere. The abbreviation 2FA stands for exactly this method.

There are three categories: something you **know**, something you **have** and something you **are**. A password or a PIN belongs to knowledge. A mobile phone or a security key belongs to possession. A fingerprint or your face belongs to biometrics, something you are. Two passwords together are not real 2FA, because both come from the same category.

After the password, the service asks for a second proof. Often this is a six-digit code from an **authenticator app**, which changes about every 30 seconds. Other services send a code by text message or a confirmation request to your phone. Small **security keys** for the USB port, which you plug in or hold against your phone, are especially secure.

If you receive a code by text message even though you did not want to log in, someone probably knows your password. Never pass the code on, and change your password straight away. When you set up 2FA you get **recovery codes**, which you should keep somewhere safe, ideally on paper. With them you can get into your account if you lose your phone.

In Switzerland, banks require a second confirmation for e-banking, often via an app. E-mail services, social networks, gaming platforms and government logins also offer 2FA. Experts recommend switching it on wherever possible, especially for your e-mail account. Anyone who takes over your e-mail account can often reset the passwords of many other accounts too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Proof that you really are the person you claim to be.
A kind of proof, such as knowledge, possession or biometrics.
An app that keeps creating new short codes for logging in.
A small device that serves as the second factor when logging in.
An emergency code for getting into your account without your phone.

gewusst: The codes from an authenticator app even work without the internet, because the phone and the service work them out from the time and a shared secret.
Fraudsters sometimes phone people pretending to be from support, just to get hold of the 2FA code.
Cash machines have used two factors for decades: the card and the PIN.

teile.einleitung: Radio, also called broadcasting, transmits sounds such as music, news and radio plays using invisible radio waves. With a receiver you can listen to these programmes almost anywhere: at home, in the car or on the move. Radio was the first medium to reach people across a whole country live and at the same time.
wichtigste: Radio stations send sounds to the receiver using invisible radio waves.
From 1895, Guglielmo Marconi made radio transmission famous.
There have been regular radio broadcasts since the 1920s.
SRG is Switzerland's public broadcaster, with SRF, RTS, RSI and RTR.
Since the end of 2024, SRG programmes have been received via DAB+ instead of FM.
Households in Switzerland pay the media fee for it.
Radio can inform people, but it can also be misused for propaganda.

abschnitte.titel: How does the sound get into the radio?
abschnitte.text: In the studio, a microphone turns the sound into electrical signals. A transmitter sends these signals out as **radio waves** through an aerial. The waves travel at the speed of light and even pass through walls. The radio set picks them up with its aerial and turns them back into sound through a loudspeaker.

From 1895, the Italian **Guglielmo Marconi** transmitted signals without cables and became famous for it. In the 1920s, regular radio broadcasts began in many countries. In Switzerland, one of the first stations started in Lausanne in 1922, and in 1931 the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation **SRG** was founded. In Germany, the Nazi regime promoted the cheap “people's receiver” so that as many people as possible would hear its propaganda.

SRG is Switzerland's public broadcaster: **SRF** in German-speaking Switzerland, RTS in French-speaking Switzerland, RSI in Ticino and RTR for Romansh. Since the end of 2024, its programmes have no longer been broadcast on FM but digitally via **DAB+** and the internet. This is paid for mainly by the media fee, which all households pay, whether or not they have a set. In 2018 voters rejected the No Billag initiative to abolish the fees, with about 72 per cent voting no.

On the radio you can hear music, news, interviews, sports commentary and radio plays. The **weather forecast** and travel news about traffic jams are also part of it. Many programmes can now be listened to later as a podcast. In an emergency, the authorities also warn the population over the radio.

Media such as radio, television and newspapers are sometimes called the **fourth estate**, because they keep a check on those in power. In Switzerland, Article 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees media freedom and forbids censorship. But not every news story is true, especially on social media. When you see a surprising report, check the source and see whether reliable media report the same thing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible electromagnetic waves that carry signals through the air.
Digital radio with better sound and more stations.
The ultra-short-wave band, the usual way of receiving radio in the past.
Deliberate, one-sided influencing of the opinions of many people.

gewusst: In the Second World War many people in Germany secretly listened to the Swiss national station Beromünster to get reliable news.
Radio waves can travel round the Earth more than seven times in one second.
The first Swiss radio play was broadcast as early as the 1920s.

teile.einleitung: The RSA cryptosystem is a method for encrypting and digitally signing that works with two different keys. Anyone may know one key, but the other is kept secret. It is named after Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, who presented it in 1977.
wichtigste: RSA is an asymmetric method with a public and a private key.
Its security is based on the fact that very large numbers are hard to split into prime factors.
RSA is named after Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, who presented it in 1977.
Clifford Cocks had already developed a similar method at the British intelligence agency GCHQ in 1973.
65537 is very often used as the public exponent.
The private exponent is calculated with the extended Euclidean algorithm.
In practice, RSA is used with padding such as OAEP.
For large amounts of data, the much faster AES is used, and RSA only encrypts the key.

abschnitte.text: With RSA, every person has a **key pair**. The **public key** is like an open padlock that you hand out to everyone. Anyone can use it to lock a message. But only the person who has the matching **private key** can open it. Because the keys are different, this is called **asymmetric encryption**.

You choose two large prime numbers p and q and multiply them to get n. Then you calculate φ(n), which is (p minus 1) times (q minus 1). You choose a public exponent e and use the **extended Euclidean algorithm** to calculate the private exponent d. To encrypt, you calculate m to the power of e and take the remainder when dividing by n. To decrypt, you do the same with d.

With p equal to 3 and q equal to 11, n is 33 and φ(n) is 2 times 10, that is 20. As the public exponent we take e equal to 3. The message m equal to 4 is encrypted like this: 4 to the power of 3 is 64, and 64 divided by 33 leaves the remainder 31. The private exponent here is d equal to 7, because 3 times 7 is 21 and leaves the remainder 1 when divided by 20. If you calculate 31 to the power of 7 and take the remainder when dividing by 33, you get 4 again.

Calculating n is easy, but finding the two prime numbers from n is extremely hard with very large numbers. This task is called **factorisation**. Today numbers with hundreds of decimal digits are used. In 2020 researchers managed to split the 250-digit number **RSA-250**, but it needed enormous computing power. Future powerful **quantum computers** could endanger RSA, which is why research into new methods is going on.

In 1977 **Ron Rivest**, **Adi Shamir** and **Leonard Adleman** presented the method at MIT in the USA. Only in 1997 did it become known that the British mathematician **Clifford Cocks** had had a similar idea back in 1973 at the intelligence agency GCHQ. Until then his work had been kept secret. The three inventors received the Turing Award in 2002. RSA is still one of the best-known methods in cryptography today.

RSA is found in many secure internet connections, which you can recognise by the padlock in the browser. It is often used for **digital signatures**, with which you check whether a website is genuine. Because RSA is much slower than AES, large amounts of data are encrypted with AES, and only the AES key is protected with RSA. So that identical messages do not look the same, **padding** such as OAEP is used. The number 65537 is very common as the public exponent.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
A key that anyone may know and with which you encrypt.
A secret key with which you decrypt.
Splitting a number into its prime factors.
Extra random data that is added before encrypting.

gewusst: The number 65537 is 2 to the power of 16 plus 1 and is itself a prime number.
In examples about cryptography, the sender and the recipient are traditionally called Alice and Bob.
There are T-shirts with the RSA algorithm printed on them in a few lines of program code.

teile.einleitung: A social network on the internet is a platform on which you have a profile and connect with other people. You share photos, videos and texts, follow friends or stars and comment on posts. Well-known examples are Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat or Facebook.
wichtigste: In a social network you have a profile and connect with others.
Mark Zuckerberg founded Facebook in 2004 with fellow students.
According to their terms of use, many large networks only allow your own account from the age of 13.
If a profile is private, only accepted contacts can see the posts.
A hashtag is a keyword with a # sign in front of it.
Free social networks earn their money mainly from advertising.
Your home address does not belong in a public profile.

abschnitte.text: A **social network** is a website or app on which people create their own **profile** and connect with others. You can publish posts, write messages and react to other people's content, for example with a like or a comment. New posts from your contacts appear in the **feed**, a constantly updated list. Many networks centre on particular content, for example short videos, photos or professional contacts.

The first networks appeared as early as the 1990s. The big breakthrough came with **Facebook**, which Mark Zuckerberg founded in 2004 with fellow students at Harvard University in the USA. It was followed by Twitter, which is now called X, Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok, among others. With the smartphone, social networks became a fixed part of the everyday lives of billions of people.

Most networks are free for users, but they earn a lot of money from **advertising**. For this they collect data about what someone looks at, likes and searches for. This lets them show advertising that matches people's interests exactly. An **algorithm** also decides which posts appear in the feed and is built so that you stay as long as possible.

Many large networks only allow your own account from the age of 13. It is worth setting your profile to **private** so that only accepted contacts can see your posts. Your home address, phone number or the name of your school do not belong in a public profile. Once something is online, it can hardly be deleted completely, because others can take screenshots. If you are treated nastily or harassed, you should block and report the account and turn to someone you trust.

A **hashtag** is a keyword with a # sign in front of it, for example #Switzerland. If you click on it, you see all the public posts on the same topic. The idea was invented on Twitter in 2007. In Switzerland, too, municipalities, clubs, museums and the media use social networks to spread information. But not everything there is true, so you should always check news critically.

begriffe.erklaerung: Your own page in a network with your name, picture and posts.
The constantly updated list of new posts.
A keyword with a # sign that links posts on a topic.
A set of calculation rules; here it decides which posts you get to see.
Switches with which you decide who may see what.

gewusst: In Switzerland the # sign is often called “Gartenhag” (garden fence) or “Raute”.
Facebook was at first only meant for students at certain universities.
Billions of people worldwide use at least one social network.

teile.einleitung: Swiss, whose full name is Swiss International Air Lines, is the largest airline in Switzerland. Its aeroplanes have a red Swiss cross on the tail and fly from Zurich and Geneva to many countries around the world. Swiss was founded in 2002 after the end of the famous Swissair.
wichtigste: There is a Swiss cross on the tail of Swiss aeroplanes.
Swiss was founded in 2002 after Swissair had to ground its planes in 2001.
The most important airport for Swiss is Zurich Airport.
Since 2007, Swiss has belonged to the German Lufthansa Group.
Swiss is a member of the Star Alliance, a group of airlines.
Swiss flies to destinations in Europe, America, Africa and Asia.

abschnitte.text: Swiss is Switzerland's **national airline**. Every year it carries many millions of passengers and also cargo. Its registered office is in Basel, and its most important **hub** is Zurich Airport. From there, large long-haul aircraft fly to places such as New York, Tokyo or Johannesburg.

Swissair, founded in 1931, was the well-known Swiss airline for about 70 years. In October 2001 it ran out of money and all its aircraft had to stay on the ground; this event is called the **grounding**. For many people in Switzerland it was a shock. The regional airline **Crossair** then became the new Swiss in 2002.

In 2005 the German airline **Lufthansa** bought Swiss, and since 2007 it has belonged entirely to the Lufthansa Group. However, Swiss still flies under its own name with the Swiss cross. It is a member of the **Star Alliance**, so travellers can easily change to flights of other partner airlines. The holiday airline Edelweiss also belongs to the same group.

Swiss flies Airbus and Boeing aircraft. For short routes it uses, among others, the **Airbus A220**, which it was one of the first airlines in the world to use. Large aircraft such as the Boeing 777 fly the long routes. The aircraft are looked after by pilots, cabin crew and engineers.

On flights, passengers often get a small piece of **Swiss chocolate**. Announcements are usually made in German, French and English. The red tail with the white cross is a well-known symbol at airports all over the world. Many aircraft are named after Swiss cantons or places.

begriffe.erklaerung: When an airline has to keep all its aircraft on the ground.
A large airport where many of an airline's flights start and passengers change planes.
A group of many airlines that work closely together.
All the aircraft of an airline together.

gewusst: Swiss was one of the first airlines in the world to use the Airbus A220, which was then still called the Bombardier CSeries.
With Swissair, Switzerland lost a company in 2001 that was seen as the country's flying calling card.

teile.einleitung: Scratch is a programming language with which children and young people learn to program in a playful way. Instead of typing commands, you put colourful blocks together like puzzle pieces. This is how games, animations and stories are made.
wichtigste: Scratch was developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
Programs are built by putting blocks together.
The objects you program are called sprites.
The area on which the sprites move is called the stage.
The centre of the stage has the coordinates x: 0 and y: 0.
The stage goes from x = -240 to x = 240.
The Scratch mascot is an orange cat.

abschnitte.text: **Scratch** is a free, visual programming language for beginners. It was developed by the Lifelong Kindergarten group at the Media Lab of **MIT** in the USA under the leadership of Mitchel Resnick. The first version appeared in 2007, and since 2019 Scratch 3.0 has run directly in the web browser. Millions of children around the world use Scratch, including in many Swiss schools.

In Scratch you drag coloured **blocks** with the mouse into the program area and snap them together. Each colour stands for a group, for example motion, looks, sound or control. Because only matching blocks fit together, there are hardly any typing mistakes. This lets you concentrate fully on the idea of the program.

The objects you program are called **sprites**; the best known is the Scratch cat. Each sprite can have several **costumes**, and quickly changing the costumes gives an animation. The sprites move on the **stage**, which can have a backdrop. You can draw your own sprites, add photos or record sounds.

The stage is 480 points wide and 360 points high. The x values go from -240 on the left to 240 on the right, the y values from -180 at the bottom to 180 at the top. The centre has the coordinates x: 0, y: 0. If a sprite is at x = 0, faces right and moves 10 steps three times, it is then at x = 30.

On the Scratch website you can publish your own projects and look at other people's projects and develop them further. This idea is called **remixing**. For younger children from about five years old there is the app ScratchJr, which appeared in 2014. Scratch is available in many languages, including German.

begriffe.erklaerung: A colourful building block that represents a command.
An object in Scratch that you can program.
The area on which the sprites move.
One appearance of a sprite; several costumes make animations.
Numbers that give a place on a surface exactly.

gewusst: The name Scratch comes from the “scratching” of DJs, who mix pieces of music and put them together in new ways.
Many millions of projects have already been shared on the Scratch website.

teile.einleitung: The von Neumann architecture is the basic blueprint on which almost all of today's computers are built. Its most important feature is that the program and the data are kept in the same memory. It is named after the mathematician John von Neumann, who described it in 1945.
wichtigste: John von Neumann described the architecture in 1945 in the “First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC”.
The central feature is that the program and the data are kept in the same memory.
The arithmetic logic unit, also called the ALU, carries out arithmetic and logical operations.
The program counter contains the address of the next instruction.
Each instruction is fetched, decoded and executed.
Because instructions and data travel over the same bus, the von Neumann bottleneck arises.
In the Harvard architecture, the memories for instructions and data are separate.

abschnitte.text: **John von Neumann** was born in Budapest in 1903 and died in the USA in 1957. He was one of the most versatile mathematicians of the 20th century. In 1945 he wrote the report **First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC** about a planned computer. In it he described how a computer with a stored program should be built, although other researchers also contributed to the ideas.

A von Neumann computer consists of a few parts. The **arithmetic logic unit** or ALU calculates and compares. The **control unit** reads the instructions and makes sure that everything happens in the right order. Then there are the memory, input and output, and a **bus** through which all the parts exchange data.

The processor works in a cycle that is always the same. First it fetches the next instruction from memory; its address is in the **program counter**. Then it decodes the instruction, that is, it works out what has to be done. Finally it executes it, and the program counter moves on to the next instruction.

Because instructions and data travel over the same bus, they have to queue up. The processor can often calculate faster than the memory can deliver data. This bottleneck is called the **von Neumann bottleneck**. Today's processors ease it with fast caches, which internally often work separately for instructions and data, as in the **Harvard architecture**.

From 1950 the **Z4** computer of the German inventor Konrad Zuse was in operation at ETH Zurich. At that time it was one of the first computers working at a university in Europe. However, the Z4 read its program from a punched tape and did not store it in memory as with von Neumann. Later ETH built its own computer, the ERMETH.

begriffe.erklaerung: The calculating centre of a computer, also called the CPU.
The arithmetic logic unit, which calculates and makes logical comparisons.
A storage place in the processor with the address of the next instruction.
A data line through which the parts of a computer are connected.
A computer design with separate memories for instructions and data.

gewusst: Because programs are stored in memory, a computer can load, change and swap them like data, which is why you can simply install apps today.
The Z4 is now on display in the Deutsches Museum in Munich.
Smartphones and games consoles also still basically follow the blueprint of 1945.

teile.einleitung: Unsupervised learning is a kind of machine learning in which a computer finds patterns and groups in data by itself. Unlike in supervised learning, nobody tells it what the correct answer is. The computer is like a child who sorts a pile of Lego bricks by colour or shape of its own accord.
wichtigste: In unsupervised learning, the data has no given target values, the labels.
An important aim is clustering, that is, forming groups of similar data.
The k-means method divides data into a chosen number of clusters.
DBSCAN recognises groups of any shape and marks isolated points as noise.
Principal component analysis reduces the number of dimensions of the data.
Banks use anomaly detection to find unusual credit card payments.
Association analysis finds rules such as “people who buy crisps often also buy drinks”.

abschnitte.text: In **supervised learning**, the computer is given examples with the correct answer, such as pictures labelled cat or dog. In **unsupervised learning**, these descriptions, called **labels**, are missing. The computer has to find out by itself which data belongs together. This is useful because labels are often expensive and laborious to obtain.

Forming groups is called **clustering**. In the k-means method, you decide beforehand how many groups there should be, and the computer keeps moving the centres of the groups until they fit well. With the elbow method you look for the bend in a curve after which more clusters hardly reduce the spread any more. In hierarchical clustering, a **dendrogram** shows as a tree which groups are merged one after another. DBSCAN, on the other hand, looks for densely packed areas and can recognise groups of any shape.

Many datasets have a great many features, which are called dimensions. **Principal component analysis** finds the directions in which the data is spread out most. In this way you can turn hundreds of features into a few important ones without losing much information. An **autoencoder** is a neural network that squeezes its input through a narrow middle layer and then rebuilds it.

Online shops divide their customers into groups with similar shopping behaviour. **Association analysis** discovers in shopping data which products are often bought together. Banks use **anomaly detection** to notice unusual credit card payments that could point to fraud. Photo programs also automatically sort pictures of similar faces into groups.

Because there is no correct answer, it is hard to say whether a result is good. The computer sometimes finds groups that make no sense to people. That is why experts always have to check and interpret the results. Unsupervised learning is often combined with other methods.

begriffe.erklaerung: The given correct answer for an example.
A group of data points that are similar to each other.
A feature of the data, for example size or weight.
Something unusual that does not fit the usual pattern.
A tree diagram that shows how groups are joined together.

gewusst: A large part of the data in the world has no labels, which is why unsupervised learning is so important.
Large language models first learn from huge amounts of text without labels by predicting the next word.
The k in k-means simply stands for the number of groups being looked for.

teile.einleitung: A direction arrow is a sign that points in a particular direction: up, down, left or right. We come across arrows on signposts, on the keyboard and in games. In programming, arrows are used to describe routes and movements precisely.
wichtigste: The arrow ↑ points up and ↓ points down.
The arrow ← points left and → points right.
The opposite direction of ↑ is ↓.
For 3 squares to the right you need 3 arrows →, one for each square.
With ↑ ↑ → you go 2 squares up and 1 to the right.
With → → ← you end up 1 square to the right of the start.
With ↑ → ↓ ← you are back at the start at the end.

abschnitte.text: An **arrow** consists of a line with a point at one end. The point shows which direction to go. The four most important directions are up ↑, down ↓, left ← and right →. The sign is reminiscent of an arrow that you shoot with a bow.

With arrows you can describe a **route** on a game board or squared paper precisely. Each arrow stands for a step of one square. So the arrows ↑ ↑ → mean two squares up and one to the right. A sequence of arrows like this is already a small program.

abschnitte.titel: Opposite direction and the way back
abschnitte.text: Every arrow has an **opposite direction**: ↑ and ↓ as well as ← and → cancel each other out. With → → ← you go two squares to the right and one back, so you are one square to the right of the start. With ↑ → ↓ ← you go round a square once and are back at the starting point. You find the way back by turning all the arrows round and going in reverse order.

On a computer keyboard there are four **arrow keys**, which you use to move around in texts, tables and games. On roads, signposts and road markings with arrows show where you may drive. At the station, arrows lead to the platforms and exits. At emergency exits, too, green signs with arrows show the escape route.

Educational robots such as the Bee-Bot have arrow buttons with which children enter a sequence of commands. Then the robot follows exactly this route. Programming languages such as Scratch have similar commands for movements. If you plan routes with arrows, you practise **order** and precise thinking.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign with a point that shows a direction.
The way in which something moves or points.
The exactly opposite way.
A key on the keyboard with a direction arrow.

gewusst: In the computer character set Unicode there are hundreds of different arrow symbols.
Arrows are understood all over the world, even without a shared language.

teile.einleitung: A robot is a machine that carries out tasks by itself and is controlled by a computer. Robots weld cars together, vacuum floors, operate alongside doctors and even drive across Mars. The word comes from Czech and originally means work.
wichtigste: A robot is a machine that carries out tasks by itself.
It is controlled by a computer and a program.
With sensors and cameras it senses its surroundings.
The word robot comes from the Czech word “robota” for work.
Especially many robot arms work in car factories.
At home, the robot vacuum cleaner cleans the floor.
Robot vehicles called rovers drive around on Mars.

abschnitte.text: A **robot** is a machine that is controlled by a computer and carries out tasks by itself. What it should do is written in a **program** that people have written. With **sensors** it measures things such as distance, light or touch, and with a camera it can see. Motors move its wheels, legs or gripping arms.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the word come from?
abschnitte.text: The word robot comes from Czech. The writer **Karel Čapek** used it in 1920 in his play “R.U.R.” for artificial workers. It comes from the word “robota”, which means work or forced labour. The science fiction author **Isaac Asimov** later wrote the famous three laws of robotics, according to which a robot must not harm people.

The first industrial robot, called Unimate, worked in a car factory in the USA from 1961. Today **robot arms** weld, paint and assemble in car factories almost without a break. They are strong and precise and never get tired. In warehouses, moving robots bring parcels to the staff.

Many families have a **robot vacuum cleaner** that moves through the flat by itself and cleans the floor. Robot lawnmowers are also common in Swiss gardens. In hospitals, surgical robots help surgeons with very delicate operations. At ETH Zurich, walking robots have been developed that, for example, inspect industrial plants.

Robots are especially useful where people cannot go. On Mars, robot vehicles called **rovers** drive around, for example Curiosity since 2012 and Perseverance since 2021. They photograph the landscape, examine rocks and look for traces of past life. Space probes are also basically robots that work by themselves far out in space.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that measures something from the surroundings, such as light or distance.
A list of commands that tells a computer what to do.
A robot vehicle that drives around on another celestial body.
A robot arm that works in factories.

gewusst: The word robot is said to have actually been suggested by Karel Čapek's brother Josef.
The Mars rover Perseverance brought along a small helicopter called Ingenuity, the first aircraft to fly on another planet.
In some factories more robots work than people.

teile.einleitung: A voice assistant is a computer program you can talk to as if it were a person. It understands spoken questions and instructions and answers with an artificial voice. Well-known voice assistants are Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant.
wichtigste: You give a voice assistant instructions by talking to it.
It listens with a microphone and answers through a loudspeaker.
Usually you first have to say a wake word.
It can, for example, set an alarm or play music.
Speaking clearly helps it to understand you well.
It gets many answers from the internet.
A voice assistant can make mistakes and give wrong answers.

abschnitte.text: A **voice assistant** is software that understands spoken language and reacts to it. It is found in smartphones, computers, cars and **smart speakers**. Apple brought Siri to the iPhone in 2011, and Amazon presented Alexa with the Echo speaker in 2014. Google followed in 2016 with Google Assistant.

The device constantly listens with a **microphone** for a **wake word** such as “Hey Siri” or “Alexa”. Only then does it record the question and usually send it over the internet to the manufacturer's servers. There, speech recognition turns the words into text, and a program looks for a suitable answer. This is then given out as an artificial voice through the **loudspeaker**.

A voice assistant can set an alarm, tell you the weather or play music. It answers general knowledge questions, does sums or translates words. It can also be used to control lights and other devices in the **smart home**. For people who cannot see well, it is a great help in everyday life.

So that the assistant understands you, you should speak **clearly** and not too fast. Many assistants understand standard German better than Swiss German, because there are so many different dialects. A voice assistant can mishear or give a wrong answer. That is why important information should be checked in another way too.

Because the device listens, recordings often end up on the manufacturer's servers. In the settings you can usually look at these recordings and delete them. Before you let a voice assistant buy something, you always ask your **parents**. Many devices also have a button with which you can switch the microphone off completely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that understands and answers spoken commands.
A word that makes the assistant start listening.
Technology that turns spoken words into text.
A home in which devices are connected and can be controlled.

gewusst: Siri, Alexa and the like can also tell jokes if you ask them to.
Modern voice assistants use artificial intelligence to understand better and better.

teile.einleitung: Tim Berners-Lee is an English computer scientist who invented the World Wide Web. He developed it around 1990 at the CERN research centre near Geneva in Switzerland. Because he did not ask for any money for it, the whole world can use the web free of charge today.
wichtigste: Tim Berners-Lee comes from England and was born in London in 1955.
He invented the World Wide Web at CERN in Switzerland.
The abbreviation www stands for World Wide Web.
In 1990 he programmed the very first web browser, called WorldWideWeb.
The first website went online in 1991.
He asked for nothing at all for the use of the web.
The British Queen gave him the honorary title Sir.
His first web server had a note stuck on it warning people not to switch it off.

abschnitte.text: Timothy Berners-Lee was born on 8 June 1955 in **London**. His parents were both mathematicians and worked on one of the first computers. He studied physics at the University of Oxford and built his own computer while he was still a student. Later he worked as a software developer, among other places at **CERN**, the large research centre for particle physics near Geneva.

Thousands of researchers from all over the world worked at CERN, and it was difficult to share information. In 1989 Berners-Lee suggested connecting documents on different computers with **hyperlinks**. You would simply be able to click on a word and jump to another document. His boss found the proposal vague but exciting and let him work on it. He was supported by the Belgian computer scientist Robert Cailliau.

In 1990 Berners-Lee programmed the first **web browser** on a NeXT computer and called it WorldWideWeb. For it he invented the page description language **HTML**, the transfer protocol HTTP and web addresses, which are called URLs. The computer was also the first web server, and a note on it warned people not to switch it off. In 1991 the first website went online; it explained what the World Wide Web is.

Berners-Lee and CERN decided not to patent the web and not to charge any fees. In 1993 CERN officially released the technology for everyone. Only because of this could the web spread so quickly around the whole world. In 1994 Berners-Lee founded the **World Wide Web Consortium**, W3C for short, which still sets the standards of the web today.

For his invention, the British Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004, and since then he has been allowed to call himself **Sir**. In 2016 he received the Turing Award, which is considered a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science. At the opening of the 2012 Olympic Games in London he appeared and sent out the message “This is for everyone”. Today he campaigns for people to have more control over their own data online.

begriffe.erklaerung: A network of linked pages on the internet, www for short.
A clickable reference that leads to another page.
A program with which you look at websites.
A language used to describe the structure of web pages.
The European research centre for particle physics near Geneva.

gewusst: The internet existed before; Berners-Lee invented the web, which is built on the internet.
The world's first website can still be seen today at its old address at CERN.
The first web server is now shown at CERN as an exhibit.

teile.einleitung: The Shift key is a key on the keyboard with which you type capital letters and many special characters. In German it is called “Umschalttaste”, and there is usually an arrow pointing upwards on it. It is one of the most frequently used keys of all.
wichtigste: With the Shift key you type capital letters.
In German it is called “Umschalttaste”; its symbol is often an arrow pointing upwards.
A normal keyboard has two Shift keys, on the left and on the right.
You hold it down and type the letter at the same time.
On the Swiss keyboard, Shift with the key 1 gives a plus and with the key 7 a slash.
Caps Lock types in capitals all the time until you press it again.
The Shift key originally comes from the typewriter.

abschnitte.text: The **Shift key** switches the keyboard to a second level for a moment. If you hold it down and type A, you get a capital A instead of a small a. With number and symbol keys, the upper character printed on the key appears. When you let go of the Shift key, you type normally again.

The Swiss keyboard has its own **keyboard layout**, which suits German and French. Shift and 1 gives a plus, Shift and 7 a slash, Shift and 0 an equals sign. A special feature is that the keys ü, ö and ä give the French letters è, é and à with the Shift key. That is why you type a capital Ü with Caps Lock.

The **Caps Lock** key is usually directly above the left Shift key. If you press it once, the keyboard types all letters as capitals until you press it again. Often a small light comes on. If you have switched on Caps Lock by mistake, you sometimes wonder why your password is not working.

The name comes from the mechanical **typewriter**. There, each type bar carried two letters one above the other, a small one and a capital one. With the Shift key, part of the machine was moved so that the other letter hit the paper. The English name shift means exactly that: to move.

The Shift key is often combined with other keys; this is called a **keyboard shortcut**. If you hold it down and click with the mouse, you can select several files or a section of text at once. With Shift and the arrow keys you select text character by character. In many games it makes the character run or creep.

begriffe.erklaerung: The English name of the key; it means to move.
A key that switches to capital letters permanently.
The arrangement of which character is on which key.
A combination of keys that carries out a command quickly.

gewusst: On the Swiss keyboard there is no key for the German sharp s (Eszett), because in Switzerland ss is always written.
If you press the Shift key five times quickly in Windows, a question appears about Sticky Keys, a function for people who can only press one key at a time.
On a smartphone, the Shift key is usually an arrow to the left of the Y or Z.

teile.einleitung: Wind energy is energy obtained from the power of the wind using large wind turbines. The wind turns the rotor blades, and a generator turns this into electricity. Because new wind keeps forming, wind energy is one of the renewable energies.
wichtigste: The wind turns the rotor blades of a wind turbine.
A generator in the nacelle turns the rotation into electricity.
Wind energy is renewable because new wind keeps forming.
According to Betz's law, a wind turbine can use at most about 59 per cent of the wind's energy.
Switzerland's largest wind farm is on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura.
In Switzerland, wind energy so far supplies only a small share of the electricity.
Countries such as Denmark and Germany obtain a great deal of electricity from wind.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the wind come from?
abschnitte.text: Wind forms because the Sun warms the Earth unevenly. Warm air rises and cooler air flows in to replace it, creating **differences in air pressure**. Because the Sun keeps shining, new wind keeps forming. That is why wind energy is a **renewable energy**. Unlike crude oil or natural gas, the wind never runs out.

A modern **wind turbine** consists of a tall tower, a nacelle and usually three long rotor blades. The wind turns the **rotor blades**, much as it turns a toy windmill. In the nacelle there is a **generator**, which turns the rotation into electricity. Large turbines are often more than 150 metres tall, and one rotor blade can be longer than a football pitch is wide. The nacelle turns into the wind automatically.

A wind turbine cannot take all the energy out of the wind, otherwise the air behind it would stand still. Around 1919, the German physicist Albert Betz calculated that at most about 59 per cent can be used. This is called **Betz's law**. In addition, the wind does not always blow with the same strength, so electricity production varies. In a storm, the turbines are switched off to protect them.

Switzerland's largest wind farm is on **Mont Crosin** in the Bernese Jura; the first turbines were built there in 1996. Another well-known wind farm has stood on the **Gotthard Pass** since 2020. Altogether only a few dozen large wind turbines turn in Switzerland so far. They currently supply less than one per cent of Switzerland's electricity. What makes them valuable is that they produce a lot of electricity in winter, when solar installations supply little.

Most of the world's wind turbines are in China, the USA and Germany. In Denmark, more than half the electricity comes from wind power. Many turbines stand at sea in **offshore wind farms**, where the wind blows more strongly and evenly. Critics complain that wind turbines change the landscape, make noise and can be dangerous for birds or bats. That is why every site is checked carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning part of the wind turbine with the rotor blades.
The housing at the top of the tower that holds the generator.
A group of several wind turbines in one place.
English for “off the coast”, that is, at sea.

gewusst: Centuries ago, windmills in Holland were already grinding grain and pumping water away.
The tips of large rotor blades can move at more than 300 kilometres per hour.
Sailing ships have also used wind energy for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: Inheritance is a basic principle of object-oriented programming. A new class takes on the properties and methods of an existing class and can add to them or change them. This means you do not have to write the same code several times.
wichtigste: With inheritance, a subclass takes on the properties and methods of a superclass.
Inheritance expresses an is-a relationship, for example: a dog is an animal.
In Java a class inherits with the keyword extends.
Every Java class inherits directly or indirectly from the class Object.
A subclass can override inherited methods.
C++ allows multiple inheritance, which can lead to the diamond problem.
The Liskov substitution principle is named after Barbara Liskov.

abschnitte.text: In object-oriented programming, a **class** describes a blueprint for objects. With **inheritance**, a subclass takes on everything from a superclass and adds something new. A class Animal, for example, has a name and a method eat. The subclass Dog inherits both and is also given the method bark.

In Java you write class Dog extends Animal; the keyword **extends** means that it extends the other class. With super you call the constructor of the superclass. Every class inherits directly or indirectly from the class Object. If a class is marked with final, nobody may inherit from it.

A subclass can rewrite an inherited method with the same signature; this is called **overriding**. A method makeSound then outputs “Miaow” for the cat and “Woof” for the dog. A program can treat all animals in the same way, and yet each animal does the right thing. This ability is called polymorphism.

Some languages such as C++ and Python allow a class to inherit from several superclasses. If a class inherits from the same base class by two routes, the **diamond problem** arises, because it is unclear which version applies. That is why Java only allows one superclass, but a class can implement several interfaces. Many experts advise using inheritance sparingly and putting objects together instead.

Inheritance was introduced in the 1960s with the Norwegian language **Simula**. In 1987 the computer scientist Barbara Liskov formulated an important rule: an object of a subclass must be usable wherever an object of the superclass is expected. This rule is called the **Liskov substitution principle**. Liskov received the Turing Award in 2008.

begriffe.erklaerung: A blueprint that sets out which properties and methods objects have.
The class from which another class inherits.
The class that inherits and can add something new.
Reprogramming an inherited method in the subclass.

gewusst: The term “diamond problem” comes from the fact that the inheritance relationships look like a diamond shape in a drawing.
Simula, the first language with inheritance, was actually meant for simulations.
In Java a class can only have one single direct superclass.

teile.einleitung: A tram is an electric railway that runs on rails right through the streets of a town. In Germany it is called “Strassenbahn”; in Switzerland simply “Tram”. Trams carry lots of people through the city quietly and without exhaust fumes.
wichtigste: A tram gets its electricity from an overhead line.
Trams run on rails that are usually set into the road.
Zurich has the largest tram network in Switzerland.
Basel, Bern and Geneva also have tram networks.
The first trams were pulled by horses.
In 1881 the world's first electric tram ran in Berlin.
Basel trams run as far as Germany and France.

abschnitte.text: Above the tracks hangs an **overhead line**, a wire carrying electric current. On the roof of the tram, a **current collector**, also called a bow or pantograph, presses against this wire. The current drives electric motors that turn the wheels. The current flows back through the rails.

The first trams were pulled by **horses**; in Switzerland from 1862 in Geneva. In 1881 the world's first electric tram ran in Berlin-Lichterfelde, built by the company of **Werner von Siemens**. Around 1900 many Swiss towns got electric trams. Later, some towns replaced their trams with buses, but today many towns are building new tram lines again.

**Zurich** has the largest tram network in Switzerland, with many blue trams. Basel has green trams whose lines reach as far as Weil am Rhein in Germany and Saint-Louis in France. Bern and Geneva also have tram networks. New lines include, for example, the Glattalbahn near Zurich and the **Limmattalbahn**, which opened as far as Killwangen in 2022.

A long tram can carry more than 200 people at once. It runs quietly and produces no **exhaust fumes** in the city. Because it runs on its own tracks, it gets stuck in traffic less often than a car. Modern **low-floor trams** have no steps, so people in wheelchairs or with pushchairs can get on easily.

A tram has a much longer **braking distance** than a car and cannot swerve. That is why in Switzerland it usually has right of way. When crossing tram tracks, you should always look carefully both ways. Cyclists should cross the rails as close to a right angle as possible so that the wheel does not get stuck in the groove.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wire carrying electric current above the tracks.
A bow on the roof that takes the current from the overhead line.
A tram with a low floor and no steps at the entrance.
The distance a vehicle needs before it comes to a stop.

gewusst: If a bus leaves every 12 minutes and a tram every 18 minutes, and both start at 8.00, they leave at the same time again at 8.36.
Zurich's Cobra tram was developed and built in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Zurich Airport is the largest airport in Switzerland and lies mainly in the municipality of Kloten. Every year hundreds of thousands of aircraft take off and land here, carrying millions of passengers. It is Switzerland's most important gateway to the world.
wichtigste: Zurich Airport is the largest airport in Switzerland.
It lies mainly in the municipality of Kloten, about 10 kilometres north of the city of Zurich.
The airport opened in 1948.
In 2024 more than 30 million passengers used it.
It has three runways for take-offs and landings.
The airport is the hub of the airline Swiss.
Beneath the airport there is a railway station with trains to many parts of the country.

abschnitte.text: **Zurich Airport** lies in the Glatt valley, about ten kilometres north of the city of Zurich. Most of it belongs to the municipality of **Kloten**, while parts are in neighbouring municipalities such as Opfikon and Rümlang. That is why it is often also called Kloten Airport. By train or tram you can get there from Zurich main station in a few minutes.

In the past, aircraft for Zurich landed at the military airfield in **Dübendorf**. Because it became too small, the new airport in Kloten was opened in 1948. In the decades that followed it was expanded several times, with new runways, terminals and docks. The underground station opened in 1980, and in 2020 the large service centre **The Circle** was added.

The airport has three **runways**; the longest is almost four kilometres long. Aircraft park at docks A, B and E, and an underground train, the **Skymetro**, takes passengers to dock E. So that people living nearby can sleep, there is a **night-time curfew**, usually with no flights between 11.30 pm and 6 am. The exact rules are set out in the airport's operating regulations.

In 2024 more than 30 million people travelled through Zurich Airport, about as many as before the coronavirus pandemic. It is the home airport of the airline **Swiss**, which flies from here to many countries. Altogether, dozens of airlines offer connections to well over a hundred destinations. Many travellers only change planes in Zurich.

The airport is one of the largest places of work in the canton of Zurich, with tens of thousands of people working there. It is run by **Flughafen Zürich AG**, in which the canton of Zurich also has a stake. As well as passengers, a lot of freight is handled there, such as medicines, watches and machines. The second largest airport in Switzerland is Geneva.

From the **observation deck** you can watch aircraft take off and land up close. On bus tours around the airport grounds you can get very close to the big jets. Around the runways there are also nature reserves where rare birds and plants live. At the edge of the airport, many plane spotters watch the aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long paved strip on which aircraft take off and land.
An airport where many travellers change planes.
A building in which passengers check in and wait for their flight.
A period at night when no aircraft should take off or land.

gewusst: Zurich Airport even has its own railway station beneath the terminal.
The Skymetro to dock E runs underneath a runway.
Rare birds such as the skylark live in protected wet meadows on the airport grounds.

teile.einleitung: ScratchJr is a free app with which even young children can make their first programs. Instead of typing commands, you put colourful picture blocks together. This is how you make your own stories and games with characters that move, talk and jump.
wichtigste: ScratchJr is meant above all for children aged 5 to 7.
The app is free.
You put the blocks together from left to right.
A program is often started with the green flag.
When you start a new project, there is already a cat there.
The blue motion blocks move the character.
ScratchJr first appeared in 2014 for the iPad.

abschnitte.text: **ScratchJr** is a programming app for younger children. It is a simplified form of the well-known programming language **Scratch**, which is intended for older children. ScratchJr is meant above all for children aged 5 to 7. You don't need to be able to read yet, because all the commands are shown as pictures. The app is free and contains no advertising.

Programs are made from **programming blocks** that fit together like puzzle pieces. You put them together **from left to right**, just as you read. Each block colour stands for a kind of command. The blue blocks are **motion blocks**; they make the character walk, jump or turn. Yellow blocks are start blocks, purple ones change the appearance, and there are also blocks for sounds.

When you start a new project, there is already a **cat** on the stage. You can choose more characters and backgrounds from a collection or paint them yourself. You can even add your own photos, such as your own face. A program is often started with the **green flag**. With other start blocks, a character reacts, for example, when you tap it.

With ScratchJr you can tell **stories** in which characters talk to each other. You can also build small **games** or animations. A project can have several pages, like a picture book. In doing so, children learn to plan sequences and to find mistakes. These skills are the basis for programming later on.

abschnitte.titel: How it came about and school
abschnitte.text: ScratchJr was developed by researchers at the **MIT Media Lab** in the USA, at Tufts University and at the company Playful Invention. The app first appeared in 2014 for the **iPad**, and later also for Android tablets and other devices. It is used in many nursery schools and schools all over the world. In Switzerland it fits well with the Lehrplan 21 curriculum, which includes computer science from the first years of school. Many teachers use ScratchJr together with educational robots such as the Bee-Bot.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program for a tablet or smartphone.
A picture building block that represents a command.
A picture on the stage that you control with commands, also called a sprite.
ScratchJr's big sister for older children.

gewusst: The abbreviation “Jr” stands for the English “junior”.
With Scratch, ScratchJr's big sister, many millions of projects have already been made and shared online.
In ScratchJr you can even give the cat your own voice by recording a sound.

teile.einleitung: The internet is a huge network that connects computers, mobile phones and other devices all over the world. Through the internet we send messages, watch videos, look for information and play together. It has changed our lives as much as printing once did.
wichtigste: The internet connects computers all over the world.
It grew out of ARPANET, which went into operation in the USA in 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN near Geneva.
Swiss websites often end in “.ch”, which stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.
You never share personal data such as your address and phone number with strangers.
You may only put photos of other people on the internet with their permission.
If something on the internet frightens you, tell an adult you trust.

abschnitte.text: The internet is a network of many millions of computers and networks connected by cables, radio and satellites. So that all devices understand each other, they use shared rules called **protocols**. Data are split into small packets, sent off and put back together at their destination. Every device on the network has its own number, the **IP address**.

The internet grew out of **ARPANET**, a research network in the USA that connected the first computers in 1969. In the 1980s it grew into a worldwide network of universities. From 1989, Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web with its linked web pages at CERN near Geneva. After that, from the 1990s, the internet also became popular in homes.

The country ending **.ch** stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name of Switzerland. Geneva is home to the International Telecommunication Union ITU, which sets worldwide rules for telecommunications and the internet. Some cantons are also trying out **e-voting**, that is, casting your vote electronically over the internet. Comparison websites also help you compare the prices of different suppliers before buying something.

Never share your address, phone number or passwords with strangers. You may only put photos of other people on the internet if they agree. If you see something that frightens you, tell an adult you trust. Before buying online, check the seller and the reviews so that you do not fall for a **scam**.

The internet makes knowledge available to a great many people, much as printing once did. In some countries, however, there is **censorship**, which means the state controls or bans what may appear on the internet. In Switzerland, freedom of opinion and of the media is protected by the Federal Constitution. Even so, the same applies on the internet: insulting others and telling lies about them is forbidden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed rule for how computers exchange data with each other.
A number by which every device on the internet is recognised.
When the state controls or bans what may be published.
Voting in a ballot or election over the internet.

gewusst: Under the oceans lie hundreds of thick undersea cables that carry almost all data traffic between the continents.
The internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing, because the Web is only one service on the internet, like e-mail.
Today about two thirds of all people in the world use the internet (as of 2024).

teile.einleitung: In a sound recording, sounds, music or voices are stored so that you can listen to them again later. Today this is very easy with a mobile phone, a tablet or a computer with a microphone. In the past you needed big machines with cylinders, records or tapes for it.
wichtigste: You record sounds and voices with a microphone.
The recording is played back through headphones or a loudspeaker.
A recording works best in a quiet room.
Outdoors, the wind in particular can badly disturb the recording.
The jagged line on the screen shows how loud the sound is.
MP3 is a well-known format for sound files.
Voice messages and podcasts are sound recordings from everyday life.

abschnitte.text: Sound consists of vibrations of the air, the **sound waves**. In the **microphone**, the sound makes a thin membrane vibrate, and this produces an electrical signal. The computer measures this signal thousands of times a second and stores it as numbers. When it is played back, the **loudspeaker** turns the numbers back into vibrations that we can hear.

When recording, a jagged line appears on the screen, the **waveform**. High peaks mean loud parts, and flat parts are quiet or silent. This lets you see quickly where someone is speaking and where there are pauses. In programs such as Audacity you can cut up this line, delete parts and put pieces together.

It is best to record in a quiet room; carpets and curtains soak up the echo. Don't speak too far from the microphone, so that the voice sounds clear, but not too close either, otherwise sounds like P and B pop. Outdoors it is above all the wind that disturbs, which is why professional microphones have a furry **windshield**. Before the real recording, a short test recording is always worthwhile.

In 1877 Thomas Edison presented the **phonograph**, which scratched sounds onto a cylinder. Later came records, tapes and cassettes. From the 1980s the CD with digital sound became established. Today sounds are almost only stored digitally as files, for example in the MP3 format.

A short recording that you send in a chat is called a **voice message**. A **podcast** is a programme to listen to on the internet that you can play at any time. Audiobooks, radio programmes and music are also sound recordings. If you want to record other people, you should always ask their permission first.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that turns sound into an electrical signal.
A jagged line that shows how loud a sound is at each moment.
A programme to listen to on the internet.
A file format that stores sound recordings in a space-saving way.

gewusst: The first recording with Edison's phonograph is said to have been a nursery rhyme.
A music CD measures the sound 44,100 times per second.
For films, many sounds such as footsteps or creaking doors are recorded afterwards in the studio.

teile.einleitung: A smartphone is a mobile phone that is also a small computer. You usually operate it with your finger on a touchscreen and can use it to make calls, take photos, surf the internet and use apps. Since the first iPhone in 2007, the smartphone has changed the everyday lives of billions of people.
wichtigste: A smartphone is a mobile phone with the abilities of a computer.
You usually operate it with your finger on the touchscreen.
The iPhone brought the big breakthrough for smartphones in 2007.
Most smartphones run on Android or iOS.
Sensors detect, for example, whether the device is held upright or sideways.
With the Swiss app TWINT you can pay without cash using your smartphone.
A hundred years ago there were no smartphones.

abschnitte.text: A **smartphone** combines a telephone, camera, music player, satnav and computer in one device. It is operated via a **touchscreen**, which recognises touches of the finger. Extra programs, the **apps**, are downloaded from an app store. With them the smartphone becomes an alarm clock, dictionary, games device or timetable.

The first mobile phones with computer functions already existed in the 1990s, but they had keys or a stylus. The big breakthrough came in 2007 with Apple's **iPhone**, which was operated only with your fingers. A year later the first smartphones with Google's **Android** operating system came onto the market. Today almost all young people in Switzerland have their own smartphone.

Inside, a small but very powerful processor does the work. An **accelerometer** detects whether the device is held upright or sideways and turns the picture to match. Other sensors measure light, nearness and direction, and a satellite receiver works out the location. A rechargeable battery supplies the power and has to be charged regularly.

**TWINT** is a Swiss app that lets you pay without cash using your smartphone. You use it in shops, in online shops or to send money to friends. The app has been widespread in its present form since 2017 and is used by millions of people in Switzerland. To pay, you need a bank account, so with children a parent usually helps.

Smartphones need rare **raw materials**, which are often mined under difficult conditions. That is why it is worth using a device for a long time and handing in old phones so that the raw materials can be recycled. Too much screen time can disturb your sleep and distract you from other things. That is why many families agree on phone rules together, for example no smartphone in the bedroom.

begriffe.erklaerung: A screen that reacts to touch.
A program that you load onto the smartphone.
The basic software that controls the device, such as Android or iOS.
A battery that can be charged again.

gewusst: A smartphone today is much more powerful than the computers that controlled the Moon landing in 1969.
The German word “Handy” for a mobile phone only looks English, because in English people say “mobile phone” or “cell phone”.
A smartphone contains dozens of different chemical elements, including gold.

teile.einleitung: A syntax error is a breach of the writing rules of a programming language. Like a sentence with wrong grammar, the computer cannot understand such a command. Syntax errors are among the most common mistakes in programming and luckily are usually easy to find.
wichtigste: A syntax error is a breach of the writing rules of the programming language.
In Python, the colon is missing at the end of “if x > 3”.
If there is a syntax error in line 10 of a Python program, the program does not start at all.
With wrong indentation, Python reports an IndentationError.
Python distinguishes between capital and small letters, which is why Print with a capital P does not work.
In “5 = x” the variable is in the wrong place; it must be to the left of the equals sign.
A program that calculates wrongly without any error message has a logic error.

abschnitte.text: Every programming language has fixed writing rules, which are called **syntax**. They lay down where brackets, colons or quotation marks have to go. For a language like English you would say grammar. If you break these rules, a **syntax error** occurs, and the computer reports, for example, SyntaxError.

In the programming language **Python**, a line such as if x > 3 needs a **colon** at the end. Python also requires correct **indentation**, otherwise an IndentationError appears. Python also distinguishes between capital and small letters, which is why Print with a capital P does not work, only print. 5 = x is wrong too, because the variable that is given a value must be to the left of the equals sign.

A syntax error is discovered before the program even runs. If it is in line 10, the program does not start at all, and lines 1 to 9 are not carried out either. The program that translates the code is called a **compiler** or **interpreter**. It usually shows which line the problem is in, but sometimes the actual mistake is one line further up.

Not every error is a syntax error. If you write print(Hello) without quotation marks and there is no variable called Hello, Python reports a **NameError**, which only occurs when the program runs. Even trickier is a **logic error**: the program runs without any message but calculates something wrong, such as a wrong average. Only someone who checks and tests the result carefully finds such mistakes.

Error messages are not a punishment but clues. You should read them calmly and look at the line given and the line before it. Many programming environments colour the code and mark syntax errors while you are still typing. It also helps to test again and again after small changes instead of writing a lot of code at once. Finding mistakes is called **debugging**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The writing rules of a programming language.
A program that translates and runs code line by line.
Space at the beginning of a line which in Python shows what belongs together.
An error in which the program runs but calculates wrongly.
Finding and fixing mistakes in a program.

gewusst: The programming language Python is named after the British comedy group Monty Python, not after the snake.
In 1947 technicians found a moth in a computer and stuck it into their logbook as the first actual bug.
Even experienced professionals make syntax errors every day, for example forgotten brackets.

teile.einleitung: A tractor is a powerful vehicle used mainly in farming. It pulls ploughs, trailers and many other machines across fields and meadows. In Switzerland people say “Traktor”; in Germany it is often called “Schlepper” or “Trecker”.
wichtigste: A tractor is used mainly in farming.
Tractors have large rear wheels with deep tread so that they do not spin on soft ground.
Many different machines can be attached to a tractor.
Using the power take-off, the tractor can also drive machines.
In Switzerland you may drive a tractor from the age of 14 with a category G licence.
The first tractors were powered by steam.

abschnitte.text: A tractor is a **towing vehicle**, a vehicle built mainly to pull and push. It is not fast, but it is very strong. The large rear wheels with deep **tread** grip the ground well. Many tractors today have four-wheel drive.

At the back and front, a tractor has **hydraulics** that can raise and lower machines such as a plough, harrow or mower. Using the **power take-off**, a turning shaft at the back, the tractor drives, for example, a hay baler or a loader wagon. With a front loader it can lift soil or manure like a small digger. In this way one tractor replaces many working animals and people.

In the past, horses and oxen pulled the plough. In the 19th century there were the first heavy **steam tractors**. Around 1890 the first tractors with petrol engines appeared in the USA. In Switzerland, the company **Hürlimann** in Wil SG built tractors from 1929; Bührer and Vevey were also well-known makers.

There are many tractors on Swiss farms because even steep meadows are farmed. For very steep ground there are special vehicles with a low centre of gravity, called **transporters**, and two-axle mowers. Young people may drive farm vehicles up to 30 km/h from the age of **14** with a category G licence. To get it, they attend a course and take a test.

Today's tractors have comfortable cabs with screens and air conditioning. With the help of **GPS**, they can drive exactly straight across a field almost by themselves. Large tractors have several hundred horsepower. Tractors powered by electricity or biogas are also being developed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A turning shaft on a tractor that drives attached machines.
A technology that lifts heavy things using oil under pressure.
A tool that breaks up the soil and turns it over.
A driving licence for farm vehicles from the age of 14.

gewusst: Some large tractor tyres are taller than an adult.
In tractor pulling competitions, modified tractors pull heavy sledges as far as they can.

teile.einleitung: Mirror writing is writing that looks like normal writing seen in a mirror. It runs from right to left, and the letters are back to front. If you hold a mirror next to it, you can read it very easily.
wichtigste: You can read mirror writing easily with a mirror.
Mirror writing runs from right to left.
