Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes in mirror writing.
On the front of some ambulances there is a word in mirror writing so that it can be read in the rear-view mirror.
The word OTTO looks exactly the same in mirror writing.
The capital letter A looks exactly the same when mirrored.
A small b turns into a d when mirrored.

abschnitte.text: In **mirror writing**, every letter is written back to front, and the line runs from right to left. It looks exactly like normal writing seen in a mirror. That is why you can read it effortlessly with a **mirror**. Without a mirror you need some practice, because the brain first has to turn the letters round.

Some capital letters look exactly the same when mirrored, for example A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y. They have **mirror symmetry**, which means their left and right halves are the same. That is why the word OTTO looks unchanged in mirror writing. Other letters change: a small b becomes a **d**, and a p becomes a q.

The Italian artist and inventor **Leonardo da Vinci** lived from 1452 to 1519. He filled thousands of pages with notes and drawings about flying machines, the human body and water. He wrote many of these notes in mirror writing. Leonardo was **left-handed**, and this way his hand did not smudge the fresh ink. We do not know for sure whether he also wanted to hide secrets in this way.

On the bonnet of some **ambulances** there is a word such as AMBULANCE in mirror writing. When the vehicle is behind a car, the driver reads the word the right way round in the rear-view mirror. With **stamps** and in printing with movable type, the characters are also mirrored so that the print comes out the right way round.

When learning to write, many children write some letters or numbers back to front; this is completely normal and usually goes away by itself. If you want to practise mirror writing, you can write a word on tracing paper and turn the sheet over. Another idea: write with both hands at the same time, and the left hand often makes mirror writing quite by itself. This is how you can make funny **secret messages** for friends.

begriffe.erklaerung: Back-to-front writing that runs from right to left.
Exactly the same on the left and right, like a butterfly.
Describes a person who writes mainly with their left hand.
Individual metal letters used for printing.

gewusst: Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks are now among the most valuable manuscripts in the world.
The number 8 and the number 0 also look the same when mirrored.
On a stamp, the letters have to be back to front so that you can read the print.

teile.einleitung: In programming, a variable is a named storage place for a value. You can imagine it as a labelled box into which you put a number or a word. Without variables a program could not remember anything, no score and no name.
wichtigste: A variable is a named storage place for a value.
The value of a variable can change while the program is running.
In Python, the instruction x = x + 1 increases the value of x by 1.
Text such as “Hello” has the data type string.
A list can store several values in an order.
To swap two variables, in most languages you need a helper variable.
Variables should be given names that are easy to understand.

abschnitte.text: A **variable** has a name and a value. If you write points = 5 in Python, a variable called points is created with the value 5. This process is called **assignment**. Later the program can read the value, output it or change it.

In Scratch there are blocks such as “set points to 5” and “change points by -2”. If you set points to 5, change it by -2 and then by 4, points has the value 7 at the end. In Python you write x = x + 1 to increase x by one. So here the equals sign does not mean “is equal to” as in maths, but “gets the value”.

With a = 3, then b = a + 2 and after that a = 10, b has the value 5 at the end. This is because b was calculated when a was still 3 and only remembers the result. If you want to swap the values of x and y, you usually need a **helper variable**, otherwise one value is lost. It is like swapping two full glasses, for which you need a third empty glass.

Every value has a **data type**. Whole numbers such as 7 are called integers, decimal numbers such as 3.5 are called floats. Text such as “Hello” is a **string**. With name = 'Lea' and print('Hello ' + name), Python outputs Hello Lea. A **list** stores several values in an order, for example the names of all the children in a class.

In most languages, a variable name must not contain spaces or begin with a digit. Good names say what is stored, for example number_of_lives instead of just a. This way others, and you yourself, understand the program much better later on. There are also variables in maths, such as the x in an equation.

begriffe.erklaerung: Storing a value in a variable.
The kind of value, for example number or text.
A data type for text.
A variable that stores several values in order.
An extra variable that briefly stores a value in between.

gewusst: In Python you can, as an exception, swap two variables without a helper variable, with x, y = y, x.
In many languages capital and small letters matter, so points and Points are then two different variables.
The word variable comes from the Latin variabilis and means changeable.

teile.einleitung: A string, called Zeichenkette in German, is a sequence of characters in computer science, such as letters, digits, spaces and punctuation marks. Every name, word and sentence in a program is a string. In Python you write strings in quotation marks.
wichtigste: A string is a sequence of characters.
In Python a string is written in quotation marks.
The characters are numbered; the first has the index 0.
With + you join strings together: "3" + "4" gives 34.
With * you repeat them: "Ha" * 3 gives HaHaHa.
Methods such as upper, replace and count change or examine strings.
In a computer every character is stored as a number, for example following the Unicode standard.

abschnitte.text: A **string** is a sequence of characters, for example "Bern" or "Hello world!". In Python you put it in single or double **quotation marks**. That way the computer knows it is text and not a command or a number. So "3" + "4" gives 34 and not 7.

Every character has a number, the **index**, and counting starts at 0. So "Bern"[0] gives B. With a range you can take out a piece: "Schoggi"[1:4] gives cho, that is the characters with index 1, 2 and 3. Such a piece is called a substring.

Python offers many **methods** for strings. "Basel".upper() turns everything into capital letters and gives BASEL. "Luzern".replace("z", "Z") replaces characters and gives LuZern. "Bananen".count("a") counts how often a appears, namely 2 times, and "Wal" in "Walensee" gives True.

With the plus sign you join strings together; this is called **concatenation**. "Ha" * 3 repeats the text three times and gives HaHaHa. If you want to combine a number with text, you first have to turn it into a string with str(). In Python you cannot change a string directly; methods such as replace always create a new one.

In a computer every character is a number. The code **ASCII** from the 1960s only had 128 characters, with no umlauts among them. Today **Unicode** is used, which covers over a hundred thousand characters from almost all the world's writing systems, including emojis. This allows programs to display German, French, Italian and Romansh just as well as Chinese or Arabic.

begriffe.erklaerung: The German word for string.
The number of a character, counted from 0.
Joining strings together with +.
A worldwide standard that gives every character a number.

gewusst: The sentence "Hello, World!" has been the best known first program for people learning to code for decades.
To a computer, every emoji is also a string of one or more Unicode characters.
An empty string "" contains not a single character and is still a valid string.

teile.einleitung: A comparison operator is a symbol with which a program compares two values. The result is always either true or false. With comparisons a program can make decisions, for example whether a game has been won.
wichtigste: Comparison operators compare two values and give true or false.
In Python you check for equality with == and for inequality with !=.
In Python the result of a comparison has the data type bool.
print(7 >= 7) outputs True, print(3 > 5) outputs False.
With text, capital and small letters count, so 'Apple' == 'apple' is false.
A number and a text are never equal, so '5' == 5 is false.
Python allows chained comparisons such as 10 < x < 15.

abschnitte.text: A **comparison operator** works like a pair of scales that weighs two things against each other. The best known are less than (<), greater than (>), less than or equal to (<=) and greater than or equal to (>=). Then there are equal to (==) and not equal to (!=). In Python the result is called True for true or False for false.

In Python, a single equals sign means an **assignment**, so x = 5 stores the 5 in x. For a comparison you therefore need two equals signs, x == 5. If you mix up the two, you often get an error message or a wrong result. This is one of the most common beginner's mistakes in programming.

Comparisons are usually found in a **condition**, for example if points >= 100: print('You win!'). Only if the comparison is true is the command carried out. Loops also often run as long as a comparison is true. With and, or and not you can combine several comparisons.

print(7 >= 7) outputs True, because 7 equals 7. print(3 > 5) outputs False. If x = 12, then print(10 < x < 15) outputs True, because 12 lies between 10 and 15. Such a **chained comparison** is a special feature of Python that many other languages do not have.

You can compare texts too. Python pays close attention to capital and small letters, so 'Apple' == 'apple' is false. The string '5' and the number 5 have different **data types**, so '5' == 5 also gives False. Texts are also compared with < and > according to the order of their character codes, similar to the alphabet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A symbol that carries out a calculation or a comparison.
A value that can only be true or false, in Python bool.
A check that decides whether a part of the program is carried out.
Storing a value in a variable.

gewusst: The data type bool is named after the English mathematician George Boole, who studied the logic of true and false in the 19th century.
In Python, when calculating, True equals 1 and False equals 0, so True + True gives the value 2.
In Scratch, comparisons are hexagonal green blocks.

teile.einleitung: A nuclear power station is a power station that produces electricity from the energy of atomic nuclei. Heavy atomic nuclei, usually of uranium, are split. Nuclear power stations supply a lot of electricity but are also controversial.
wichtigste: Nuclear power stations produce electricity by splitting heavy atomic nuclei.
The fuel is usually uranium.
Nuclear fission releases heat, which turns water into steam and drives turbines.
Switzerland's first commercial nuclear power station, Beznau, went into operation in 1969.
The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down for good in 2019.
Today Beznau 1 and 2, Gösgen and Leibstadt are still running in Switzerland.
The Chernobyl reactor accident in 1986 showed how dangerous an accident can be.

abschnitte.text: In the **reactor**, heavy atomic nuclei, usually of **uranium**, are hit with neutrons and split. This **nuclear fission** produces large amounts of heat and more neutrons. These split new nuclei in turn, creating a controlled **chain reaction**. The heat turns water into steam, which turns a turbine. Finally, a generator turns this into electric current.

Switzerland's first commercial nuclear power station was **Beznau** in the canton of Aargau; it went into operation in 1969. Later came **Gösgen** in the canton of Solothurn and **Leibstadt** in Aargau; Leibstadt is the largest. The **Mühleberg** nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down for good at the end of 2019 and is now being dismantled. Together, Switzerland's nuclear power stations supply about a third of the country's own electricity. Their safety is supervised by the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate ENSI.

In a serious accident, **radioactivity** can escape and harm people and nature. In 1986 a reactor exploded at **Chernobyl** in what is now Ukraine; the surrounding area is still closed off today. In 2011 an earthquake and a tsunami damaged the Fukushima nuclear power station in Japan. In Switzerland too, in 1969, there was an accident in the small experimental reactor in a rock cavern near **Lucens** in the canton of Vaud. That is why very strict safety rules apply to nuclear power stations.

abschnitte.titel: What to do with the waste?
abschnitte.text: Spent fuel rods remain dangerously radioactive for a very long time, in some cases for hundreds of thousands of years. They are first kept in interim stores, for example the **Würenlingen interim store**. In the long term they are to be sealed deep in the rock in a **deep geological repository**. In 2022 the organisation responsible, Nagra, proposed the Nördlich Lägern area for this. It will be many years before such a repository is built.

Nuclear power stations supply a lot of electricity day and night and give off hardly any **carbon dioxide** while doing so. On the other hand, there is the risk of serious accidents and the unsolved problem of radioactive waste. In 2017 Swiss voters approved the **Energy Strategy 2050**, which bans the building of new nuclear power stations. The existing plants may keep running as long as they are safe. Whether new nuclear power stations should be allowed again is being debated in politics once more.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, which releases a lot of energy.
A heavy, slightly radioactive metal used as fuel in nuclear power stations.
A process in which each splitting sets off further splittings.
Invisible radiation from decaying atomic nuclei that can harm living things.
A tall tower in which water is cooled, recognisable by its white cloud of steam.

gewusst: The white cloud above the cooling tower of a nuclear power station is harmless water vapour.
A single small uranium fuel pellet supplies about as much energy as roughly a tonne of hard coal.
At 144 metres, the cooling tower at Leibstadt is one of the tallest structures in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The World Wide Web, www or the Web for short, is a system of billions of web pages connected to each other by links. It was invented by the British computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee from 1989 at CERN near Geneva. The Web is not the same as the internet; it is one of its most important services.
wichtigste: The abbreviation “www” stands for World Wide Web.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the Web in 1989 at CERN near Geneva.
Web pages are connected to each other by links, also called hyperlinks.
On 30 April 1993, CERN released the Web for everyone to use freely.
You look at web pages with a program called a browser.
The Web is a service on the internet, like e-mail.
Today there are more than a billion websites worldwide.

abschnitte.text: The **World Wide Web** consists of web pages containing texts, pictures and videos. If you click on a **link**, you jump to another page, no matter which computer in the world it is stored on. With a **browser** such as Firefox, Chrome or Safari you can look at these pages. Every page has its own address, the URL, for example with www at the beginning.

**CERN** is a large research centre for particle physics near Geneva on the border with France. Thousands of researchers from many countries worked there and wanted to share their information. So in March 1989 the Briton **Tim Berners-Lee** proposed a system of linked documents. In 1990 he built the first web server and the first browser on a NeXT computer.

Berners-Lee invented three important building blocks: **HTML** is the language in which web pages are written. HTTP is the rule for how browsers and servers exchange pages. The URL is the address where a page can be found. These building blocks are still used today, in further developed form, on every website.

On 30 April 1993, CERN released the technology of the Web for **free use**. Nobody had to pay fees for it, and everyone was allowed to build their own web pages. This was an important reason why the Web spread so quickly all over the world. From the mid-1990s, more and more companies, newspapers and private individuals went online.

Today billions of people use the Web for learning, shopping, playing and communicating. Online encyclopedias, video platforms and social networks are part of the Web. In 1994 Tim Berners-Lee founded the **W3C**, which still sets shared rules for the Web today. The very first website can still be visited at CERN at its old address.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single page on the World Wide Web that you can look at.
A clickable reference that takes you to another page.
A program for displaying web pages.
The language in which web pages are written.
The address of a web page.

gewusst: Tim Berners-Lee's boss wrote the words “vague but exciting” on the first proposal.
On the first web server there was a note saying that the computer must not be switched off.
The very first photo on the Web showed a band made up of CERN staff members.

teile.einleitung: Social engineering means cleverly deceiving people so that they give away secrets or do something wrong. Attackers do not crack the computer; instead they take advantage of trust, helpfulness, curiosity or fear. If you know the tricks, you are much less likely to fall for them.
wichtigste: In social engineering, people are manipulated.
Phishing with fake emails or websites is the most common form.
Quishing is phishing with a manipulated QR code.
In shoulder surfing, someone looks over your shoulder while you type in your PIN.
In baiting, an attacker leaves behind a prepared USB stick, for example.
In tailgating, someone sneaks through a secured door behind an authorised person.
In CEO fraud, fraudsters pretend to be the boss of a company.
The well-known hacker Kevin Mitnick wrote the book “The Art of Deception” about social engineering.

abschnitte.text: **Social engineering** means something like “social manipulation”. Instead of attacking technology, fraudsters exploit human qualities. These include helpfulness, respect for authority, curiosity and time pressure. It is often easier to ask someone for their password than to crack it. That is why people are considered the most important weak point, but also the most important protection.

In **phishing**, fraudsters send fake emails or text messages that look as if they come from a bank, the post office or a parcel service. A link leads to a fake website where you are supposed to enter passwords or card details. In **quishing**, a manipulated **QR code** leads to such a page, for example a fake code on a parking meter. Typical warning signs are time pressure, threats and spelling mistakes. Real banks never ask for passwords by email.

In **shoulder surfing**, someone secretly watches as you type in a PIN or password. In **tailgating**, an unauthorised person sneaks through a secured door behind an authorised person. In **baiting**, an attacker leaves behind a prepared USB stick in the hope that someone curious will plug it in. Then malicious software gets onto the computer. That is why you should never plug a USB stick you have found into your own computer.

In **pretexting**, the attacker makes up a believable story as a pretext, for example as a supposed technician or police officer. In **CEO fraud**, a fraudster pretends to be the boss of a company and asks for an urgent, secret bank transfer. The so-called grandchild trick played on elderly people is also part of this kind of fraud. The criminals often seem very friendly and well informed. They collect information beforehand, for example from social networks.

The American **Kevin Mitnick** was one of the best-known hackers in the world in the 1980s and 1990s. Many of his break-ins succeeded not through technology but through clever phone calls and lies. After a prison sentence he worked as a security consultant and helped companies protect themselves. In 2002 his book “The Art of Deception” appeared. He died in 2023.

Be suspicious if someone puts pressure on you or asks for something secret. Never give away passwords and codes, not even to supposed employees of a company. Check senders and links carefully, and if in doubt, phone the real organisation yourself. Cover the keypad when you enter a PIN. In Switzerland you can report suspicious emails to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity NCSC.

begriffe.erklaerung: Secretly influencing someone so that they do something they would not otherwise do.
Fraud using fake messages to steal passwords or data.
A square code that you scan with a mobile phone.
A fraud using a made-up story as a pretext.

gewusst: The word phishing is a variation of the English “fishing”, as in fishing for passwords.
In tests in companies, a surprising number of people plug a USB stick they have found into their computer.
Phone calls with a faked telephone number, called spoofing, are also used for social engineering.

teile.einleitung: Encryption means changing a message so that only people who are in on the secret can read it. Anyone who knows the right key can turn the secret text back into normal text. In the past it was mainly rulers and armies who used secret writing; today encryption protects our messages and passwords on the internet every day.
wichtigste: A message before encryption is called plain text.
In the Caesar cipher, each letter is shifted a few places along the alphabet.
With a shift of 3, HELLO becomes the word KHOOR.
With symmetric encryption, you need the same key for encrypting and decrypting.
Asymmetric encryption works with a public and a private key.
The “S” in HTTPS shows that the connection is encrypted.
The German encryption machine Enigma was cracked at Bletchley Park in the Second World War.

abschnitte.text: A readable message is called **plain text**. With a method and a **key**, it is turned into an unreadable **cipher text**. Only someone who knows the key can decrypt the cipher text again. The science of encryption is called cryptography, from Greek words for “hidden” and “writing”.

The Roman general Julius Caesar is said to have encrypted his letters by shifting each letter three places along the alphabet. A becomes D, B becomes E and so on, so HELLO becomes the word KHOOR. To decrypt, you shift back: WUHH becomes TREE again. This **Caesar cipher** is easy to crack, because there are only 25 possible shifts.

In the Second World War the German armed forces encrypted their radio messages with the **Enigma** machine. It looked like a typewriter and changed the encryption with every key press. At **Bletchley Park** in England, thousands of people worked on cracking the code, including the mathematician Alan Turing. Polish mathematicians had done the groundwork, and the success helped the Allies in the war.

With **symmetric encryption**, sender and recipient use the same key, as with a front door. The problem is handing over the key safely. With **asymmetric encryption**, there is a public key that everyone may know and a private one that only the owner has. You can imagine it like a letter box: anyone can post something in it, but only the person with the key can open it.

If a web address begins with **HTTPS**, the connection to the website is encrypted, often recognisable by a little padlock. This is important when logging in or paying on the internet. Messengers such as Signal or the Swiss app Threema use **end-to-end encryption** so that only the sender and the recipient can read the message. Mobile phones, bank cards and Wi-Fi networks are also encrypted.

begriffe.erklaerung: The message before it is encrypted.
The encrypted, unreadable message.
The secret information with which you encrypt or decrypt.
The science of encryption.
An encrypted connection between browser and website.

gewusst: Even the ancient Spartans used a staff, the scytale, to encrypt secret messages.
The Enigma had so many possible settings that you could not simply try them all out.
Modern encryption is so strong that even fast computers could not crack it by guessing in millions of years.

teile.einleitung: A computer is a machine that processes data with the help of programs. It can calculate, write, show pictures, play music and much more. Today computers are found not only in laptops but also in smartphones, cars and washing machines.
wichtigste: A computer processes data according to the commands of a program.
Inside, a computer calculates only with the two digits 0 and 1.
In 1941 Konrad Zuse built the first working programmable computer.
The first computers were as big as a room.
Today there is also a small computer inside a smartphone.
The Swiss Niklaus Wirth developed the programming language Pascal at ETH Zurich.
To keep your computer safe, you should never tell anyone your password.

abschnitte.text: The word computer comes from the English “to compute”, which means to calculate. A computer works on the principle of **input, processing, output**. You enter something, the computer processes it and shows a result. The commands telling it what to do are in a **program**. Without programs, a computer would just be a box of metal and plastic.

Inside, a computer calculates only with the two digits 0 and 1, the so-called **binary system**. You can imagine it like a light switch that is either off or on. A single 0 or 1 is called a **bit**; eight bits together make a byte. With many millions of such switches, a computer can represent numbers, letters, pictures and sounds.

The computer's brain is the **processor**; it carries out the commands. The working memory holds data that are needed right now. Files are stored permanently on the hard disk or an SSD. You type letters with the **keyboard**, and you move the pointer on the screen with the mouse. The well-known Swiss company Logitech, founded in the canton of Vaud, makes such mice and keyboards.

In 1941 the German engineer **Konrad Zuse** built the Z3 in Berlin, the first working programmable computer. The first computers were as big as a room and weighed several tonnes. A later machine by Zuse, the Z4, was used at ETH Zurich from 1950. Thanks to small electronic components, transistors and microchips, computers became smaller and faster. From the 1980s, home computers moved into many living rooms.

The Swiss computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** developed the programming language **Pascal** at ETH Zurich around 1970. Many people all over the world learned to program with it. For his work, Wirth received the Turing Award in 1984, a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science. Not far away, at CERN near Geneva, the World Wide Web was invented in 1989.

In 1997 the computer **Deep Blue** beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match. In March 2016 the program AlphaGo by DeepMind won 4 to 1 against the Go professional Lee Sedol. Programs like these show what **artificial intelligence** can do. Safety is also important, though: you should never tell anyone your password. You should also only install programs from safe sources.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a computer that carries out commands and calculates.
A list of commands that tells the computer what to do.
The smallest unit of information, a 0 or a 1.
A number system that works only with the digits 0 and 1.
A secret word that protects a computer or an account.

gewusst: A smartphone today is much more powerful than the computers used to fly the first people to the Moon in 1969.
The American computer ENIAC from 1946 weighed about 27 tonnes.
The word “bug” for a computer fault became famous when a real moth was found in a computer in 1947.

teile.einleitung: The Grande Dixence is a huge dam in the canton of Valais that holds back the reservoir Lac des Dix. At 285 metres, it is the highest gravity dam in the world. Its water is turned into electricity in power stations for the whole of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Grande Dixence dam is in the canton of Valais.
It is 285 metres high, making it the highest gravity dam in the world.
It was built from 1951 to 1961.
The lake it holds back is called Lac des Dix.
Most of the water comes from glaciers and is brought in through long tunnels.
The plant supplies valuable electricity, especially in winter.
The dam contains about six million cubic metres of concrete.

abschnitte.text: The Grande Dixence lies high up in the **Val des Dix**, a side valley of the Val d'Hérens in the canton of **Valais**. It belongs to the municipality of Hérémence south of Sion. The top of the dam is at about 2365 metres above sea level. Behind it, the reservoir **Lac des Dix** stretches for several kilometres. All around rise high Valais mountains and glaciers.

The Grande Dixence is 285 metres high, more than twice as tall as the Prime Tower in Zurich. It is a **gravity dam**, which holds back the water by its enormous weight alone. At the bottom it is almost 200 metres thick; at the top only about 15 metres. The crest is about 750 metres long. Inside, there are inspection galleries in which experts monitor the dam.

Today's dam was built from 1951 to 1961 and replaced a smaller, older dam. Thousands of workers worked at great height, often in cold and snow. Altogether about six million cubic metres of **concrete** were used. It is often said that this would be enough to build a wall round the Earth. The Grande Dixence is still regarded as a masterpiece of Swiss **civil engineering** today.

The Lac des Dix can store about 400 million cubic metres of water. Most of the water comes from the meltwater of dozens of **glaciers**, including from the area around Zermatt. Pumping stations and about 100 kilometres of **tunnels** carry it to the lake. From there it flows down through penstocks into the Rhône valley to power stations such as Bieudron and Fionnay. Because the water is collected in summer and used in winter, the plant supplies important **winter electricity**.

In summer, buses go up to the foot of the dam. By cable car or on foot you can reach the crest and the lake. On guided tours you can also visit the inside of the dam. Popular hiking trails lead around the Lac des Dix, for example to the Cabane des Dix. The Grande Dixence is one of the best-known sights in Valais.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wall that blocks a valley and holds back water to form a lake.
A dam that holds back the water by its great weight alone.
An artificial lake behind a dam.
An underground passage through which water is channelled.

gewusst: The Grande Dixence is higher than any building in Switzerland.
The Bieudron power station uses a drop of almost 1900 metres; when it opened, that was a world record.
So that the water from Zermatt can reach the Lac des Dix, some of it is pumped up the mountain.

teile.einleitung: Transport Layer Security, TLS for short, is a method that encrypts connections on the internet. It makes sure that nobody can read or change what goes back and forth between your device and a website. You can recognise it by the https in the address and by the little padlock in the browser.
wichtigste: The forerunner of TLS was called SSL and was developed by the company Netscape.
TLS 1.3 was published in 2018 as RFC 8446.
After the handshake, the actual data is encrypted symmetrically with a shared session key.
Perfect forward secrecy prevents a key stolen later from decrypting old sessions.
Heartbleed was a serious security hole in the OpenSSL library in 2014.
Server Name Indication tells the server the desired host name as soon as the connection is set up.
Since 2015 Let's Encrypt has issued free, automatically renewable certificates.
In the network stack, TLS lies between the transport protocol and the application protocol.

abschnitte.text: Without encryption, data travels on the internet like a postcard that anyone along the way can read. **TLS** puts it into a sealed envelope. It protects three things: nobody can read along, nobody can change anything unnoticed, and you know who you are really connected to. If an address begins with **https**, the connection is secured with TLS.

In the mid-1990s the company Netscape, which made a popular browser at the time, developed the **SSL** method. It was developed further and standardised in 1999 as TLS 1.0. Today's version, **TLS 1.3**, was published in 2018 as RFC 8446; it is faster and more secure than its predecessors. Old versions such as SSL are now considered insecure and are rejected by browsers.

At the start of a connection there is the **handshake**, a kind of greeting. The server shows a **certificate**, a digital ID card signed by a trustworthy body. Then both sides use clever mathematics to agree on a secret session key without ever sending it openly. After that, the actual data is encrypted **symmetrically**, that is, with this shared key, which is very fast.

In the network stack, TLS lies between the **transport protocol** TCP and application protocols such as HTTP or the protocols for email. With the extension Server Name Indication, the browser says right at the start which website it wants to reach, because many websites are often on the same server. Modern connections offer **perfect forward secrecy**: there are new keys for each session, so a server key stolen later cannot decrypt old, recorded conversations.

In 2014 the **Heartbleed** hole was discovered in the widely used program library OpenSSL. Attackers could use it to read parts of servers' memory, sometimes including passwords, and millions of servers around the world had to be updated. Certificates used to cost money, which put off many small websites. Since 2015 the non-profit organisation **Let's Encrypt** has issued free, automatically renewable certificates, and since then the vast majority of websites have been encrypted.

begriffe.erklaerung: Changing data so that only authorised people can read it.
A digital ID card that shows who a website belongs to.
A greeting at the beginning in which keys are agreed.
A web address with a secured, encrypted connection.
A secret key that is only valid for one connection.

gewusst: The padlock in the browser only shows that the connection is encrypted, not that the website is honest.
Heartbleed was one of the first security holes to get its own logo, a bleeding heart.
Messengers, email programs and online banking also use TLS.

teile.einleitung: A stack is a data structure that works like a pile of plates. You always put things on top and only take them off from the top again. So whatever went in last comes out first.
wichtigste: A stack works on the LIFO principle: last in, first out.
With push you put an element on top of the stack.
With pop you remove the top element and get it back.
If you put 1, 2 and 3 on an empty stack, pop then gives you the 3.
When functions are called, programs put the return addresses on the call stack.
With a stack you can check, for example, whether brackets are placed correctly.
Friedrich L. Bauer developed the stack principle with Klaus Samelson.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a pile of plates in the cupboard. You put a new plate on top, and when you need one, you take the top one. This is exactly how a **stack** works. This principle is called **LIFO**, which stands for last in, first out. The opposite is a queue, in which whoever comes first is also served first.

A stack has two main operations. With **push** you put an element on top, with **pop** you take the top element off and get it back. If you put 1, 2 and 3 one after another on an empty stack, pop gives first the 3, then the 2 and finally the 1. There is often also peek or top, with which you only look at the top element without removing it.

Every running program uses a special stack, the **call stack**. When one function calls another, a note is put on top saying where the program has to jump back to afterwards. When the inner function is finished, this entry is taken off again. If a function calls itself endlessly, the stack grows until there is no more room; this is called a **stack overflow**.

With a stack you can work out calculations in **reverse Polish notation**, in which the operators come after the numbers. With the expression 3 4 + 2 *, you put 3 and 4 on the stack, and the plus calculates 3 plus 4 equals 7. Then the 2 is added, and the times sign calculates 7 times 2, which gives 14. Some calculators made by the company Hewlett-Packard worked exactly like this. The notation goes back to the Polish logician Jan Łukasiewicz.

In the 1950s the German computer scientists **Friedrich L. Bauer** and Klaus Samelson described the so-called **cellar principle** and had it patented. That is why in German the stack is sometimes also called a “Kellerspeicher”, a cellar store. We often come across it in everyday life, for example with the undo function: the last step is undone first. The back button in the browser also works on this principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particular way of organising data in the computer.
Last in, first out: what came last goes first.
An operation that puts an element on top of the stack.
An operation that takes the top element off.
An error when the stack overflows because it gets too full.

gewusst: One of the best-known question-and-answer sites for programmers is called Stack Overflow.
When checking brackets, you put every opening bracket on the stack and take it off again at the matching closing bracket.
Friedrich L. Bauer also helped coin the term software engineering.

teile.einleitung: The wheel is a round disc that turns around an axle, and it is one of the most important inventions of humankind. It was invented about 5500 years ago and made it much easier to move heavy loads. Without wheels there would be no bicycles, cars or trains, and no clocks with cogwheels either.
wichtigste: A wheel turns around an axle in its centre.
The wheel was invented about 5500 years ago.
The first wheels were made of wood.
Early wheels were heavy discs without spokes.
Later, lighter spoked wheels appeared.
Very old wooden wheels have also been found in lake-dwelling settlements in Switzerland.
Wheels are found not only in vehicles but also in machines and clocks.

abschnitte.text: A **wheel** is a round object that turns around an **axle**. Because the wheel rolls instead of scraping along the ground, you need much less force to move a load. The wheel and axle together are one of the simple machines in physics. Cogwheels, pulleys and flywheels are also based on this idea.

The wheel was invented about 5500 years ago, that is, around 3500 BC. The oldest finds come from Mesopotamia, Eastern Europe and the Alpine region. Potters probably used turning discs early on, the **potter's wheel**. Soon afterwards, people built carts and wagons pulled by cattle.

The first wheels were made of wood and were heavy **disc wheels** made of one or more planks. In lake-dwelling settlements on Lake Zurich and in Slovenia, archaeologists found wooden wheels about 5000 years old. They survived in the damp lake bed because hardly any air could get to them. Finds like these show that the wheel spread quickly across Europe.

Around 2000 BC, lighter **spoked wheels** appeared. With them, fast chariots and travelling carts could be built. Later, wooden wheels were protected with iron tyres, and in the 19th century air-filled rubber tyres were added. These still make bicycles and cars quieter and more comfortable today.

Today we come across wheels everywhere: on bicycles, cars, trains, pushchairs and wheeled suitcases. In machines, **cogwheels** pass on forces, for example in gearboxes or in mechanical Swiss watches. Wind turbines and water wheels use the power of nature. Even a Ferris wheel at the fair is basically a giant wheel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rod around which a wheel turns.
A rod that connects the centre of a wheel to its rim.
A wheel with teeth that can drive other wheels.
Houses on stilts on lake shores from the Stone and Bronze Ages.

gewusst: The peoples of ancient America knew the wheel in toys but did not use it for carts.
A bicycle has spoked wheels, which are very light and yet strong.
One of the oldest wooden wheels in the world was found in Ljubljana in Slovenia.

teile.einleitung: A memory card is a small, flat card on which devices such as cameras, mobile phones or games consoles store data. Photos, videos, music or saved games end up on it. Although it is often smaller than a fingernail, thousands of pictures fit on it.
wichtigste: In a digital camera, the memory card stores the photos.
The particularly small microSD card fits into many mobile phones.
The storage space of a card is often given in gigabytes.
More photos fit on a 64 GB card than on a smaller card.
A long video usually needs much more space than a photo.
On a computer you read a memory card with a card reader.
You should not take the card out while data is being saved.

abschnitte.text: A **memory card** is a small data store with no moving parts. Inside there is **flash memory**, a chip that keeps data even without electricity. You can store data on it, delete it and write to it again, a great many times. That is why it is well suited to devices that have to be small and light.

In a **digital camera**, the memory card stores the photos and videos. Action cameras, drones, games consoles such as the Nintendo Switch and many Android phones also use memory cards. When the card is full, you cannot save any more photos. Then you have to transfer pictures to the computer and delete them from the card, or put in a second card.

The best known is the **SD card**, which is about the size of a postage stamp. It was introduced in 1999. Even smaller is the **microSD** card, which is about the size of a fingernail and fits into many phones. Older or large professional cameras sometimes use other formats such as CompactFlash. With an adapter you can also put a microSD card into an SD slot.

How much fits on a card is usually given in **gigabytes**, GB for short. A gigabyte is about a billion bytes. Many more photos fit on a 64 GB card than on an 8 GB card, several thousand depending on the camera. A long video in high resolution needs much more space than a single photo. As well as size, **speed** is also important, especially when filming.

On a computer you read a card with a **card reader**, which is built in or connected by USB. While the device is saving, you must not pull the card out, otherwise files can be damaged. Memory cards should be protected from water, heat and scratches on the contacts. You should also save important photos in a second place, because cards can fail too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A memory chip that keeps data even without electricity.
A unit of storage space, about a billion bytes.
A very small memory card that fits into many phones.
A device with which a computer can read memory cards.
Preparing a card for use; everything on it is deleted.

gewusst: Many SD cards have a small slider on the side with which you can lock them against being overwritten.
The biggest memory cards today hold more data than a whole computer used to.

teile.einleitung: A 3D printer is a machine that makes real objects you can hold. It builds them up layer by layer out of plastic, metal or other materials. In this way it makes toy figures, spare parts and even parts for medicine.
wichtigste: A 3D printer builds objects up layer by layer.
As a template, it needs a three-dimensional computer model.
In home 3D printers, the plastic is fed in as a thread from a reel.
A nozzle melts the plastic thread and lays it down in thin lines.
The first 3D printers were developed in the 1980s.
Experts call the process additive manufacturing.
3D printers are used in industry, medicine, schools and at home.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary printer puts ink onto a flat sheet of paper. A 3D printer, on the other hand, creates objects with length, width and height. It only adds material where it is needed. That is why it is called **additive manufacturing**, because additive means adding. When milling or carving, by contrast, material is taken away.

It starts with a **3D model**, which you draw on a computer or create with a 3D scanner. A special program, the **slicer**, cuts the model into many thin slices. For each slice it works out the exact path of the nozzle. The computer then sends these commands to the printer.

Most home printers use **fused deposition modelling**. A plastic thread, the **filament**, is unwound from a reel and heated to about 200 degrees in a hot nozzle. The nozzle moves back and forth and lays the soft plastic down in fine lines, which quickly harden again. When one layer is finished, it carries on one step higher. With layers of 0.2 millimetres, an object 3 centimetres tall therefore needs 150 layers.

There are also 3D printers that work with liquid resin. A beam of light hardens the resin layer by layer; this is called **stereolithography**. The American Chuck Hull patented this method in the 1980s. Other machines melt fine metal powder together with a **laser**; this is how parts for aircraft are made, for example.

In medicine, made-to-measure **prostheses**, dental splints and models of organs for planning operations are printed. Companies use them to build samples of new products quickly, called prototypes. If you have a broken plastic part, you can sometimes print a spare part yourself. In several countries, small houses have even been built with giant concrete printers.

Many Swiss schools, libraries and so-called makerspaces have their own 3D printers. There, children and teenagers can design and print their own ideas. Universities such as **ETH Zurich** also research new printing methods, for example for concrete buildings. In this way you learn technology, maths and design at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plastic thread on a reel that a home 3D printer prints with.
A computer program that splits a 3D model into many thin layers.
Making things by adding material layer by layer.
The first sample of a new product, made for testing.

gewusst: A 3D printer has already been tested on the International Space Station ISS so that astronauts can make tools themselves.
A larger object can take many hours or even days in a 3D printer.
A commonly used plastic is PLA, which is made from plants such as maize.

teile.einleitung: A search engine is a program on the internet that finds websites matching a search term. You type in a few words and get a list of results in a fraction of a second. The best-known search engine is Google, but there are also Bing, DuckDuckGo or the Swiss search engine Swisscows.
wichtigste: A web crawler automatically searches websites for the search engine and records them.
Quotation marks around several words search for exactly that sequence of words.
A minus sign in front of a word excludes pages with that word.
With site:admin.ch you search only on that website.
With filetype:pdf you find PDF documents specifically.
You can recognise paid entries by a label such as Ad or Sponsored.
The legal notice usually says who is responsible for a website.
The best way to check information is to compare several reputable sources.

abschnitte.text: A search engine does not search the whole internet every time you ask it something. Beforehand, a program called a **web crawler** constantly visits billions of websites and follows all the links. What it finds is stored in a huge **index**, similar to the index at the back of a book. When you type something in, the search engine looks it up in this index and sorts the results by importance.

Which page is at the very top is decided by a **ranking** algorithm. Google was founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin and became famous for a clever idea: a page counts as important if many other important pages link to it. Today hundreds of features play a role, such as whether the page matches the search term, is up to date and loads quickly. But at the very top there are often paid entries, labelled Ad or Sponsored.

With **quotation marks** around several words you search for exactly that sequence of words. A **minus sign** excludes words: with jaguar -car you are more likely to get pages about the big cat. With site:admin.ch you search only the pages of the Swiss federal administration. And with filetype:pdf you find PDF documents specifically, for example information sheets or reports.

Not everything a search engine finds is true. That is why it is worth looking at who is behind a page; this is usually stated in the **legal notice**. A good strategy is to compare a piece of information with several **reputable sources**, such as newspapers, encyclopedias or official bodies. The date is also important, because some pages are out of date.

Large search engines often store what someone searches for and show matching advertising. Some providers promise not to collect any personal data, including DuckDuckGo and **Swisscows**, which was developed in Switzerland. Since the 1990s there has also been a Swiss search portal, search.ch. For children there are special search engines such as fragFINN or Blinde Kuh, which only show checked pages.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that automatically visits and records websites.
A huge directory of all the recorded pages and words.
A special character or command that makes a search more precise.
Information on a website about who is responsible for it.
The order in which the results are shown.

gewusst: The name Google comes from the word googol, which is the name for a 1 followed by a hundred zeros.
The first search engine on the internet was called Archie and was created in 1990, even before the World Wide Web.
Billions of searches are made worldwide every day.

teile.einleitung: Saving energy means using less energy without going without important things. Saving energy protects the environment and your wallet. Even small everyday habits can make a big difference.
wichtigste: Saving energy means using electricity, heat and fuel carefully and wisely.
The cleanest energy is the energy you never use in the first place.
When cooking, a lid on the pan saves a lot of energy.
In winter the most economical way to air a room is briefly, with the window wide open.
LED lamps use much less electricity than old light bulbs.
When buying, the energy label shows how economical an appliance is.
Well-insulated houses need much less energy for heating.

abschnitte.text: A large part of the world's energy still comes from crude oil, natural gas and coal. Burning them produces **carbon dioxide**, which makes climate change worse. Renewable energy also needs space, materials and money for power stations. So using less protects the **climate** and saves money. In winter 2022/23 the federal government called on the population to save energy because an **energy shortage** was threatening.

Heating uses the most energy in Swiss households. Just one degree less room temperature saves a few per cent of heating energy. In winter it is best to air a room briefly with the window wide open; this is called **shock ventilation**. Windows left tilted open, on the other hand, let heat escape for hours. Taking a shower instead of a bath saves hot water and so also saves energy.

A lid on the pan makes the water boil faster and saves a lot of energy. Appliances on **standby** secretly use electricity even when switched off; a power strip with a switch helps against this. **LED lamps** use only a fraction of the electricity of an old light bulb and last much longer. When buying, the coloured **energy label** shows whether a fridge or washing machine is economical. Class A is the best.

Short journeys on foot or by bike use almost no energy and keep you fit. Trains, trams and buses use much less energy per person than a car. Switzerland has one of the densest **public transport networks** in the world. Air travel also uses a great deal of energy per person. So if you go on holiday closer to home, you save energy.

Good **insulation** in walls, roof and windows keeps the heat in the house like a thick winter coat. Since 1998 Switzerland has had the **Minergie** building standard for especially economical houses. Heat pumps take heat from the air or the ground and need little electricity to do so. The federal programme SwissEnergy gives tips on saving. Many municipalities support renovations with money.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ready mode in which an appliance seems to be off but still uses electricity.
Airing a room for a few minutes with the window wide open.
A layer on house walls and roofs that keeps heat inside the house.
A coloured label that shows how much energy an appliance uses.

gewusst: One LED lamp can shine as long as many old light bulbs one after the other.
A fridge standing next to the oven has to work harder and uses more electricity.
Heating water takes much more energy than you might think, so short showers save a lot.

teile.einleitung: A railway is a means of transport that runs on rails and carries people and goods. Since the 19th century it has completely changed travel and trade. Switzerland has one of the densest rail networks in the world and the longest railway tunnel on Earth.
wichtigste: A railway runs on steel rails.
The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in England in 1825 as the first public railway with steam locomotives.
George Stephenson is regarded as the father of the railway; his locomotive Rocket won the Rainhill Trials in 1829.
Standard gauge, about 1,435 millimetres, is the most common gauge in the world today.
The first railway entirely on Swiss soil ran from Zurich to Baden in 1847 and was called the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn.
At 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
The railway made it possible to transport goods faster and more cheaply.

abschnitte.text: On a railway, steel wheels roll on steel **rails**. Because there is very little friction, a locomotive can pull many heavy wagons. The distance between the rails is called the **gauge**; standard gauge measures about 1,435 millimetres. Many mountain railways in Switzerland run on narrower metre gauge tracks.

In 1825 the **Stockton and Darlington Railway** opened in England, the first public railway with steam locomotives. The engineer **George Stephenson** built the locomotives with his son Robert and is regarded as the father of the railway. In 1829 their locomotive Rocket won the Rainhill Trials. In 1830 the line from Liverpool to Manchester followed, the first to run to a fixed timetable.

In 1835 the locomotive Adler ran between Nuremberg and Fürth in Germany. In Switzerland the line from **Zurich to Baden** opened on 9 August 1847. It was called the **Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn**, after a popular pastry from Baden. A network soon grew up, most of which was brought together in 1902 as the Swiss Federal Railways, SBB.

To cross the Alps, Swiss engineers built spectacular lines. The first Gotthard tunnel opened in 1882. In 2016 it was followed by the **Gotthard Base Tunnel**, at 57 kilometres the longest railway tunnel in the world. The Albula and Bernina lines of the Rhaetian Railway have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 2008.

In the 19th century the railway completely changed travel. Goods could be transported much faster and more cheaply, and new factories sprang up along the lines. People could now cover distances in one day that used to take a week by coach. Because the same time had to apply everywhere, standard clock times were introduced.

Hardly any other people travel by train as much as the Swiss. Trains run to a **regular interval timetable**, so they leave at the same minute every hour. Almost the whole network is **electrified**, meaning the trains run on electricity. The Swiss railway clock is also famous: its red second hand pauses briefly before each full minute.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the two rails of a track.
A vehicle that pulls or pushes a train.
A timetable in which trains run at regular intervals.
The most common gauge in the world, about 1,435 millimetres.

gewusst: George Stephenson's Rocket already reached around 45 km/h in 1829.
Building the Gotthard Base Tunnel took about 17 years.
The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn took around 45 minutes for the roughly 23 kilometres from Zurich to Baden.

teile.einleitung: A bicycle is a vehicle with two wheels that you power with your muscles. In Germany it is called “Fahrrad”; in Switzerland “Velo”. It is quiet, healthy, environmentally friendly and one of the most important means of transport in the world.
wichtigste: You power a bicycle with your muscles.
The chain connects the pedals to the back wheel.
Karl Drais's running machine from 1817 did not yet have pedals.
A dynamo turns the movement of the wheel into electricity for the lights.
Friction slowly brings a rolling bicycle to a stop.
In Switzerland many children take a cycling test at school.
The tread on the tyre helps it grip better.

abschnitte.text: A bicycle has a **frame**, two wheels with tyres, handlebars, a saddle and pedals. When you push the pedals, the chainring at the front turns, and the **chain** passes the force on to the back wheel. With the **gears** you can ride uphill more easily or go faster on the flat. A little oil on the chain reduces friction.

In 1817, **Karl Drais** in Mannheim invented the running machine, also called the draisine. It did not yet have pedals; you pushed yourself along with your feet. Later came the **penny-farthing** with its huge front wheel and, around 1885, the safety bicycle with chain drive, which looks like our bicycles today. In 1888, John Boyd Dunlop's air-filled tyre made riding much more comfortable.

In Switzerland a roadworthy bicycle needs two brakes, a bell, lights at the front and back, and reflectors. A **dynamo** turns the movement of the wheel into electricity for the lights; today there are also battery lights. When you stop pedalling, **friction** and air resistance slowly bring the bicycle to a stop. If you ride at 15 kilometres per hour, you travel 30 kilometres in two hours.

In Switzerland there are thousands of kilometres of **cycle paths** and signposted cycle routes from “Veloland Schweiz”. Children up to 12 may ride on the pavement if there is no cycle lane, and they must be considerate towards pedestrians. Many schools have a **cycling test**. A cycle helmet is not compulsory but is strongly recommended.

Cycle races such as the **Tour de France** or the Tour de Suisse, which has existed since 1933, are very popular. There are racing bikes, mountain bikes, BMX bikes and **e-bikes** with electric motors. When you cycle, you get exercise and produce no exhaust fumes. That is why the bicycle is good for your health and for the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first two-wheeler, by Karl Drais, without pedals.
A small generator that makes electricity from movement.
A device that lets you pedal more easily or with more effort.
A force that slows down a movement.

gewusst: It is estimated that there are more than twice as many bicycles as cars in the world.
On a penny-farthing the front wheel was often more than 1.5 metres tall, so that each turn of the pedals took you a long way.

teile.einleitung: A fire engine is a special vehicle that quickly brings firefighters, water and tools to fires and accidents. With blue lights and a siren, it may even cross a junction at a red light in an emergency. In Switzerland you call the fire brigade on the emergency number 118.
wichtigste: The emergency number for the fire brigade in Switzerland is 118.
Fire engines are usually red and have blue lights and a siren.
A water tender has a large water tank and a pump on board.
A turntable ladder is used to reach high floors.
Fire engines carry hoses, breathing apparatus, ladders and rescue tools.
The fire brigade does not only put out fires but also helps with accidents, storms and floods.
In Switzerland, most firefighters are volunteers in militia fire brigades.

abschnitte.text: A **fire engine** quickly brings the crew and the equipment to where they are needed. It is usually bright red so that it can be seen easily. On the roof it has **blue lights**, as well as a loud warning signal, the **siren**. Other road users must then make way immediately.

The most important vehicle is the **water tender**. It has a water tank that often holds several thousand litres and a powerful pump. This means the fire brigade can start putting out the fire straight away, even before a hydrant is connected. The compartments on the side hold hoses, nozzles, breathing apparatus and tools.

The **turntable ladder** is a long ladder on a lorry that can turn and extend. Many turntable ladders reach about 30 metres high, about the height of a house with around ten floors. At the very top is a cage in which firefighters stand and can rescue people from windows. From there they can also spray water on a fire from above.

There are many other fire brigade vehicles. A rescue vehicle has heavy tools such as **hydraulic cutters** and spreaders to free people trapped in cars. Other vehicles are equipped for chemical accidents, oil spills or floods. At airports there are especially large airport fire engines that can spray firefighting foam a long way.

In Switzerland you dial **118** in an emergency. Most municipalities have a **militia fire brigade**, whose members do fire brigade service alongside their job. Larger cities such as Zurich, Basel, Bern, Geneva and Lausanne also have a professional fire brigade. When there is an alarm, firefighters today usually receive a message on their mobile phone or a pager.

If there is a fire, the rule is: stay calm, raise the alarm, rescue people and then put out the fire if it is safe to do so. When you call 118, say who is calling, what has happened and **where** the fire is. Leave a burning building immediately and do not use the lift. Many fire brigades have a **youth fire brigade** that children and young people can join.

begriffe.erklaerung: Flashing blue warning lights on emergency vehicles.
A connection to the water mains to which the fire brigade attaches hoses.
A ladder on a fire engine that can turn and extend.
A fire brigade whose members do the service alongside their job.

gewusst: In the past, fire engines were pulled by horses and the water was pumped with hand pumps.
A fire engine often weighs more than ten tonnes.
Many fire brigades hold open days when children can climb into a fire engine.

teile.einleitung: The PostBus is the yellow bus that links villages, valleys and mountain passes in Switzerland. It belongs to Swiss Post and also goes to places no train can reach. It is famous for its three-tone horn, which can be heard from far away in the mountains.
wichtigste: A PostBus is yellow.
PostBuses belong to the company PostBus (PostAuto), a subsidiary of Swiss Post.
The first PostBus ran near Bern in 1906.
The tune of the PostBus horn comes from the overture to “William Tell” by Rossini.
PostBuses drive over many Alpine passes such as the Grimsel or the Furka.
Every year a great many people travel by PostBus, schoolchildren, commuters and tourists.

abschnitte.text: The PostBus is a public transport bus. It is run by the company **PostBus**, which belongs to Swiss Post. PostBuses run mainly in the countryside and in the mountains and take people to the nearest railway station. The timetables are coordinated with trains and boats.

In the past, horse-drawn **mail coaches** carried letters, parcels and travellers across the country and over the passes. In 1906 the first PostBus ran between Bern and Detligen. After the First World War, PostBuses gradually replaced the horse-drawn coaches on the Alpine passes. For a long time the company **Saurer** in Arbon built many of the PostBuses.

On winding mountain roads, the PostBus uses its **three-tone horn** to warn of tight bends. The three notes sound like “dü-da-do”. They come from the overture to the opera **“William Tell”** by Gioachino Rossini. In Switzerland only PostBuses may use this horn, and on certain mountain roads the PostBus also has right of way.

PostBuses drive over famous passes such as the **Grimsel**, Furka, Susten, Klausen or Bernina. The route from Reichenbach to the Griesalp in the Bernese Oberland is considered the steepest PostBus route in Europe. For tourists, a trip over a pass is a special experience. The drivers have to be very skilled, because the roads are narrow and steep.

Yellow is the colour of the **Post**. That is why you recognise a PostBus immediately. Today there are also PostBuses powered by electricity or hydrogen. In the Principality of Liechtenstein, yellow buses that look similar run as well.

begriffe.erklaerung: Means of transport such as trains, buses and trams that anyone may use.
A horse-drawn carriage that used to carry post and travellers.
The PostBus horn, which plays three notes one after another.
A route over a mountain from one valley to another.

gewusst: The three notes of the PostBus horn are C sharp, E and A.
On mountain roads, PostBus drivers often have to pass rock faces with millimetre precision.

teile.einleitung: A web browser is a program with which you can fetch and look at websites on the internet. Well-known browsers are Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge. The very first web browser was created in 1990 at the CERN research centre in Geneva.
wichtigste: The main job of a web browser is to fetch and display web pages.
Well-known browsers are Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Safari, Apple's browser.
You type the web address into the address bar.
With tabs you can have several pages open at the same time.
A small padlock next to the address shows a secure connection.
The rendering engine turns HTML and CSS into a visible page.
In the cache, the browser stores copies of loaded files for quicker access.

abschnitte.text: A **web browser** is a program that fetches web pages from the internet and displays them on the screen. The English word “to browse” means roughly to look around or leaf through. Well-known browsers are Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge and Apple's Safari, which you find on the iPad, for example. At least one browser is installed on every computer, tablet and mobile phone.

At the top of the browser is the **address bar**, into which you type a web address and which shows the address of the open page. With the back arrow you get to the page before, and the circular arrow reloads the page. Small tabs at the top, the **tabs**, let you have several pages open at the same time. With a **bookmark** you remember a favourite page.

When you enter an address, the browser sends a request to a server somewhere in the world. The server answers with files in the languages HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The browser's **rendering engine** turns this code into a page with texts, pictures and buttons. So that it is quicker next time, the browser stores copies in the **cache**.

The British researcher Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at **CERN** in Geneva and in 1990 wrote the first browser, called WorldWideWeb. In 1993 the Mosaic browser made the web with pictures popular with many people. After that came Netscape Navigator and Microsoft's Internet Explorer. Firefox appeared in 2004, Google Chrome in 2008, and Chrome is now the most widely used browser in the world.

A small padlock next to the address shows that the connection is encrypted; the address then begins with https. This protects passwords, for example, from prying eyes, but it does not say whether the page itself is trustworthy. Browsers warn about dangerous pages and often block advertising windows. In a private window the browser does not store any history, but you are still not invisible on the internet.

It is worth always keeping your browser up to date, because updates close security holes. Extensions, small add-on programs, should only be installed from trustworthy sources. With questions such as “Do you want to allow cookies?”, you may also say no. And if you are unsure whether a page is genuine, it is best to ask an adult.

begriffe.erklaerung: A page on the internet with texts, pictures or videos.
A computer that stores web pages and sends them out on request.
The language in which the structure of web pages is described.
A temporary store in which the browser keeps files for later.
A small file with which a website can remember you.

gewusst: The very first web page in the world went online at CERN in 1991 and can still be called up today.
Many browsers use the same rendering engine inside, which is why pages look almost the same in them.

teile.einleitung: A bus, originally called an omnibus, is a large vehicle that carries many people at the same time. The Latin word omnibus means for everyone, because anyone can ride. In Switzerland, buses run in towns, in the countryside and right up into mountain villages.
wichtigste: Omnibus is Latin and means for everyone.
Buses are part of public transport and run to a timetable.
A trolleybus gets its electricity from an overhead line above the road.
The first omnibuses were pulled by horses.
In Switzerland, the yellow PostBuses also connect small mountain villages.
Articulated buses consist of two parts joined by a flexible section and offer lots of space.
More and more buses run on electricity and without exhaust fumes.

abschnitte.text: A bus is a motor vehicle with many **seats and standing places**. It runs on fixed **routes** and stops at bus stops. Passengers buy a ticket for this or have a travel pass. A normal city bus is about 12 metres long and has room for around 80 to 100 people.

In the early 19th century the first **horse-drawn omnibuses**, carriages for many passengers, ran in France. From around 1900, motor buses replaced the horses. In Switzerland the first PostBus ran from Bern to Detligen in 1906. Soon **PostBuses** were carrying post and people over Alpine passes too.

A **trolleybus** runs on electricity, which it takes through two poles from an **overhead line** above the road. Trolleybuses run, for example, in Zurich, Bern, Lucerne, Lausanne and Geneva. Modern electric buses instead have large batteries that are charged at the last stop or in the depot. Both are quiet and give off no exhaust fumes while driving.

The yellow **PostBuses** are a landmark of Switzerland. They run on hundreds of routes and also serve remote valleys. On mountain roads you can hear their famous **three-tone horn**, which warns of tight bends. On some routes, for example over passes, a PostBus ride is even seen as an excursion in itself.

As well as city buses there are **articulated buses**, which bend in the middle, and even double articulated buses with three parts. Coaches take groups on excursions and holidays. In London, the red double-decker buses are famous. In rural areas, school buses pick children up and take them to school.

A full bus replaces many cars and so saves space on the road and fuel. That is why public transport is more environmentally friendly than lots of individual cars. In many Swiss towns buses have their own **bus lanes** so that they do not get stuck in traffic. Many transport companies are gradually switching their fleets to electric buses.

begriffe.erklaerung: Latin for for everyone, the original word for the bus.
An electric cable stretched above the road.
A long bus made of two parts joined by a flexible joint.
A list of when a bus or train leaves and arrives where.

gewusst: The word bus is actually just the ending of omnibus.
The notes of the PostBus horn come from the overture to the opera William Tell by Gioachino Rossini.
In Switzerland, PostBuses even drive over passes more than 2,000 metres high.

teile.einleitung: A ship is a large watercraft that carries people and goods across seas, lakes and rivers. People were already building ships out of wood thousands of years ago; today the largest are made of steel and are longer than three football pitches. Even though they are so heavy, they do not sink.
wichtigste: A steel ship floats because it pushes aside a lot of water and buoyancy holds it up.
Large cargo ships travel up the Rhine as far as Basel.
In the past, the wind drove the explorers' ships.
Columbus set off in 1492 with three ships; the largest was the Santa María.
From 1519 to 1522, Magellan's expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world.
Today, container ships carry most of the world's goods.
Switzerland also has ocean-going ships; their home port is Basel.

abschnitte.text: A ship's hull pushes water aside; we say it **displaces** water. The water pushes back from below, and this force is called **buoyancy**. If the displaced water weighs as much as the whole ship, the ship floats. The Greek scholar Archimedes discovered this more than 2000 years ago.

The front part is called the **bow**, the back part the **stern**. Looking forward, the left side is **port** and the right side is starboard. The rudder is used for steering, and a propeller under the water drives modern ships. The ship is steered from the bridge, where the captain is in command.

For a long time, the **wind** drove ships across the seas. In 1492, Christopher **Columbus** set off with three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, and first stopped in the Canary Islands. He then crossed the Atlantic and reached America. From 1519 to 1522, Ferdinand **Magellan**'s expedition was the first to sail all the way around the Earth.

There are **container ships**, tankers for crude oil, ferries for cars, cruise ships for holidays and fishing boats. The largest container ships are about 400 metres long and carry more than 20,000 containers. Icebreakers can break through thick ice. Warships and submarines belong to a country's navy.

Although Switzerland has no coast, large cargo ships travel up the **Rhine** as far as **Basel**. In the Rhine ports, containers, grain and fuel are unloaded and reloaded. Since 1941 there has been a Swiss ocean-going fleet whose ships are registered in Basel. Many passenger boats also take people on trips on the Swiss lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of water that pushes floating things upwards.
The front part of a ship.
The back part of a ship.
The left side of a ship when you look forward.
A large metal box of standard size for goods.

gewusst: Because they can travel through the desert for weeks, camels are also called “ships of the desert”.
In 1912 the Titanic was thought to be unsinkable, yet it sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg.

teile.einleitung: A drone is a flying machine with nobody sitting inside. It is remote-controlled or flies on its own with the help of a computer. Drones take aerial photos, deliver parcels, help rescue people and are also a popular hobby.
wichtigste: Nobody sits in a drone; it is an unmanned aircraft.
Most small drones have four rotors and are therefore called quadcopters.
Drones are remote-controlled or fly on their own using GPS and sensors.
In Switzerland, flying drones near airports is forbidden.
In Switzerland, drones weighing 250 grams or more must be registered.
Drones are used for photos, surveying, farming, rescue and parcel deliveries.
The name drone comes from male bees, which also buzz.

abschnitte.text: A drone is an **unmanned aircraft**, a flying machine with no pilot on board. It is controlled from the ground with a **remote control** or a mobile phone. Larger drones can fly a route by themselves using a computer program. There are tiny drones that fit in your hand, and others as big as an aeroplane.

Most small drones are **multicopters** with four, six or eight propellers. By turning the propellers at different speeds, the drone can climb, descend, hover and fly in any direction. **Sensors** such as an acceleration sensor, a compass and GPS keep it steady in the air. A camera on board sends pictures straight to the screen on the ground.

With drones you can take spectacular **aerial photos** of landscapes and buildings. Farmers use them to monitor fields or to find fawns hidden in tall grass before mowing. Rescue services use thermal imaging cameras to search for missing people. In some countries drones also deliver medicines or parcels.

Since 2023, Switzerland has had rules similar to those in the EU. Drones weighing 250 grams or more, or with a camera, must be registered with the Federal Office of Civil Aviation **FOCA**, and heavier drones also require an online test. Flying is forbidden near **airports**, over crowds and in some protected areas. You must always keep the drone within sight and respect other people's privacy.

Switzerland is regarded as an important centre for **drone research**. At ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne, researchers develop drones that recognise obstacles by themselves or fly through caves and buildings. Some Swiss companies build drones for surveying or for inspecting narrow spaces. The army also uses drones for reconnaissance.

The word **drone** originally refers to the male honeybee. Drones in a bee colony have no sting and are larger than the worker bees. In autumn they are often driven out of the hive. Because flying machines buzz in a similar way, they were given the same name.

begriffe.erklaerung: With no people on board.
A drone with four propellers.
A satellite system you can use to find your own location.
The Federal Office of Civil Aviation, responsible for the rules in Swiss skies.
A camera that makes heat visible, for example from people or animals.

gewusst: Every spring in Switzerland, drones help to save fawns from mowing machines.
The smallest drones are no bigger than a coin.
In 2021 a small helicopter drone called Ingenuity flew on Mars.

teile.einleitung: A counting loop is a loop in programming that repeats commands a fixed number of times. A loop variable keeps count of which round you are in. In Python you usually write it with for and range.
wichtigste: A counting loop repeats commands a number of times known in advance.
The variable that keeps count is called the loop variable.
In Python, range(3) produces the numbers 0, 1 and 2.
range(2, 6) produces 2, 3, 4 and 5; the end value is never included.
A third value sets the step size, even backwards.
With for you can also go through the letters of a word.
Counting loops are good for adding up and multiplying many numbers.

abschnitte.text: A **counting loop** repeats something exactly as often as you set. The **loop variable**, often called i, takes the next value in each round. In many languages such as Java or C you write a start value, a condition and a step. Python counts with for i in range(...).

The function **range** produces a sequence of numbers. range(3) gives 0, 1 and 2, because Python starts at 0 and stops before the end value. range(2, 6) gives 2, 3, 4 and 5. With a step size, range(0, 10, 2) gives the numbers 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8, and range(5, 0, -1) counts backwards from 5 to 1.

With a counting loop you can add many numbers together. With s = 0 and for i in range(1, 5): s = s + i you get 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. If you replace plus with times and start with p = 1, you get 1 times 2 times 3 times 4 = 24. Such a collecting variable is called an **accumulator**.
