In Python, for can go through not only numbers but also letters and lists. for b in "Uri": print(b) prints U, r and i, each on its own line. In the same way you can print every town from a list one after another. After the loop for i in range(7), i has the last value, which is 6.

Even the programming language **Fortran** from 1957 had a counting loop, the DO loop. In BASIC you wrote FOR I = 1 TO 10. If you know the number of rounds in advance, a counting loop is clearer than a **while loop**. If the number is unknown, it is better to use while.

begriffe.erklaerung: A variable that keeps count in each round of a loop.
A Python function that produces a sequence of numbers.
How much the loop variable goes up or down in each round.
A variable in which results are collected step by step.

gewusst: Programmers often call the loop variable i because of old habits from mathematics and Fortran.
In Python counting starts at 0, so range(10) gives ten numbers, but 10 is not among them.
With two nested counting loops you can, for example, print out all the times tables.

teile.einleitung: Responsive web design means that a website automatically adapts to the size of the screen. The same page then looks good on a mobile phone, a tablet and a big monitor. Today almost all modern websites are built this way.
wichtigste: With responsive web design, the page adapts to the screen size.
With media queries in CSS, you react to different screen widths.
Mobile first means designing for small screens first.
The viewport meta element in the head section is important for mobile phones.
The CSS unit vw depends on the width of the browser window.
CSS Grid and Flexbox are layout systems for flexible arrangements.
The width at which a layout changes is called a breakpoint.

abschnitte.text: In the past, websites were mostly designed for a fixed computer screen. With the success of smartphones from 2007 this became a problem, because you saw tiny writing on your phone. With **responsive web design**, the page reacts to the available width. The term was coined by the web designer Ethan Marcotte in 2010.

With **media queries**, you write rules in CSS that only apply from a certain screen width. The width at which the layout changes is called a **breakpoint**. An example: on a mobile phone, three boxes are shown one below the other, and from a width of 768 pixels side by side. This keeps the page easy to read everywhere.

In responsive layouts, widths are often given in **percent** so that elements adapt to the available space. The unit vw stands for one hundredth of the width of the browser window. Pictures are often given the rule never to become wider than their container. The **viewport** meta element in the head section tells the mobile phone not simply to show the page shrunk down.

**Flexbox** arranges elements flexibly in a row or column and shares out the space automatically. **CSS Grid** divides the page like a grid into rows and columns. Both techniques make it much easier to build layouts for different screens. They are supported by all common browsers today.

With the **mobile first** approach, you design the version for small screens first. There you have to limit yourself to the essentials, which makes the page clearer. For bigger screens you then add more columns and elements. Because many people today mainly browse on their phones, this approach is widespread.

begriffe.erklaerung: A language used to set the appearance of websites.
A CSS rule that only applies at certain screen sizes.
The screen width at which a layout changes.
The visible area of a website in the browser window.
The arrangement of texts, pictures and elements on a page.

gewusst: Search engines rate websites better if they also work well on mobile phones.
In a browser's developer tools you can test how a page looks on different mobile phones.

teile.einleitung: A battery is an energy store that turns chemical energy into electric current. It supplies electricity for torches, remote controls, clocks and toys without any plug socket. A rechargeable battery is found in every mobile phone and every electric car.
wichtigste: A battery turns stored chemical energy into electric current.
Around 1800, Alessandro Volta built the first usable battery, the voltaic pile.
A battery that can be recharged is called a rechargeable battery or accumulator.
Batteries supply direct current, which always flows in the same direction.
A lamp only lights up when the circuit is closed.
Empty batteries go back into the collection box in the shop.
The unit volt is named after Alessandro Volta.

abschnitte.text: A **battery** has two terminals, a positive one and a negative one. Inside, chemical reactions take place that release electrons at one terminal. If you connect the two terminals with a wire and a device, the electrons flow and an electric current is produced. When the supply of chemicals is used up, the battery is flat.

For a simple **circuit** you need at least a battery, wires and something that uses the current, such as a lamp. The lamp only lights up when the circuit is closed and the current can flow all the way round. A switch opens or closes the circuit. Batteries supply **direct current**, which always flows in the same direction, whereas the current from a plug socket is alternating current and regularly changes direction.

Around 1800, the Italian **Alessandro Volta** stacked discs of zinc and copper on top of each other in turn and put cardboard soaked in salt water between them. This **voltaic pile** was the first usable battery that supplied current continuously. Volta was inspired by experiments with frogs' legs by his fellow Italian Luigi Galvani. The unit of electrical voltage, the volt, is named after Volta.

A battery that can be charged again is called a **rechargeable battery** or accumulator. Mobile phones, laptops, e-bikes and electric cars usually contain lithium-ion batteries. They are light and store a lot of energy. In 2019 three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing them.

Batteries contain metals that are valuable but in some cases also poisonous. In Switzerland you are required to hand back empty batteries, and every shop that sells batteries must take them back. There are **collection boxes** there; handing them in is free because a fee has already been paid when you buy them. Damaged lithium batteries can catch fire and so must never go in the rubbish bag.

begriffe.erklaerung: The connection of a battery, positive or negative.
A closed path through which electric current flows.
A battery that can be charged again.
The unit of electrical voltage.

gewusst: Some animals also produce electricity: the electric eel can give off shocks of several hundred volts.
A bicycle dynamo also makes electricity, but from the movement of the wheel instead of from chemistry.
With a lemon, a piece of copper and a galvanised nail you can make a small battery.

teile.einleitung: A hot air balloon is an aircraft that rises into the sky using heated air. Beneath a large, colourful envelope hangs a basket in which people ride. It is the oldest flying machine in which people have risen into the air.
wichtigste: A hot air balloon rises because warm air is lighter than cold air.
A burner using propane gas heats the air in the envelope.
The Montgolfier brothers invented the hot air balloon in France in 1783.
A balloon cannot be steered; it drifts with the wind.
The pilot only controls the height, by heating or letting air out.
In German, people say a balloon travels rather than flies.
Every year a famous balloon festival takes place in Château-d'Oex in the canton of Vaud.

abschnitte.text: When air is heated, it expands and becomes lighter. That is why warm air floats above cold air, rather as wood floats on water. In the balloon, a **burner** heats the air in the envelope to about 100 degrees. This creates enough **lift** to carry the envelope, the basket and the passengers. When the air cools down, the balloon sinks again.

The **envelope** is made of light, tear-resistant fabric such as nylon or polyester. A normal balloon holds several thousand cubic metres of air and is as tall as a house with several floors. The **basket** is usually made of woven willow, because this is light and cushions the landing. The gas cylinders with propane for the burner stand in the basket. At the top of the envelope there is an opening through which the pilot can let warm air out.

The French brothers Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne **Montgolfier** launched the first hot air balloons in 1783. At a demonstration in Versailles, a sheep, a duck and a cockerel were the first to fly. On 21 November 1783 people travelled in a hot air balloon for the first time, in Paris. After its inventors, a hot air balloon is also called a **montgolfière**. Modern balloons with gas burners have existed since the 1960s.

Balloons usually take off early in the morning or in the evening, because the wind is calm then. You cannot steer a balloon; it drifts with the **wind**. But the wind often blows in different directions at different heights, and the pilot makes clever use of this. A chase vehicle follows on the ground and picks up the balloon and passengers after landing.

An international balloon festival takes place every January in the village of **Château-d'Oex** in the Pays-d'Enhaut in Vaud. Then dozens of colourful balloons float in front of the snow-covered mountains. In 1999 the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3, with Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones, took off from there. They became the first to fly around the world in a balloon without stopping. However, this balloon was a combination balloon using helium and hot air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that heats the air in the balloon with a large flame.
A force that pushes something upwards because it is lighter than its surroundings.
A flammable gas carried in cylinders in the basket.
Another word for a hot air balloon, named after its inventors.

gewusst: The first passengers of a hot air balloon, in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a cockerel.
Because the balloon drifts with the wind, you feel almost no breeze in the basket.
After a balloon trip there is often a balloon christening for people who have travelled for the first time.

teile.einleitung: In a survey, you ask lots of people the same question and collect their answers. This way you find out what a group thinks, likes or does. There are surveys in school classes, in market research and before votes in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In a survey you ask lots of people the same thing.
The answers are counted, for example with a tally chart.
Each person may only answer once.
The results are shown well with a bar chart.
Answers must not be changed afterwards.
In class you can vote quickly with a show of hands.
Online surveys are often filled in on a computer or mobile phone today.

abschnitte.text: In a **survey**, you ask many people the same question. A good question for the class is, for example, “What is your favourite animal?”. Often fixed answers are given to choose from so that they are easier to count. Several questions together on one sheet are called a **questionnaire**.

The answers are counted with a **tally chart** or on the computer. If 8 children say “pizza”, 5 “spaghetti” and 3 “soup”, then 16 children were asked altogether. The most popular is then pizza. In a spreadsheet you can add up such results quickly.

With a **bar chart** you can see at a glance which answer was the most common. If the bar for “dog” is 9 high and the bar for “cat” is 6 high, dog has 3 votes more. A pie chart shows what proportion of the people asked chose something. Percentages also help with comparing.

In a survey, each person may only answer once. The answers must not be changed or made up. The question should be neutral and not push anyone towards a particular answer. In secret surveys you don't write any names down, so that everyone can answer honestly.

Before federal votes and elections, research institutes ask a few thousand people who are entitled to vote. From this they estimate how the vote might turn out. Because only part of the population is asked, a so-called **sample**, there is always some uncertainty. Companies also carry out surveys to find out which products their customers want.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sheet or form with several questions.
A list on which you make a mark for each answer.
A picture in which bars show how often an answer came up.
A selected part of all the people that you ask.

gewusst: Five marks on a tally chart are often drawn as a bundle so that you can count faster.
With just about a thousand well-chosen people, you can roughly estimate the opinion of a whole country.
How a question is worded can strongly influence the result of a survey.

teile.einleitung: A stop-motion film is a film made of many single photos. Between two photos you move the figures only a tiny bit, and when the photos are played quickly one after another, they seem to come to life. This is how famous animated films such as Pingu or Shaun the Sheep are made.
wichtigste: A stop-motion film consists of many single photos.
Between two photos you move the figure a tiny bit each time.
If you play the photos quickly, you see a smooth movement.
Figures made of modelling clay are especially popular because they are easy to shape.
The camera stands on a tripod so that it stays completely still.
The famous clay penguin Pingu comes from a Swiss animated series.
A tablet with a camera is enough to make your own stop-motion film.

abschnitte.text: In stop motion, a figure is photographed, then moved a tiny bit and photographed again. You repeat this hundreds or thousands of times. When it is played back, the film shows many pictures per second, and our eye sees a **movement** in them. This technique belongs to **animation**, that is, to animated films.

For a single second of film you often need 10 to 24 photos. If Lina needs 10 photos per second, that is already 30 photos for 3 seconds. A 90-minute cinema film can therefore have more than a hundred thousand single pictures. Professionals sometimes manage only a few seconds of finished film in a working day. If you move the figure too far, you get a **jerky** movement.

Figures made of **modelling clay** are very popular; this is also called claymation. But you can also use Lego figures, toys, scraps of paper or even food. Professionals build puppets with a movable wire frame inside so that they stay in any position. Small sets with furniture, trees and houses bring the figures' world to life.

The little penguin **Pingu** was invented in Switzerland by the animator Otmar Gutmann and has been on television since 1990. Wallace and Gromit and Shaun the Sheep come from the English studio Aardman. As early as the 1933 film King Kong, the giant ape was moved with stop motion. The Swiss director Claude Barras made the stop-motion film “My Life as a Courgette”, which was nominated for an Oscar in 2017.

For a simple film, a tablet or mobile phone with a stop-motion app is enough. The camera goes on a **tripod** so that it does not wobble between photos. Even lighting is important; a lamp is best rather than sunlight, which keeps changing. Many apps show the last photo see-through, so you can see exactly how far you have already moved the figure. At the end you can add music and sounds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single photo from which, together with many others, a film is made.
A stand with three legs that holds the camera completely still.
A stop-motion film with figures made of modelling clay.
How many pictures per second a film shows.

gewusst: For many cinema films with clay figures, several identical heads or mouths are built for each figure so that the faces can be swapped quickly.
Stop motion is one of the oldest animation techniques and was already being used more than a hundred years ago.
Because modelling clay gets soft under warm light, animators often have to reshape their figures.

teile.einleitung: A robot vacuum cleaner is a small, usually round robot that vacuums the floor by itself. It drives through the home, avoids obstacles and goes back by itself to recharge. This makes it one of the best-known robots in the household.
wichtigste: A robot vacuum cleaner vacuums the floor all by itself.
Many robot vacuum cleaners are round and flat.
When its battery is almost empty, it drives to its charging station.
Sensors detect the edges of stairs so that it does not fall down.
If it bumps into a chair leg, it notices that there is an obstacle.
It collects the dust in its dust container.
Some robot vacuum cleaners make a map of the home as they drive around.

abschnitte.titel: What is a robot vacuum cleaner?
abschnitte.text: A robot vacuum cleaner is a **robot** that cleans the floor without help from people. It is usually round and so flat that it can drive under beds and sofas. It is controlled by a small computer inside. Many models can be started and scheduled with an app on a mobile phone.

At the front, **side brushes** turn and get dust out of corners and from along edges. A brush underneath the device loosens the dirt, and a motor sucks it up. The dust ends up in the **dust container**, which has to be emptied regularly. Some models can also mop the floor.

A robot vacuum cleaner has many **sensors**, feelers that measure its surroundings. A bumper notices when it hits a chair leg, and the robot turns away. Sensors on the underside detect the edges of stairs so that it does not fall down. Modern devices measure the rooms with laser light or cameras and draw a **map** of the home.

Robot vacuum cleaners run on a **rechargeable battery**, which lasts for one to two hours depending on the model. When the battery gets low, the robot finds its charging station by itself. There it recharges and can then carry on vacuuming. Some charging stations even empty the dust container automatically.

Before starting, you should tidy socks, cables and small toys off the floor so that the robot does not get tangled up. Rugs with long fringes are difficult for many devices. One of the first robot vacuum cleaners on sale was the Trilobite from Electrolux around 2001. The Roomba from the company iRobot became well known in 2002 and sold millions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that carries out tasks by itself.
A feeler that measures something, for example distance or touch.
A battery that can be charged again.
The place where the robot vacuum cleaner charges its battery.

gewusst: In some videos, cats ride round the home on robot vacuum cleaners.
A robot vacuum cleaner does not clean as thoroughly as a person, but it does it every day without grumbling.

teile.einleitung: A telephone is a device that lets people talk to each other over long distances. It turns the voice into electrical signals or radio waves and, at the other end, back into sound. In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell received the patent for the telephone; today almost everyone carries a mobile phone in their pocket.
wichtigste: With a telephone you can talk over great distances.
In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone.
In the past, all telephones were connected to the telephone network by cable.
A mobile phone is a telephone you can take anywhere.
In Switzerland you dial 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 144 for an ambulance.
At payphones you paid with coins.
The International Telecommunication Union ITU in Geneva sets worldwide rules for telecommunications.

abschnitte.text: In the telephone's **microphone**, the voice makes a thin membrane vibrate. These vibrations are turned into electrical signals and passed on by cable or radio. At the receiving end, a small **loudspeaker** turns the signals back into sound. So you hear the voice even though the other person is far away.

Several inventors were working at the same time on the idea of transmitting speech electrically. The German **Philipp Reis** demonstrated a device that transmitted sounds as early as 1861. **Alexander Graham Bell**, who was born in Scotland, filed his patent in the USA in 1876 and is therefore usually regarded as the inventor of the telephone. Soon telephone networks were set up in many towns.

abschnitte.titel: From the switchboard operator to the mobile phone
abschnitte.text: At first, a telephone operator connected calls by hand using plugs at an **exchange**. Later, automatic systems took over this work, and people dialled the number with a rotary dial. On the street there were phone boxes with **payphones**, into which you put coins. From the 1990s the **mobile phone** spread, and since 2007 smartphones with touchscreens have been usual.

In an emergency the telephone can save lives. In Switzerland you dial **117** for the police, **118** for the fire brigade and **144** for an ambulance. The Europe-wide emergency number 112 also works. On the phone, say calmly who you are, where you are and what has happened.

For telephones all over the world to work together, shared rules are needed. They are drawn up by the **International Telecommunication Union** ITU, which has its headquarters in Geneva and is an organisation of the UN. Today many calls go over the internet or mobile networks instead of copper cables. With video calls you can even see each other while you talk.

begriffe.erklaerung: A legal right that reserves an invention for its inventor.
The place that used to connect telephone calls with each other.
A telephone number for help when you are in danger.
Making calls using radio waves and masts instead of cables.

gewusst: The first telephones had no numbers; you simply told the operator who you wanted to talk to.
Many old phone boxes in Switzerland have been turned into mini-libraries.
Bell wanted people to answer the phone with “Ahoy”.

teile.einleitung: SQL injection is an attack on websites and apps in which someone smuggles their own database code into an input field. If the program is badly written, the database runs this foreign code. In this way attackers can read or change data or even delete whole tables.
wichtigste: In an SQL injection, harmful code gets into a database query through input fields.
A classic example is entering ' OR '1'='1 into a login field.
The characters -- often turn the rest of the query into a comment.
With UNION, attackers attach data from another table to the result.
In blind SQL injection, the attacker only draws conclusions from how the page behaves.
The most important protection is prepared statements with parameters.
OWASP lists injection in its well-known top 10 list of risks.
The principle of least privilege limits the damage of an attack.

abschnitte.text: Many websites build an **SQL query** from what you type in, for example when you log in. If the input is simply inserted into the command, an attacker can type in their own SQL commands instead of a name. The database can then no longer tell what is data and what is a command. It is as if a waiter read out and carried out every note, even if it said: give me the till.

A classic example is entering **' OR '1'='1** into a login field. Because 1 always equals 1, the condition is always true, and the attacker may get in without a password. With the characters **--**, the rest of the query becomes a comment and is therefore ignored. With the keyword **UNION**, data from other tables can be attached, such as user names and passwords.

Sometimes a page does not show any data from the database at all. In a **blind SQL injection**, the attacker then asks questions that can only be answered with yes or no. For example, he watches whether the page loads normally, shows an error message or takes a noticeably long time. In this way he can guess secret information character by character, which is slow but effective.

The most important protection is **prepared statements** with parameters. Here the SQL command is first sent to the database without any input, and the input is only sent afterwards as pure data. The **principle of least privilege** also helps: the database user of a website may only do what it really needs. Checking input and not showing error messages publicly make attacks even harder.

SQL injection has been known since the end of the 1990s and yet is still one of the most common weaknesses today. The non-profit **OWASP** has listed injection for many years in its top 10 list of the biggest risks for web applications. The webcomic xkcd with **Little Bobby Tables** is famous: a mother has named her son so that his name contains the command DROP TABLE, and in this way deletes the school's database of pupils. The joke shows why you must never build input into commands without checking it.

begriffe.erklaerung: Literally “injecting”; here: sneaking in foreign code.
A prepared query in which input only counts as data.
A placeholder in a query that is later filled with a value.
A non-profit organisation for the security of web applications.
Every program may only do what it really needs.

gewusst: The command DROP TABLE deletes a whole table together with all its data.
SQL injection does not only work with login fields but with any input that gets into a query.
Many modern programming tools protect against SQL injection automatically if you use them correctly.

teile.einleitung: A tunnel is an underground passage that leads through a mountain, under a river or under a city. Tunnels shorten journeys, protect against avalanches and connect valleys that would otherwise be separated by mountains. Switzerland is a land of tunnels: it is home to the Gotthard Base Tunnel, the longest railway tunnel in the world.
wichtigste: A tunnel is an artificially built underground route.
The longest railway tunnel in the world is the Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland.
It opened in 2016 and is about 57 kilometres long.
Tunnels are blasted or dug with huge tunnel boring machines.
The first Gotthard railway tunnel opened in 1882.
Small tunnels are also built under roads for animals such as frogs and toads.
Moles and badgers are nature's tunnel builders.

abschnitte.text: A **tunnel** is an underground passage through which roads, railways, water or pipes and cables run. In mountainous countries such as Switzerland, tunnels connect valleys and make long, winding pass roads unnecessary. In cities, underground trains and other trains run through tunnels beneath the houses. Under the sea, tunnels even connect countries, for example the Channel Tunnel between England and France.

In hard rock, blasting is often used: holes are drilled, filled with **explosives**, and afterwards the rock is cleared away. For long tunnels, huge **tunnel boring machines** are used today, which eat their way through the mountain with a rotating cutting head. Then the tunnel is lined with concrete so that nothing collapses. Ventilation, lighting and emergency exits make it safe.

The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** between Erstfeld in the canton of Uri and Bodio in Ticino is the longest railway tunnel in the world, at about 57 kilometres. It opened in 2016 after 17 years of construction. Because it runs deep down in the mountain, trains hardly have to climb any more and can travel much faster. It is part of the **NRLA**, which also includes the Lötschberg Base Tunnel and the Ceneri Base Tunnel.

As early as 1882 the first **Gotthard railway tunnel** opened, about 15 kilometres long. Many workers died during its construction; most of them came from Italy. In 1980 came the Gotthard road tunnel for cars, almost 17 kilometres long. Today Switzerland has hundreds of railway and road tunnels.

Animals are tunnel builders too. The **mole** digs long passages with its shovel-like front paws and spends almost its whole life underground. The badger builds large setts with several entrances, sometimes more than ten. In Switzerland, small **amphibian tunnels** are built under some roads so that common frogs and common toads can travel safely to their spawning waters in spring.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge machine that bores through rock with a rotating head.
New Railway Link through the Alps, the Swiss project for new Alpine tunnels.
A tunnel deep down at the foot of a mountain range.
A small tunnel under a road for frogs and toads.

gewusst: At its highest point, the rock above the Gotthard Base Tunnel is more than 2000 metres thick.
The miners from both sides met in the Gotthard Base Tunnel almost to the centimetre.
Saint Barbara is regarded as the patron saint of tunnel builders, which is why her figure often stands at the tunnel entrance.

teile.einleitung: Unicode is a worldwide standard that gives every written character in the world its own number. Thanks to Unicode, a computer can show Latin letters, Chinese characters, Arabic script and even emojis at the same time. Without Unicode, a message would often arrive on another device as a jumble of strange characters.
wichtigste: Unicode aims to give every written character in the world its own code.
Every character has a code point; the capital A, for example, is U+0041.
Unicode includes over 150,000 characters (as of 2025).
The first 128 code points are the same characters as in the ASCII code.
Emojis are also part of the Unicode standard.
UTF-8 is an encoding that stores Unicode characters as bytes.
The standard is maintained by the Unicode Consortium.

abschnitte.text: A computer can really only deal with numbers. That is why every letter needs a number so that the computer can store it. In Unicode this number is called a **code point** and is usually written with U+ and a hexadecimal number. The capital A has the code point U+0041, the small a the code point U+0061.

In the past there were many different character tables, for example for Western Europe, for Russian or for Japanese. If you opened a text with the wrong table, you saw a strange **jumble of characters** instead of umlauts. Unicode solves this problem with one single big table for all scripts. It contains over 150,000 characters (as of 2025), including Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, Chinese and even old scripts such as Egyptian hieroglyphs.

The older **ASCII code** from the 1960s had only 128 characters, mainly English letters, digits and punctuation marks. Umlauts such as ä, ö and ü were missing from it. At the end of the 1980s, experts began working on a shared code for all languages. In 1991 the first version of Unicode appeared, maintained by the **Unicode Consortium**, and since then new characters have been added regularly.

Unicode only sets out which number a character has. How this number is stored as bytes is decided by an **encoding**. The most important is **UTF-8**, which is used on the vast majority of websites today. English letters need only one byte in it, umlauts two bytes and many Chinese characters three bytes, and emojis usually four.

**Emojis** are also Unicode characters with their own code points. The grinning face 😀, for example, has the code point U+1F600. Anyone who wants to suggest a new emoji can submit a proposal to the Unicode Consortium. But the look of the emojis is decided by the companies themselves, which is why the same emoji looks a bit different on different phones.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fixed number of a character in Unicode.
An old character code with only 128 characters.
The rule for how characters are stored as bytes.
The most common encoding for Unicode text on the internet.
A small unit of storage made of 8 bits.

gewusst: The Swiss flag emoji is not a character of its own but is made from two special characters for the letters C and H.
Unicode has room for over a million code points, so it is a long way from being full.
New emojis are added to Unicode every year, such as new animals, foods or faces.

teile.einleitung: A paddle steamer is a ship driven by large paddle wheels. The wheels are turned by a steam engine. Several paddle steamers more than a hundred years old still sail on Swiss lakes today, and you can visit them and travel on them.
wichtigste: The wheels of a paddle steamer are driven by a steam engine.
From 1823 the first steamship in Switzerland, the “Guillaume Tell”, sailed on Lake Geneva.
The paddle wheels are usually fitted on the left and right of the ship.
Many paddle steamers still sail on Swiss lakes today.
Switzerland has one of the largest paddle steamer fleets in the world.
Later, paddle steamers were replaced by ships with propellers.

abschnitte.text: Deep inside the ship, water is heated in a **boiler** until it turns into steam. In the **steam engine**, the steam pushes pistons back and forth. Through a shaft, this movement turns the large **paddle wheels**. The paddles push the water backwards, and the ship moves forwards.

In 1807 Robert Fulton's steamship sailed on the Hudson River in America. Soon there were steamships on rivers and lakes all over the world. From 1823 the **“Guillaume Tell”**, the first steamship in Switzerland, sailed on Lake Geneva. On the Mississippi, **sternwheelers**, with one large wheel at the stern, became famous.

On **Lake Geneva** several splendid paddle steamers from the Belle Époque sail, for example the “Montreux” and the “La Suisse”. On **Lake Lucerne** there are five paddle steamers, including the “Uri” from 1901. There are others on Lake Zurich, Lake Thun, Lake Brienz and Lake Maggiore. Many people like to look into the engine room, where you can see the steam engine at work.

Paddle steamers need only a shallow **draught**, so they are well suited to rivers and lakes. But the paddle wheels are large and easily damaged. From the middle of the 19th century the **propeller** took over at sea. It sits under the water and is more efficient.

The old paddle steamers are valuable cultural treasures. Associations and shipping companies raise money to **restore** them. Many boilers are now heated with oil instead of coal. This means the ships can keep sailing and offer trips on the lake.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that produces movement using hot steam.
A large wheel with boards that push the water away.
How deep a ship sits in the water.
The period around 1900, known for beautiful and richly decorated buildings.

gewusst: The “Uri” on Lake Lucerne has been sailing since 1901, which makes it more than 120 years old.
More historic paddle steamers sail on Swiss lakes than in most other countries.

teile.einleitung: A keyboard shortcut is a command that you give by pressing several keys at the same time. Instead of clicking through menus with the mouse, you can do tasks such as copying or saving in a flash. Such combinations are also called shortcuts.
wichtigste: In Windows, Ctrl + Z undoes the last step.
With Ctrl + V you paste what you have copied.
Ctrl + X cuts.
Ctrl + A selects everything in a document.
In most programs, Ctrl + F opens the search for a word.
With Alt + Tab you switch between open windows in Windows.
In most programs, Ctrl + S saves.
On a Mac, the Command key usually takes over the role of the Ctrl key.

abschnitte.text: With a **keyboard shortcut**, you hold down one or more special keys and press another key as well. Important special keys are **Ctrl**, Alt and Shift; on German keyboards Ctrl is often called Strg, short for “Steuerung”. On their own these keys usually do nothing; only together with another key do they trigger a command. If you know the most important shortcuts, you work much faster at the computer.

The best-known shortcuts are to do with the **clipboard**, an invisible store for things you have copied. With Ctrl + C you copy something, with Ctrl + X you cut it, and with Ctrl + V you paste it again. The letters are next to each other on the keyboard so that you can reach them with one hand. Beforehand, Ctrl + A selects everything in a document.

With **Ctrl + Z** you undo the last step, which often saves you trouble. Ctrl + S saves your work, and Ctrl + F opens the search for a word. With **Alt + Tab** you switch between open windows in Windows. In many programs Ctrl + P opens printing, and with the Windows key and L you lock the computer when you go away for a moment.

On Apple computers, the **Command key** takes over the role of the Ctrl key for many shortcuts. It has the symbol ⌘, which is reminiscent of a loop with four eyelets. So on a Mac, copying is Command + C. The idea of cutting, copying and pasting with keyboard shortcuts was developed back in the 1970s and 1980s and became known through the first Apple computers with a mouse.

The **Swiss keyboard** has its own layout with keys for ä, ö, ü as well as é, è and à. That is why some characters such as brackets or the @ are in different places from a German keyboard. In many programs, the menus show the matching shortcut next to each command. A good trick is to learn a new shortcut every week and use it deliberately.

begriffe.erklaerung: A keyboard shortcut, a quick key combination.
An invisible store for copied or cut content.
The Control key, often called Strg on German keyboards.
The key with the symbol ⌘ on Apple keyboards.
Cancel the last step of your work.

gewusst: In Windows, Ctrl + Alt + Del calls up a special menu, for example for the Task Manager.
The symbol ⌘ on the Mac Command key comes from a sign used to mark places of interest.
With Ctrl + Shift + T you can reopen a tab you closed by mistake in the browser.

teile.einleitung: A sailing ship is a ship driven by the wind. The wind blows into large pieces of cloth, the sails, and pushes the ship forward. For centuries, sailing ships were the fastest way to travel across the seas.
wichtigste: A sailing ship is driven by the wind.
The sails hang from masts and are adjusted with ropes.
Many explorers used caravels.
With clever technique, a sailing ship can even travel at an angle against the wind.
The Swiss team Alinghi won the America's Cup in 2003.
Today most people sail in their free time or as a sport.

abschnitte.text: A sailing ship has a **hull**, one or more **masts** and sails made of cloth. All the ropes and masts together are called the **rigging**. Under the hull, a keel stops the ship drifting sideways or capsizing. It is steered with the rudder at the stern.

If the wind comes from behind, the ship is simply pushed along. If it blows from the side, the sail works like a wing and pulls the ship forward. No sailing ship can sail directly into the wind. That is why it sails in a zigzag; this is called **tacking**.

In the 15th and 16th centuries, Portuguese and Spanish seafarers used **caravels**. These nimble ships could sail well even when the wind was unfavourable. In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed to America with two caravels and one larger ship. Later the Dutch and the English built large merchant ships for the route to Asia.

In the 19th century the fast **clippers**, which brought tea from China to Europe, were famous. The “Cutty Sark” from 1869 can still be seen in London today. Huge cargo sailing ships were called windjammers. When steamships came along, the great sailing ships gradually disappeared.

People sail on many Swiss lakes, especially Lake Geneva, Lake Constance and Lake Zurich. Every year the **Bol d'Or** regatta takes place on Lake Geneva. The Geneva team **Alinghi**, owned by Ernesto Bertarelli, won the America's Cup in 2003 as the first European team and defended it in 2007. That was a sensation for a country without a sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the masts, sails and ropes of a sailing ship together.
Sailing in a zigzag against the wind.
A nimble sailing ship used by explorers in the 15th and 16th centuries.
A race between sailing boats.

gewusst: The America's Cup is one of the oldest sports trophies still contested in the world and dates from 1851.
Today some cargo ships are being fitted with large sails again to save fuel.

teile.einleitung: A server is a computer that provides data and services for other computers. When you open a website, watch a video or send a message, a server is working in the background. It is a bit like a waiter who waits for orders and delivers them.
wichtigste: A server is a computer that provides data.
Most servers on the internet work day and night.
When you watch a video, a server delivers the video to you.
Messages are often stored on a server before they reach the recipient.
Many people can fetch data from a server at the same time.
Servers need electricity and get warm, which is why server rooms are cooled.
If a website's server fails, the website can no longer be reached.

abschnitte.text: The word **server** comes from the English “to serve”. A server waits for requests and answers them. The device that asks is called the **client**, for example your mobile phone or laptop. This interplay is called the **client-server principle**. By “server” people sometimes mean the device and sometimes the program running on it.

When you open a website, a **web server** sends you the page. When you watch a video, a video server delivers the data piece by piece. Your chat messages first land on a server and are forwarded from there to your friend. Online games, email and cloud storage also work with servers. A good server can serve a huge number of people at the same time.

Large companies run thousands of servers in huge halls, the **data centres**. The servers are placed one above the other in cabinets called racks. They run day and night, all year round. Because they need a lot of **electricity** and get warm, they have to be cooled. Some data centres use their waste heat to heat homes or swimming pools.

If a server fails, a website, for example, can no longer be reached. That is why important services have **backup servers** that take over straight away. Emergency power systems make sure that servers keep running even during a power cut. Servers are popular targets for attackers, so they are protected with firewalls and updates. The data is backed up regularly.

The world's first **web server** was at CERN near Geneva from 1990. It ran the first website, which **Tim Berners-Lee** had programmed. It was a black computer made by the company NeXT, with a note stuck on it saying not to switch it off. Today there are many data centres in Switzerland, because the country is considered safe and politically stable. Some are even housed in former military facilities in the mountains.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer or program that provides data and services.
A device or program that requests something from the server.
A building with a great many servers.
Storage and programs that run on servers on the internet.

gewusst: The note on the first web server at CERN warned in English that the machine was a server and must not be switched off.
Large data centres can use as much electricity as a small town.
Some servers are cooled with water, similar to a car engine.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower is energy obtained from flowing or falling water. Centuries ago, water wheels were already driving mills; today hydropower stations produce electricity. In Switzerland, hydropower is the most important source of electricity.
wichtigste: Hydropower is a renewable energy source, like solar or wind power.
In a hydropower station, the water turns a turbine that drives a generator.
For more than a hundred years, Switzerland has obtained most of its electricity from hydropower.
Because it replaced the missing coal, hydropower was called “white coal”.
A pumped storage power station stores energy by pumping water uphill.
In 1769 Richard Arkwright invented the water frame, a spinning machine powered by water.
Hydropower helped Switzerland to industrialise early.

abschnitte.text: Water that flows downhill or falls from above has a lot of **kinetic energy**. This energy can be captured and used. In the past, **water wheels** drove mills, saws and hammer works. Today hydropower stations turn the power of water into electricity. Because the Sun keeps making water evaporate and fall again as rain, hydropower is **renewable**.

The water flows through pipes onto a **turbine** and makes it turn. The turbine is connected to a **generator**, which turns the rotation into electricity. The more water and the greater the drop, the more electricity is produced. Depending on the location, different turbines are used, such as the Pelton, Francis or Kaplan turbine. The electricity then flows through high-voltage lines to the consumers.

**Run-of-river power stations** are on rivers such as the Rhine and the Aare and supply electricity all the time. **Storage power stations** in the Alps hold back water in reservoirs behind high dams and release it when electricity is needed. **Pumped storage power stations** pump water up into an upper lake when there is surplus electricity. When electricity is needed later, it is let flow down again, so the power station works like a giant battery. Examples in Switzerland are Nant de Drance in Valais and Linth-Limmern in the canton of Glarus.

In the 18th century, in 1769, the Englishman Richard Arkwright invented the **water frame**, a spinning machine driven by water power. Because Switzerland has hardly any coal, many factories here were built on rivers and used water power. Together with the tradition of home working and exports, this helped Switzerland to **industrialise** early. Only the steam engine made factories elsewhere independent of water power. From about 1900, large power stations for producing electricity were built in Switzerland, and people spoke of **white coal**.

Thanks to the Alps, plenty of rain and glaciers, Switzerland has ideal conditions. There are about 700 larger hydropower stations here. They supply about 60 per cent of the country's own electricity (as of 2024). The highest dam is the **Grande Dixence** in Valais at 285 metres. One problem is that dams change rivers and block the way for fish, so **fish ladders** are built and care is taken to leave enough residual water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that is turned by the water.
A machine that turns rotation into electric current.
A power station that stores energy by pumping water into a higher lake.
A stepped waterway that lets fish swim past a power station.

gewusst: The largest hydropower station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze in China.
The caverns of the Nant de Drance pumped storage power station lie deep in the rock; the large machine hall is almost 200 metres long.
Even in ancient Rome, water wheels were used to grind grain.

teile.einleitung: Dance instructions describe step by step which movements you make in which order. This makes them surprisingly similar to a computer program. In computer science lessons, dances are used to learn what commands, sequences and repetitions are.
wichtigste: Like a program, dance instructions have steps in a fixed order.
With clap 2 times and turn 1 time, the whole thing 2 times, you clap 4 times.
With repeat 3 times hop and turn, you turn 3 times.
Instructions with 4 steps, danced 3 times, make 12 steps.
With right, left, right, left, the 5th step is right again.
A foot symbol in dance instructions stands for stamping.
So that everyone dances at the same time, the group needs the same beat.
In musical statues, everyone stands completely still as soon as the music stops.

abschnitte.text: **Dance instructions** are a list of commands such as clap, hop, turn or stamp. You carry them out in a fixed order, just as a computer carries out the commands of a program. In computer science, such exact step-by-step instructions are called an **algorithm**. If you swap two steps, the whole dance looks different, just as a program then does something different.

Many dances consist of parts that repeat. Instead of writing everything down several times, the instructions say, for example: repeat 3 times hop, turn. In computer science this is called a **loop**. With clap 2 times and turn 1 time, the whole thing repeated 2 times, you clap 4 times altogether. If instructions have 4 steps and you dance them 3 times, that makes 12 steps.

Dance instructions for children often show **symbols** instead of words: a hand for clap, a foot for stamp, an arrow for turn. This means you can understand them even without reading. There are often **patterns** such as right, left, right, left. If you recognise the pattern, you also know that the 5th step is right again.

So that everyone in a group dances at the same time, they need the same **beat**. The beat is like a clock that sets the rhythm; often you count out loud one, two, three, four. In **musical statues** there is a rule: when the music stops, everyone stands completely still. In computer science, such an if-then rule is called a **condition**.

Professionals also write dances down so that they can be danced exactly again later. The dancer **Rudolf von Laban** developed his own dance notation for this, Labanotation. Around 1913 he also gave courses on Monte Verità near Ascona in Ticino. Today dances are mostly recorded on video, and robots can even dance by themselves with programmed dance steps.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions.
A part that is repeated several times.
An if-then rule that decides what happens.
A steady rhythm that everyone dances to.
The planned sequence of all the steps of a dance.

gewusst: Someone who invents a choreography is called a choreographer.
In Swiss folk dance there are long-established sequences of steps that are passed down from generation to generation.
Computers and robots can also dance if you give them the steps as a program.

teile.einleitung: A satellite is a spacecraft that circles the Earth in space on a fixed path. Satellites provide weather pictures, transmit television and phone calls and show us the way with navigation. The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, went into space in 1957.
wichtigste: An artificial satellite is a device that circles the Earth in an orbit.
The first artificial satellite was Sputnik 1 in 1957.
Geostationary satellites circle about 35,800 kilometres above the equator.
Navigation satellites such as those of Galileo help you find your own location.
In 2009 SwissCube was the first satellite built entirely in Switzerland.
The space mission CHEOPS is led by the University of Bern.
The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth.

abschnitte.text: A **satellite** is a celestial body or a device that circles a larger body. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth. Artificial satellites are taken into space by rockets. They do not fall down because they fly so fast that, because of the curve of the Earth, they keep falling past it.

On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the first artificial satellite, into space. It was a metal ball about 58 centimetres across and sent out a beeping radio signal. The USA was shocked, and so the space race between the two superpowers began. Only a few months later came the first American satellite, Explorer 1.

Many satellites fly a few hundred kilometres up; the International Space Station ISS is at about 400 kilometres. **Geostationary** satellites circle about 35,800 kilometres above the equator. They take exactly as long for one orbit as the Earth takes to turn once, so they seem to stand still in the sky. That is why satellite dishes for television can be pointed at them in a fixed position.

**Weather satellites** photograph clouds and help with weather forecasts. Communication satellites transmit television programmes, phone calls and the internet. Navigation satellites, such as those of the European system **Galileo**, help you find your exact location. Research satellites and space telescopes such as Hubble observe distant stars and galaxies.

In 2009 **SwissCube** was launched, a small cube-shaped satellite built by students at EPFL in Lausanne. The University of Bern leads the **CHEOPS** mission, which has been studying planets around other stars since 2019. The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier helped repair the Hubble Space Telescope in 1993 and 1999. Switzerland is a founding member of the European Space Agency ESA.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path on which a satellite circles the Earth.
A satellite that seems always to stay above the same point on Earth.
Old satellites and pieces of wreckage that circle the Earth uselessly.
A vehicle that carries satellites into space.

gewusst: Today several thousand active satellites circle the Earth, more than ever before.
At night you can see some satellites with the naked eye as moving points of light in the sky.
Sputnik 1 circled the Earth about every 96 minutes.

teile.einleitung: Hydrogen is the lightest and most common chemical element in the universe. In the periodic table it has the atomic number 1 and the symbol H. As an energy carrier, hydrogen could make lorries, trains and factories more climate-friendly in future.
wichtigste: In the periodic table, hydrogen has the atomic number 1.
Shortly after the Big Bang, mainly hydrogen and helium were formed.
The Sun shines because hydrogen fuses into helium inside it.
With electricity, water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen; this is called electrolysis.
A fuel cell turns the energy of hydrogen and oxygen directly into electricity.
Only water comes out of the exhaust of a fuel cell vehicle.
Hydrogen catches fire very easily and must be handled carefully.

abschnitte.text: Hydrogen is the simplest element; its atom consists of just one **proton** and one **electron**. It has the atomic number 1 and the chemical symbol H. At normal temperature, hydrogen is a colourless, odourless gas. It only becomes liquid at minus 253 degrees. Niels Bohr developed his **atomic model**, in which electrons circle the nucleus in fixed shells, using the hydrogen atom.

Shortly after the **Big Bang**, mainly hydrogen and helium were formed, hydrogen most of all. At that time helium made up about 25 per cent of the mass of normal matter, and almost all the rest was hydrogen. The first stars were also made mainly of these two gases. Our Sun shines because, inside it, hydrogen fuses into helium through **nuclear fusion**. Hydrogen is still the most common element in the universe today.

The English scientist Henry **Cavendish** described hydrogen as a separate substance in 1766. The Frenchman Antoine Lavoisier later gave it its name, which means “water maker”. This is because when hydrogen burns with oxygen, **water** is formed. On Earth, hydrogen hardly ever occurs on its own but is usually bound up, above all in water. All living things also contain a lot of hydrogen.

With electricity, water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen; this is called **electrolysis**. If the electricity comes from the sun, wind or water, it is called **green hydrogen**. In a **fuel cell**, hydrogen and oxygen combine again, producing electricity and water. A fuel cell vehicle therefore gives off only water from its exhaust. In Switzerland, lorries have been running on hydrogen since 2020, among others for retailers.

Hydrogen catches fire very easily and can form an explosive mixture with air. In 1937 the hydrogen-filled airship **Hindenburg** went up in flames in the USA. Today strict safety rules apply to tanks and filling stations. One problem is that a lot of energy is lost when hydrogen is produced. In addition, most hydrogen is still made from natural gas; it is called **grey hydrogen**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen with the help of electricity.
A device that produces electricity directly from hydrogen and oxygen.
The joining of light atomic nuclei, which releases a great deal of energy.
The number of an element in the periodic table; it shows the number of protons in the nucleus.

gewusst: A balloon filled with hydrogen rises even faster than one filled with helium.
About two thirds of all the atoms in your body are hydrogen atoms.
Every second, the Sun turns hundreds of millions of tonnes of hydrogen into helium.

teile.einleitung: The World Wide Web, WWW or Web for short, is the worldwide network of web pages connected to one another by links. It was invented by the Briton Tim Berners-Lee at the CERN research centre in Geneva. Today billions of people use the Web every day for learning, playing and communicating.
wichtigste: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web.
The Web was created at the end of the 1980s at CERN in Geneva.
The structure of web pages is described in the language HTML.
You use a browser to display web pages.
A hyperlink is a clickable word or picture that leads to another page.
The Web is not the same as the internet, but a service that uses the internet.
In 1993 CERN made the Web technology freely available to everyone.

abschnitte.text: The World Wide Web is a huge collection of **web pages** stored on computers all over the world. These pages are linked by **hyperlinks**, so you can jump from one page to the next with a click. That is why it is called a net or web. The Web runs on the **internet**, the network of cables, radio links and computers underneath it. E-mail and online games also use the internet but are not part of the Web.

Tim Berners-Lee worked as a computer scientist at **CERN**, the large research centre for particle physics near Geneva. Thousands of researchers worked there with different computers, and it was difficult to exchange information. In March 1989 Berners-Lee therefore proposed a system of linked documents. At the end of 1990 the first web page ran on his computer, a NeXT machine. Together with the Belgian Robert Cailliau, he made the idea known.

The Web is based on three inventions by Berners-Lee. **HTML** describes how a page is built, that is where headings, texts, pictures and links go. Every page has its own address, the **URL**, for example an address beginning with https. The HTTP protocol sets out how the browser requests a page from a server and receives it. These three building blocks are still used today.

A **browser** is a program that fetches and displays web pages, for example Firefox, Chrome, Safari or Edge. The pages themselves are stored on **servers**, computers that can be reached around the clock. When you enter an address, the browser sends a request and the server sends the page back. Search engines help you find the right one among billions of pages. From 1993 the Mosaic browser made the Web popular with many people thanks to pictures and simple controls.

On 30 April 1993 CERN declared that anyone could use the Web technology free of charge. Berners-Lee and CERN thus gave up patents and fees. That is why the Web was able to spread very quickly. In 1994 Berners-Lee founded the W3C, a body that still develops the rules for the Web today. He was knighted by the British Queen for his invention.

On the Web you find a great deal of knowledge, but also false information and advertising. So you should check who wrote a page and whether other sources say the same. A small padlock next to the address shows that the connection is **encrypted**. You only enter passwords and personal data on trustworthy sites. If you are unsure, it is best to ask an adult.

begriffe.erklaerung: A clickable word or picture that leads to another web page.
The language used to describe the structure of a web page.
A program you can use to display web pages.
The address of a web page.
A computer that stores web pages and sends them out on request.

gewusst: The very first web page in the world had the address info.cern.ch and can still be viewed today.
Berners-Lee's NeXT computer had a note stuck on it warning people not to switch it off, because it was the first web server.
The Web was actually invented so that physicists could share their research results more easily.

teile.einleitung: A Trojan is a computer program that looks useful or harmless but secretly does damage. Its name is a reminder of a famous trick from an ancient Greek legend. If you know how Trojans work, you can protect yourself against them much better.
wichtigste: A Trojan disguises itself as a useful program and secretly does damage.
The name comes from the wooden horse in the legend of the war over Troy.
Unlike a computer virus, a Trojan usually does not copy itself.
Trojans especially often disguise themselves as free games or programs.
A Trojan with a back door lets attackers control the computer remotely.
Banking Trojans are after login details for online banking.
The best way to protect yourself is to download programs only from trustworthy sources.

abschnitte.text: In the Greek legend, the Greeks besieged the city of **Troy** for ten years without success. Then they built a huge **wooden horse** and hid soldiers inside it. The Trojans thought the horse was a gift and pulled it into their city. In the night the soldiers climbed out and opened the city gates. This is exactly how a Trojan works in the computer: it is brought in voluntarily and then opens the door to the attackers.

A Trojan is a form of **malicious software**, malware for short. It looks like a normal program, for example a game, a tool or an update. While you are using the program, a second, harmful part is secretly running in the background. The user often notices nothing for a long time.

A **computer virus** attaches itself to other files and spreads further by itself. A Trojan usually cannot do this. It needs a person to download and start it. That is why the attackers rely on tricks and deception; this is called **social engineering**.

A Trojan with a **backdoor** allows attackers to control the computer remotely. A **downloader** secretly loads more malicious programs from the internet. A **banking Trojan** spies out passwords and login details for online banking. Other Trojans record keystrokes or encrypt files in order to extort a ransom.

Only download programs and apps from trustworthy sources, such as the official website or the official app store. Be suspicious if something expensive is suddenly offered for free. Don't open unknown attachments in emails or messages. Keep your operating system up to date and use an **antivirus program**. In Switzerland, the Federal Office for Cybersecurity provides information about current dangers on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: Programs that were made to harm computers or people.
A secret back door through which strangers can get into a computer.
A Trojan that secretly loads more malicious programs.
Tricks used to get people to do something careless.
A program that recognises and removes malware.

gewusst: The story of the Trojan Horse is about 3,000 years old and is already told in the works of Homer and Virgil.
Many Trojans today disguise themselves as fake apps or as supposed cheats for popular games.
A Trojan can stay on a computer unnoticed for weeks before it becomes active.

teile.einleitung: A rocket is a flying object that forces hot gases out backwards with great power and so flies forwards. Only with rockets can people, satellites and space probes reach space. Rockets even work where there is no air.
wichtigste: A rocket pushes hot gases out backwards and so flies in the opposite direction.
This principle is called recoil.
People fly into space with rockets.
In 1957 a rocket took the first satellite, Sputnik 1, into space.
The huge Saturn V took astronauts to the Moon.
Europe sends satellites into space with Ariane rockets.
The Swiss Claude Nicollier flew into space four times on the Space Shuttle.

abschnitte.text: In the rocket, **fuel** and oxygen burn together to form hot gases. These stream out of the nozzle downwards or backwards at great speed. The **recoil** pushes the rocket in the opposite direction, just like a balloon with air escaping from it. An octopus, by the way, swims on the same principle by pushing water out through a funnel.

Large rockets are made up of several **stages** stacked on top of each other. When a stage has used up its fuel, it is dropped so that the rocket becomes lighter. Right at the top sits the payload, for example a satellite or a space capsule with astronauts. Before launch, people count backwards to zero in the **countdown**.

Many hundreds of years ago the Chinese were already using gunpowder rockets as fireworks and weapons. In 1926 the American Robert Goddard launched the first rocket with liquid fuel. On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put **Sputnik 1** into space, which also caused military concern, because rockets like this could carry nuclear warheads as far as the USA. In 1969 the **Saturn V** with Apollo 11 took the first people to the Moon.

Before people flew into space, animals were sent up on rockets. In 1949 the **rhesus monkey Albert II** became the first primate in space. In 1959 the female rhesus monkey Able and the squirrel monkey Miss Baker flew into space on a Jupiter rocket and came back alive. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space.

Europe launches its **Ariane** rockets from the Kourou spaceport in French Guiana in South America. Swiss companies build important parts for them, for example the nose cone in which the satellites sit protected. **Claude Nicollier** from Vaud flew into space four times on the Space Shuttle between 1992 and 1999. Today some rockets land again after launch and can be used again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force created when something is pushed out forcefully in one direction.
A part of a rocket with its own engine, which is dropped.
What the rocket carries, such as a satellite.
Counting backwards to the launch.

gewusst: The Saturn V was about 110 metres tall, taller than a 30-storey building.
To get into orbit around the Earth, a rocket has to reach a speed of about 28,000 km/h.
Rockets do not need air because they carry their own oxygen with them.

teile.einleitung: The Unified Modeling Language, UML for short, is a graphical language used to plan and describe software. Instead of only writing text, developers draw diagrams with fixed symbols. This lets everyone in the team see at a glance how a program is built and how it works.
wichtigste: UML is a standardised language of diagrams for describing software.
It is maintained by the Object Management Group.
Grady Booch, James Rumbaugh and Ivar Jacobson are known as the “Three Amigos” of UML.
UML 2.5 defines 14 types of diagram.
In a class diagram, a minus sign stands for a private attribute.
Inheritance is drawn as an arrow with an empty triangular head.
The sequence diagram shows the order in time of messages between objects.

abschnitte.text: UML is something like the **blueprint** for software. An architect draws a plan before a house is built, and in the same way experts plan a program with UML diagrams. The symbols are laid down exactly so that everyone understands them in the same way. UML is not a programming language but a **modelling language**.

In the 1990s there were many different methods of drawing software. **Grady Booch**, James Rumbaugh and Ivar Jacobson brought their approaches together and were therefore called the “Three Amigos”. In 1997 the **Object Management Group**, OMG for short, adopted UML as a standard. Since 2005 there has been the heavily revised version UML 2, and the current version, UML 2.5, has 14 types of diagram.

The best-known UML diagram is the **class diagram**. Each class is a rectangle with three parts: name, attributes and methods. In front of each attribute there is a sign for its visibility, a plus for public and a minus for private. A line with an empty triangular head means **inheritance**, and a line with a filled diamond means **composition**, that is, a part that cannot exist without its whole.

Other diagrams show what happens in a program. The **sequence diagram** shows from top to bottom which messages objects exchange one after another. The **use case diagram** shows actors as stick figures and the functions a system provides for them. An activity diagram looks similar to a flowchart with decisions.

UML is used in companies, at universities and in training, including in Switzerland, for example in computer science apprenticeships. With UML you can discuss a program before writing a single line of code. Some tools can even generate program code automatically from UML diagrams. In big projects, the diagrams also serve as **documentation** for later changes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simplified representation of something complicated.
A blueprint for objects of the same kind in a program.
A property of an object, for example name or age.
A class takes on properties from another class.
Someone or something that works with a system, such as a customer.

gewusst: UML is also recognised as an international ISO standard.
The 14 diagram types of UML 2.5 are divided into structure diagrams and behaviour diagrams.
In a use case diagram, a person is simply drawn as a stick figure.

teile.einleitung: An order says what comes first, what comes next and what comes at the end. It is very important in everyday life and in programming, because steps in the wrong order often lead to a wrong result. A computer always carries out commands exactly in the order in which they are written.
wichtigste: The sequence “first, then, next, finally” is called an order.
When washing your hands: wet them, soap them, rinse them.
When planting, you first dig a hole, put the seed in and then water it.
Before you ride your bike, you put on your helmet first.
A computer carries out the commands A, B and C one after another: A, then B, then C.
If a robot turns too early, it moves off in a different direction.
When sending a letter, you post it last.

abschnitte.text: An **order** is the sequence in which things happen one after another. Words like “first”, “then”, “next” and “finally” help to describe it. Sometimes the order doesn't matter, for example whether you put on your left or your right shoe first. But often it is crucial, for example with socks and shoes.

Many activities have a fixed sequence of **steps**. When washing your hands, you wet them, soap them and rinse them. For a slice of bread and butter, you first take the slice of bread and then spread the butter on it. When baking a cake, taking it out of the oven comes right at the end.

A computer works through commands **one after another** from top to bottom. If the commands A, B and C are written one below the other, it first carries out A, then B and then C. If a robot is supposed to move forward two squares first and then turn right, you must not swap the commands. Otherwise it turns first and moves off in a completely different direction.

Some steps build on each other, which means one needs the result of the other. You can only plant a seed once the hole has been dug. You can only post a letter once it has been written, put in an envelope and stamped. If you think like this, you are already practising **algorithmic thinking**, which is important in programming.

With picture stories you can practise putting events in the right order. Recipes, craft instructions and game rules are also good examples. At school, children learn in the subject media and computer science to write instructions for robots such as the Bee-Bot. You quickly notice how exact **instructions** have to be.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sequence in which things happen one after another.
A single part of an action or a process.
A description of how to do something step by step.
An exact sequence of steps for solving a task.

gewusst: Even a simple recipe often contains more than ten steps in a fixed order.
A computer always sticks to the order, even when it is obviously wrong.

teile.einleitung: A structogram is a drawing that shows the steps of a program clearly. It consists of rectangles placed one below the other and nested inside each other. After its inventors it is also called a Nassi-Shneiderman diagram.
wichtigste: After its inventors, a structogram is also called a Nassi-Shneiderman diagram.
Structograms were invented in the 1970s.
A structogram is built from rectangles placed one below the other.
Unlike in a flowchart, there are no arrows that jump back and forth anywhere.
A branch is shown with a triangle at the top and two columns for yes and no.
In a loop, a block surrounds the repeated instructions from the left.
Instructions that are simply placed one below the other form a sequence.

abschnitte.text: Before writing a program, it helps to draw the **algorithm** first. A **structogram** shows the steps as rectangles that are read from top to bottom. Each rectangle contains an instruction, for example read in a number or output the result. Because it is drawn independently of any particular programming language, everyone understands it.

The structogram was invented by the two Americans **Isaac Nassi** and **Ben Shneiderman** at the beginning of the 1970s. At that time many experts wanted to get away from confusing programs in which there were wild jumps back and forth. This movement was called **structured programming**. In Germany the symbols for structograms were later laid down in a DIN standard.

The **sequence** consists of instructions that are simply placed one below the other and carried out one after another. A **branch** (if, then, else) is drawn with a triangle at the top and two columns for yes and no. In a **loop**, a block surrounds the repeated instructions from the left, like an upside-down L. With these three building blocks, any algorithm can be shown.

A **flowchart** connects boxes with arrows. These arrows can jump back and forth anywhere, which quickly leads to a muddle in large programs. In a structogram there are no such arrows; the steps always go from top to bottom. On the other hand, a structogram is a bit more laborious to draw and harder to change afterwards.

A structogram contains three steps: number gets the value 4, then repeat 3 times number gets number plus 2, then output number. At the start, number equals 4. After the first repetition it is 6, after the second 8 and after the third **10**. This number is output at the end. Swiss pupils also practise such tasks in the subject **media and computer science**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
Instructions that are carried out one after another.
A point at which a different route is taken depending on a condition.
Instructions that are repeated several times.
A diagram of steps with boxes and arrows.

gewusst: Ben Shneiderman later became known above all as a researcher on user-friendly computer interfaces.
A structogram always fits exactly into one single large rectangle.

teile.einleitung: A car, or automobile, is a vehicle that usually has four wheels and moves with its own engine. The word automobile means something like self-moving. Since Carl Benz built his first car in 1886, it has greatly changed people's lives.
wichtigste: Carl Benz built the first modern car in 1886.
Cars run on a combustion engine, an electric motor or both.
In Switzerland you need a motorway vignette to drive on the motorway.
In Switzerland you can apply for a learner's permit for a car from the age of 17.
If you lease a car, you pay monthly to use it, but it does not belong to you.
In winter, stone martens like to visit warm car engines and sometimes bite through cables.
Cars give people freedom, but they also cause exhaust fumes, noise and traffic jams.

abschnitte.text: A car has a **body**, a shell made of sheet metal or plastic, and usually four wheels. An engine drives the wheels, and you steer with the steering wheel. You speed up with the accelerator and stop with the brake. Modern cars have many safety systems such as **airbags**, seat belts and brake assistants.

In 1886 **Carl Benz** applied for the patent for his motor car, which is regarded as the first modern car. At first cars were expensive and only a few people owned one. From 1913 Henry Ford built cars on an **assembly line**, which made them much cheaper. Today there are well over a billion cars worldwide.

For a long time almost all cars ran on **petrol** or diesel in a combustion engine. An electric car runs on electricity from a battery and gives off no exhaust fumes while driving. Hybrid cars have both, a combustion engine and an electric motor. The energy of movement of a moving car is called **kinetic energy**.

In Switzerland you can apply for a **learner's permit** from the age of 17, and you can take the test at 18 at the earliest. If you want to drive on the motorway, you need a **motorway vignette**, which is valid for one year and costs 40 francs. On motorways the limit is usually 120 km/h, outside built-up areas 80 and in built-up areas 50 km/h. Children must travel in a child seat until they are 12 years old or 150 centimetres tall.

A car costs a lot of money, not only when you buy it but also for petrol or electricity, insurance, taxes and repairs. Some people buy a car with a **consumer loan**, which is borrowed money that you pay back with interest. With **leasing** you pay every month to use the car, but it belongs to the leasing company. An alternative is car sharing, where many people share cars.

In winter, the **stone marten** likes to visit warm engine compartments and sometimes bites through cables and hoses. Cars produce exhaust fumes that contribute to climate change, and noise. Every year many animals such as deer, foxes and hedgehogs are run over on the roads. That is why wildlife bridges are built and public transport is promoted.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sticker on the windscreen that shows you have paid the motorway fee.
A permit that lets you practise driving with someone accompanying you.
Using a car for a monthly fee without owning it.
The outer shell of a car.
The energy a body has because it is moving.

gewusst: The heart of a blue whale is about as big as a small car.
About 4.7 million passenger cars are registered in Switzerland (2024).
The first cars were hardly faster than a running person.

teile.einleitung: An electric car does not run on petrol or diesel but on electricity from a large battery. Instead of going to a petrol station, you charge it at a charging station or at a socket at home. Because it gives off no exhaust fumes while driving, it is seen as an important part of more climate-friendly transport.
wichtigste: An electric car runs on electricity from a battery.
Instead of petrol, an electric car is filled up with electricity.
An electric motor drives the wheels and is very quiet.
When braking, the electric motor can produce electricity again.
Electric cars give off no exhaust fumes while driving.
There were electric cars as early as 1900, but they were then pushed out by petrol cars.
In Switzerland about one in five new cars is a fully electric car (2024).

abschnitte.text: Instead of a fuel tank and combustion engine, an **electric car** has a **battery** and one or more electric motors. The battery usually lies flat in the floor of the car and is very heavy. It is made up of thousands of small battery cells. An electric car has no gearbox with lots of gears and needs fewer oil changes and less maintenance.

The **electric motor** turns electrical energy directly into movement. It is much more efficient than a petrol engine, which loses a large part of its energy as heat. When braking, the motor works the other way round as a generator and produces electricity again; this is called **regenerative braking**. In this way part of the energy of movement is fed back into the battery.

At home you can charge the car overnight at a **wallbox** in the garage. On the road there are fast charging stations where the battery is mostly full in about half an hour. The **range** of modern electric cars is often 300 to 600 kilometres. Switzerland now has thousands of public charging stations.
