Electric cars are older than many people think. In 1899 the Belgian electric car **La Jamais Contente** became the first car to go faster than 100 km/h. Because petrol was cheap and petrol cars could travel further, electric cars then almost completely disappeared. Only with better lithium-ion batteries did they become popular again from about 2010.

Electric cars give off no **exhaust fumes** while driving and are quieter. How climate-friendly they are depends on where the electricity comes from. In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from hydropower, which is good for electric cars. However, making the batteries requires raw materials such as **lithium**, nickel and cobalt, and mining them can cause environmental problems.

The number of electric cars in Switzerland is growing fast. About one in five new cars sold in 2024 was a fully electric car. Many municipalities and companies are building charging stations, and PostBuses and delivery vans are also increasingly electric. An electric car uses about 15 to 20 kilowatt hours of electricity for 100 kilometres.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rechargeable store for electrical energy.
Recovering electricity when braking.
How far an electric car can go on one battery charge.
A place where you charge an electric car with electricity.
A unit of measurement for electrical energy.

gewusst: Around 1900, some cities in the USA had more electric cars than petrol cars.
Electric cars are so quiet that at low speeds they have to make an artificial sound so that pedestrians can hear them.
An electric car can accelerate especially strongly when pulling away, because the motor has its full power immediately.

teile.einleitung: Copyright protects works that people have created, for example music, texts, pictures, films or computer programs. It lays down that the creator may decide for themselves what happens with their work. In Switzerland this is regulated by a law of its own.
wichtigste: The Swiss Copyright Act (URG) protects works such as music, texts and pictures.
In Switzerland a work is usually protected until 70 years after the creator's death.
After that a work is in the public domain and may be used freely.
Copyright does not protect a mere idea.
If you quote someone else's text, you must always give the source.
If you pass off someone else's work as your own, you are committing plagiarism.
Offering protected music publicly for download is forbidden.

abschnitte.text: A **creator** is the person who made a work, for example a singer, an author or a photographer. **Copyright** gives them the right to decide whether and how their work is copied, sold or shown. This way artists can earn money with their work. A work is protected automatically as soon as it has been created; you don't have to register it anywhere.

In Switzerland the **Copyright Act**, URG for short, from 1992 applies. It protects works with their own personal character, that is, music, texts, pictures, films, buildings and software. Since a revision in 2020, simple photos have also been protected. Societies such as SUISA collect money for musicians when their songs are played on the radio or at concerts.

A work is usually protected until **70 years** after the creator's death. After that it enters the **public domain**, which means everyone may use it freely. That is why, for example, pictures by Albert Anker or fairy tales by the Brothers Grimm may be used freely today. For computer programs, a shorter period of protection of 50 years applies in Switzerland.

A mere **idea** is not protected, only the concrete way it is carried out. So anyone may have the idea of a story about a young wizard, but copying out a whole book is not allowed. Pure facts such as “The Rhine flows through Basel” are not protected either. Laws and official documents are also free.

For private use you may use many things in Switzerland, for example downloading a song for yourself. But it is forbidden to offer protected music or films **publicly** for download. If you show pictures from the internet on your own website or on social networks, you usually need permission. Many creators allow their work to be used with so-called Creative Commons licences, provided you give their name.

At school you may use short passages from other people's texts if you **quote** them properly. To do this, you put the quotation in quotation marks and give the source. If, on the other hand, you pass off someone else's work as your own, you are committing **plagiarism**. That is unfair and can lead to bad marks or penalties at school and university.

begriffe.erklaerung: The person who made a work.
No longer protected and free for everyone to use.
Someone else's work is passed off as your own.
A passage taken word for word, with the source given.
Permission to use a work under certain conditions.

gewusst: The © symbol is not necessary in Switzerland; a work is protected even without it.
A photo you take yourself with your phone is also protected, and you are then its creator.
Works by Wilhelm Busch, such as “Max and Moritz”, have long been in the public domain.

teile.einleitung: A steam engine is a machine driven by hot steam. It turns the heat from burning fuel into movement. Without it there would have been no Industrial Revolution with its factories, steam locomotives and steamships.
wichtigste: A steam engine is driven by hot steam.
In 1712 Thomas Newcomen built the first workable steam engine.
The first steam engines mainly pumped water out of mines.
James Watt improved the steam engine decisively and patented it in 1769.
The fuel burned was mainly coal.
The steam engine was the driving force of the Industrial Revolution.
The unit of power, the watt, is named after James Watt.

abschnitte.text: In a **boiler**, water is heated by a fire until it turns into steam. Steam takes up much more space than water and therefore pushes hard against a movable **piston** in a cylinder. The piston moves back and forth. Using a rod and a flywheel, this is turned into a rotating movement that drives wheels, pumps or machines.

In 1712 the Englishman **Thomas Newcomen** built the first steam engine that really worked reliably. It was used mainly in coal and tin mines, where groundwater kept flowing into the tunnels. The engine pumped this water up so that the miners could dig deeper. However, it was huge and slow and used a great deal of coal.

The Scot **James Watt** realised that Newcomen's engine wasted a lot of energy because the cylinder was cooled down again and again. He invented a separate **condenser**, in which the steam is cooled outside the cylinder. In 1769 he patented his improved engine. It needed only about a quarter of the coal and could later also supply rotating movement for factories. To show how strong his engines were, Watt compared them with horses and introduced the unit **horsepower**.

The **Industrial Revolution** is the name for the change to working with machines and factories from the 18th century onwards. Before that, factories needed a water wheel and therefore had to stand beside a river. With the steam engine they could be built anywhere, for example in towns or next to coal pits. Spinning and weaving mills now produced much more cloth in much less time.

At the beginning of the 19th century, steam engines were put on wheels, and so the **steam locomotive** was born. Steamships also now sailed across seas and lakes. The first railway entirely on Swiss soil ran between Zurich and Baden in 1847 and was called the “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn”. Historic paddle steamers still sail on many Swiss lakes today, for example Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva.

Today our machines are mostly driven by electric motors and combustion engines. But the principle of steam has not disappeared. In many power stations, steam turbines turn the generators that produce electricity. In honour of James Watt, the unit of power is called the **watt**, which you will find on every light bulb and every hairdryer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movable part in the cylinder that the steam pushes back and forth.
A container in which steam is cooled and turns back into water.
The period from the 18th century in which machines and factories replaced handwork.
An old unit of power, abbreviated hp.

gewusst: Even in ancient Greece, Hero of Alexandria built a small steam ball that spun round, but only as a toy.
The “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn” got its name because servants could use it to bring fresh pastries from Baden to Zurich.
The steamships on Lake Geneva are among the largest paddle steamer fleets in the world.

teile.einleitung: A fact file is a short, clear collection of the most important details about a person, an animal or a thing. Instead of long sentences it has keywords under clear headings such as name, size or habitat. This lets you take in the most important information at a glance.
wichtigste: A fact file contains important details in a short, clear form.
An animal fact file includes details such as size and food.
A fact file about you includes, for example, your name and age.
A fact file often also shows a picture.
Under “Habitat”, the fact file for a squirrel says, for example, “forest”.
Your address has no place in a fact file on the internet.
In the past, the police used wanted posters to search for wanted people.

abschnitte.text: A **fact file** sums up the most important things about a topic in **keywords**. It is divided into boxes with headings so that you can find details quickly. There are fact files about animals, plants, countries, famous people or yourself. At school they are a popular way of organising knowledge.

An animal fact file has headings such as name, appearance, size, **habitat**, food and enemies. For the squirrel, under habitat it says “forest” and under food something like “nuts, seeds and cones”. From details such as “lives in water, has fins, breathes with gills” you can guess that it is about a fish. A photo or a drawing makes the fact file clearer.

A personal fact file includes your name, age, hobbies, favourite food or favourite colour. Such fact files are often found in friendship books or at the start of the school year. If a fact file is published on the **internet**, your address, phone number and school do not belong in it. A made-up name or just your first name is safer there.

abschnitte.titel: How to write a fact file
abschnitte.text: First collect information from books, encyclopedias or trustworthy websites. Then think of suitable **headings** and write short keywords under them instead of whole sentences. Make sure that all the details are correct, and note down where you got them from. Finally you can add a picture and lay the whole thing out clearly.

In the past, the police used wanted posters, called “Steckbriefe” in German, to search for **wanted people**. They contained a description of the person's appearance, often a picture and sometimes a reward. Such posters were put up in public on walls and doors. Today this is called a manhunt, and it often also runs on the internet and on television.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short overview of the most important details about a topic.
A single word or short phrase instead of a whole sentence.
The surroundings in which an animal or a plant lives.
The police's search for a person.

gewusst: Well-known wanted posters from the Wild West often had the English word “Wanted” in big letters.
Databases in the computer are also divided into fixed fields, much like fact files.

teile.einleitung: Routing is deciding the route that data packets take through a network. On the internet, your data travels through many intermediate stations, the routers, until it arrives at its destination. This works much like the post office, which takes a letter to the recipient via several sorting centres.
wichtigste: Routing decides which route data packets take to reach their destination.
Routers read the destination address of each packet and send it to the next station.
If there are several matching routes, the router chooses the most specific one.
In IPv4 the default route is 0.0.0.0/0.
The BGP protocol exchanges routes between the autonomous systems of the internet.
With RIP, a destination counts as unreachable from 16 hops.
With traceroute you can see the routers on the way to a destination.
Home routers use network address translation to hide many private addresses behind one public one.

abschnitte.text: On the internet, data is split into small **packets**. Each packet carries a destination address, the **IP address**. A **router** is a device that receives packets and decides where to send them next. To do this, it looks in its **routing table**. Each step from one router to the next is called a hop.

The routing table says which address ranges can be reached by which route. If several entries match, the most specific one wins; this is called **longest prefix match**. If a router knows, for example, 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16, it sends a packet for 10.1.2.3 via the route 10.1.0.0/16. If no entry matches at all, it takes the **default route** 0.0.0.0/0. This is like a signpost saying “all other directions”.

With **static routing**, an administrator enters the routes by hand. This is simple, but it does not adapt if a line fails. With **dynamic routing**, routers exchange information about routes themselves. An old protocol for this is RIP, which counts the hops and regards a destination as unreachable from 16 hops. With such distance-vector protocols, the **count-to-infinity** problem can occur when routers report out-of-date distances to each other.

The internet consists of many tens of thousands of networks belonging to companies, universities and providers. Each large network is called an **autonomous system**. Between these networks, routes are exchanged with the protocol **BGP**, the Border Gateway Protocol. In Switzerland, many providers connect at exchange points, for example in Zurich and Geneva. Mistakes with BGP can mean that large websites cannot be reached worldwide for hours.

There is a router at home too, usually from the internet provider. All the devices in the household have private addresses, for example 192.168.1.20. To the outside world, the router appears with a single public address. This method is called **network address translation**, NAT for short. The router remembers which answer belongs to which device.

With the tool **traceroute** you can see which routers a packet travels through to reach its destination. In Windows the command is called tracert. It often turns out that a packet from Switzerland to an American website passes through 10 to 20 stations. Even so, the whole journey usually takes only a fraction of a second. Packets of the same message can even take different routes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that passes data packets on between networks.
The address of a device on the internet.
A step from one router to the next.
A list in the router of which destinations can be reached by which route.
A protocol with which the large networks of the internet exchange their routes.

gewusst: In October 2021, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp could not be reached for about six hours because of a BGP mistake.
The internet was built so that data automatically finds another route if something fails.
Every packet has a counter for its lifetime so that it does not wander round in circles endlessly.

teile.einleitung: The keyboard is the most important input device for typing letters, numbers and commands into a computer. Its layout comes from the typewriter of the 19th century. In Switzerland the top row of letters begins with QWERTZ.
wichtigste: With the keyboard you enter text, numbers and commands into the computer.
The Swiss keyboard is called a QWERTZ keyboard after its top row of letters.
It has its own keys for ä, ö and ü and for French letters such as é, è and à.
The flashing line on the screen is called the cursor.
With the backspace key you delete the letter to the left of the cursor.
The Enter key starts a new line.
In touch typing you type with all ten fingers without looking at the keys.

abschnitte.titel: How a keyboard is laid out
abschnitte.text: Most keys are **letter keys** and number keys. Then there are special keys such as the space bar, the Shift key for capital letters and the Esc key for cancelling. With the four **arrow keys** you move the cursor up, down, left and right. Many keyboards have a **numeric keypad** on the right, laid out like a calculator.

Because several languages are spoken in Switzerland, the Swiss keyboard has ä, ö and ü for German and é, è and à for French. There is no key for the German sharp s, because in Switzerland ss is always written instead. The layout is called **QWERTZ**; in England and the USA it is called QWERTY. So there, Y and Z are swapped.

The arrangement of the letters goes back to the **typewriter**, which the American Christopher Latham Sholes developed in the 1870s. Common pairs of letters were placed apart so that the type bars did not get caught on each other. When computers came along later, this familiar layout was kept. That is why we still type today on a layout that is over 150 years old.

In **touch typing**, each finger rests on a fixed home position. The index fingers rest on F and J, which usually have small bumps you can feel. This lets you find the home position without looking. If you practise the system, you can type much faster and with fewer mistakes.

With key combinations, lots of things go faster. In Windows, Ctrl and C copies a selected text and Ctrl and V pastes it; on a Mac you use the Command key. Ctrl and Z undoes the last step. The Esc key often closes a full-screen game or cancels a process.

begriffe.erklaerung: The flashing line that shows where the next letter will appear.
A key that deletes the character to the left of the cursor.
A separate block of number keys, usually on the right of the keyboard.
A combination of keys that quickly triggers a command.

gewusst: The small bumps on F and J also help people who cannot see to find their way around the keyboard.
On the Swiss keyboard there is no key of its own for the sharp s that is used in Germany.
In France the keyboard begins with AZERTY instead of QWERTZ.

teile.einleitung: Submarine cables are cables that lie on the seabed and connect continents with each other. Almost all the internet traffic between the continents flows through them. When you watch a video from America, the data very probably travels through a cable in the Atlantic.
wichtigste: Submarine cables lie on the seabed and connect continents.
Most internet data from Europe to America runs through submarine cables.
In modern submarine cables, light flows through glass fibres.
Submarine cables are laid with special ships.
A ship's anchor can damage a submarine cable.
Switzerland is connected to the submarine cables by cables on land.
More than 150 years ago, telegrams were sent through the first Atlantic cable.

abschnitte.text: A **submarine cable** is a cable that is laid through seas or large lakes. Most of them simply lie on the **seabed**, sometimes thousands of metres deep. Today there are more than 500 such cables worldwide. Together they are over a million kilometres long, which is enough to go round the Earth many times. Satellites, on the other hand, carry only a small part of the data between the continents.

Modern submarine cables contain **glass fibres** that are thinner than a hair. Data is sent through them as **pulses of light**. A single cable can carry huge amounts of data in this way, much more than a satellite connection. Over long distances, the light is regularly refreshed in amplifiers. In the deep sea, such a cable is often only about as thick as a garden hose; near the coast it is armoured with steel.

Submarine cables are laid by **cable-laying ships** that have thousands of kilometres of cable on board. The cable is slowly unrolled and sinks to the bottom. The main dangers come from **ships' anchors** and fishing nets in shallow water. Earthquakes under the sea can also tear cables apart. For repairs, a special ship pulls the cable up to the surface with a hook and mends it.

The first cable across the Atlantic, between Ireland and Newfoundland, was laid in 1858. It made it possible to send **telegrams** between Europe and America for the first time, but the cable failed after a few weeks. In 1866 a lasting connection was achieved with the huge steamship Great Eastern. In 1956 the first telephone cable across the Atlantic went into operation. From 1988 the first fibre-optic cables were laid across the Atlantic.

Switzerland has no coast and therefore no landing point of its own for submarine cables. It is connected to its neighbouring countries by **land cables**. From there the data travels on to coasts, for example in France, Italy or on the North Sea, where the submarine cables come ashore. Large internet exchange points are located, for example, in Frankfurt, Marseille and Zurich. In this way a message from Switzerland reaches other continents in a fraction of a second.

Submarine cables are part of the **critical infrastructure**; without them the worldwide internet would be badly disrupted. Today large internet companies such as Google or Meta also build their own submarine cables. If a cable is damaged, other cables take over the traffic. Because the cables are so important, many states now pay more attention to protecting them. Even so, many cables around the world fail every year because of accidents and have to be repaired.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very thin thread of glass through which light carries data.
A special ship for laying submarine cables.
A short message that used to be sent over electrical lines.
Facilities without which a country cannot function properly.

gewusst: Sharks used to bite submarine cables sometimes, probably because of the weak electric fields.
The first message through the Atlantic cable of 1858 was a greeting from the British Queen Victoria to the US President.
A submarine cable in the deep sea is often hardly thicker than a thumb.

teile.einleitung: Wikipedia is a free online encyclopaedia written by volunteers from all over the world. It was launched in January 2001 and is now one of the most visited websites in the world. All articles can be read free of charge and edited by almost anyone.
wichtigste: Wikipedia was launched in January 2001.
It was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger.
The Hawaiian word wiki means quick.
The articles are written by volunteers from all over the world.
Wikipedia is run by the Wikimedia Foundation and funded mainly by donations.
The texts are published under the free licence CC BY-SA.
Wikipedia requires statements to be backed up by reliable sources.

abschnitte.text: Wikipedia is an **encyclopaedia**, a reference work covering all areas of knowledge. Unlike a printed encyclopaedia, it is on the internet and is constantly being added to. It exists in over 300 languages, including Alemannic and Romansh. The English edition alone has more than six million articles (as of 2025).

Wikipedia was launched on 15 January 2001. It was founded by **Jimmy Wales** and Larry Sanger. The name combines the Hawaiian word wiki, which means quick, with the English word encyclopaedia. A **wiki** is a website whose pages you can edit directly in the browser, and the German-language Wikipedia followed as early as March 2001.

The articles are written by **volunteers** from all over the world who are not paid for it. Every change is saved and can be checked and undone by others. Wikipedia requires statements to be backed up by **sources** that are reliable, such as specialist books or newspapers. In addition, articles should be written neutrally and not express a personal opinion.

Wikipedia is run by the **Wikimedia Foundation**, a non-profit organisation based in San Francisco. It is funded mainly by donations and shows no advertising. The texts are published under the licence **CC BY-SA**. This means you may reuse them if you name the source and pass on the result under the same licence.

Wikipedia is very good for getting a first overview of a topic. But because anyone can write for it, it can contain mistakes that nobody has noticed yet. That is why it is worth checking important facts in the sources at the end of the article. In Switzerland, the association Wikimedia CH supports the volunteers, for example with writing workshops.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reference work with knowledge about many topics.
A website that people can edit together directly in the browser.
Rules that set out how a work may be used.
A reference that shows a statement is true.
Presenting a topic without taking sides.

gewusst: The name wiki comes from the Wiki Wiki buses at the airport in Honolulu, Hawaii.
Every single change to a Wikipedia article is saved in the version history and can still be viewed.
The pictures in Wikipedia mostly come from Wikimedia Commons, a huge free collection of media.

teile.einleitung: A television is a device that receives moving pictures and sounds and shows them on a screen. The word “television” actually means “seeing far away”. Since the 1950s, television has changed the way people experience news, sport and entertainment.
wichtigste: The television shows pictures and sounds that are transmitted from far away.
In 1926 in London, John Logie Baird was one of the first to show moving television pictures.
The first television pictures were black and white.
Switzerland has had regular television since 1953.
A screen picture is made of tiny dots, the pixels.
In 1969 millions of people watched the Moon landing live on television.
Swiss households pay a media fee for radio and television with a public service mission.

abschnitte.text: A television receives broadcasts via aerial, cable, satellite or the internet and turns them into picture and sound. The picture is made up of millions of tiny **pixels** that light up in red, green and blue. Because the pictures are shown very quickly one after another, our eyes see smooth movement. With the **remote control** you can change channels comfortably from the sofa.

Many inventors were working on television at the same time. In 1926 in London, the Scot **John Logie Baird** was one of the first to show moving television pictures. His pictures were small, flickered and were black and white. Later, electronic sets with a **picture tube** took over; for a long time they were heavy and bulky.

In Switzerland regular television broadcasting began in 1953, at first only on a few evenings a week. Today **SRG** broadcasts in all the national languages; in German-speaking Switzerland it is called **SRF**. It is financed mainly by the media fee, which is collected by the company Serafe. Every household pays it, whether or not it owns a set.

On 21 July 1969, millions of people all over the world watched live as Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon. Football World Cups and the Olympic Games are also watched on television by billions of people. From the 1960s and 1970s, colour televisions came into living rooms. Today flat screens with **LED** or OLED technology are usual.

**Screen time** is the time you spend in front of a mobile phone, tablet or television. Too much of it can make you tired and leaves less time for exercise, friends and sleep. It helps to agree rules with your parents and to choose programmes on purpose. Many televisions today are connected to the internet as smart TVs and also serve as a screen for games consoles such as the Nintendo Switch.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny dot that a screen picture is made of.
A large glass tube that produced the picture in old televisions.
A charge in Switzerland for radio and television with a public service mission.
A television with an internet connection for apps and streaming.

gewusst: A modern 4K picture is made up of more than eight million pixels.
John Logie Baird's first television pictures had only 30 lines.
Old tube televisions were so deep that they looked almost like a box.

teile.einleitung: Solar energy is energy that comes from the Sun. With solar installations, electricity or heat can be obtained from sunlight. Every day the Sun sends many times more energy to the Earth than humankind needs.
wichtigste: Solar energy comes from the Sun.
The technology by which solar cells turn light into electricity is called photovoltaics.
Solar collectors can be used to heat water; this is called solar thermal energy.
Solar energy is renewable and produces no exhaust gases while running.
In Switzerland, much more solar electricity is produced every year than the year before.
In winter and at night, solar installations supply little or no electricity.
Solar cells are usually made of the semiconductor silicon.

abschnitte.text: Inside the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, producing an enormous amount of energy. This energy reaches us as light and heat; the light takes about eight minutes to get here. Without the Sun's energy there would be no life on Earth, because plants need light for **photosynthesis**. The wind and the water cycle are also driven by the Sun. Using the Sun's energy directly is called **solar energy**.

Solar cells turn light directly into electric current; this technology is called **photovoltaics**. They are usually made of the **semiconductor** silicon, which is obtained from sand. When light hits the cell, electrons are set in motion and a current flows. Many cells together form a **solar panel**, and many panels a solar installation. The Frenchman Edmond Becquerel discovered this physical effect as early as 1839.

With **solar thermal energy**, the Sun directly heats water or another liquid. Dark **solar collectors** on the roof, in which the liquid flows through tubes, are used for this. In this way you can heat water for showers or help the heating. In very sunny countries such as Spain or Morocco there are also large solar power stations with mirrors. These concentrate the sunlight and use it to produce steam for turbines.

In Switzerland solar energy is growing very fast, especially on the roofs of houses. Around 2024, solar electricity covered about a tenth of Switzerland's electricity consumption. A well-known installation is **AlpinSolar** on the dam wall of the Muttsee in the canton of Glarus, which went into operation in 2022. In the mountains the sun often shines above the fog in winter, and snow reflects extra light. That is why **Alpine solar installations** are also being planned and built.

Sunlight is free and inexhaustible and produces no **exhaust gases** when making electricity. Solar installations are quiet and can be placed on almost any roof. But they supply no electricity at night, and much less in winter than in summer. That is why **storage** such as batteries or pumped storage power stations is needed. Making the panels needs energy and raw materials, but this is made up for after a few years of operation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technology by which solar cells turn light directly into electricity.
Using the Sun's heat, for example to heat water.
A semiconductor material made from sand, from which most solar cells are made.
A panel made of many solar cells connected together.

gewusst: The sunlight falling on you today left the Sun about eight minutes ago.
In 2016, the solar aeroplane Solar Impulse of the Swiss Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg flew around the Earth using only solar energy.
Pocket calculators and garden lights often have small solar cells too.

teile.einleitung: A dictionary is a book or website in which words are collected and explained in a fixed order. You can look up how to spell a word correctly, what it means or what it is called in another language. If you know how the alphabet works, you can find any word in a few seconds.
wichtigste: In a dictionary the words are arranged in alphabetical order.
Words beginning with A, such as “Ameise”, come right at the front, words beginning with Z, such as “Zebra”, right at the back.
The guide words at the top of each page show which words are on that page.
Words are usually listed in their basic form, so “gehen” rather than “ging” and “Maus” rather than “Mäuse”.
The Duden is the best known spelling dictionary of the German language.
There are monolingual dictionaries and bilingual dictionaries for translating.
Today many people also use online dictionaries on a computer or mobile phone.

abschnitte.text: A dictionary is a **reference work**, a book in which you look for something specific rather than reading it from front to back. Each word explained in it is called a **headword**. For each headword it says how to spell it and where it can be split, often also whether it is a noun, verb or adjective. For German nouns you will also find the article, that is der, die or das.

All the words are arranged by the **alphabet**, first by the first letter, then by the second and so on. If you are looking for “Katze” and the page goes from “Kamel” to “Kanu”, you have to turn further back, because after “Ka” the word “Katze” has a “t”. The **guide words** at the top of the page show the first and last word on the page. So you do not have to read every line, just compare the guide words.

A dictionary almost always lists the **basic form** of a word. You find verbs in their basic form, the infinitive, so “gehen” and not “ging” or “gegangen”. Nouns are listed in the singular, which is why you look up “Maus” and not “Mäuse”. Adjectives are given in their simple form, so “gross” and not “grösser”.

A **spelling dictionary** such as the Duden mainly shows the correct spelling. A bilingual dictionary helps with translating, for example from German into French, which is important in language lessons in Switzerland. There are also picture dictionaries for young children and specialist dictionaries for medicine or technology. The Swiss Idiotikon has been collecting words from the Swiss dialects since the 19th century.

Even in ancient times people wrote down lists of words to learn foreign languages. The brothers **Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm**, famous for their fairy tales, began a huge German dictionary in the 19th century, which was only finished in 1961. Konrad Duden published a dictionary in 1880 that helped to standardise German spelling. His name still appears on the yellow Duden books today.

Many dictionaries are now also available as an **online dictionary** or app. There you simply type in the word and do not have to turn pages. Word processing programs also have a built-in spell checker based on a dictionary. Even so, it is worth knowing how to use a printed dictionary, because it teaches you the alphabet and you often discover new words.

begriffe.erklaerung: The word that is printed in bold in the dictionary and explained.
The word at the top of a page that shows which words are on it.
The simple form of a word under which it is listed in the dictionary, for example “gehen”.
The fixed order of the letters from A to Z.
A book in which you look for something specific, for example a dictionary or encyclopaedia.

gewusst: The German dictionary of the Brothers Grimm took more than 120 years to finish.
The Duden is regularly published in a new edition, and each time new words are added.
In Switzerland people write “ss” instead of the sharp s, so Swiss school lessons always use “Strasse”.

teile.einleitung: The hook-and-loop fastener is a fastening made of two strips of fabric that stick firmly together when pressed. It was invented by the engineer George de Mestral from French-speaking Switzerland after he noticed burrs in his dog's fur. Today this handy fastener is found in shoes, jackets, bags and even spacesuits.
wichtigste: The hook-and-loop fastener was invented by the Swiss engineer George de Mestral.
He had the idea after a walk with his dog.
His model was the burdock, a plant with tiny hooks on its fruits.
A hook-and-loop fastener has a hook side and a loop side.
Inventions modelled on nature are called bionics.
The brand name Velcro combines the French words “velours” and “crochet”.
Hook-and-loop fasteners can be opened and closed thousands of times.

abschnitte.text: **George de Mestral** came from the canton of Vaud and was an engineer. After a walk with his dog in 1941, he noticed burrs stuck everywhere in its fur and on his clothes. Curious, he looked at the fruits under a microscope. He discovered lots of tiny hooks that catch in hair and fabric fibres.

The **burdock** is a plant that grows along paths and on waste ground. Its fruits are covered with hundreds of small, curved hooks. In this way they cling to animals brushing past and are spread far and wide. This trick of nature helps the plant settle in new places.

When people copy inventions from nature, it is called **bionics**. The hook-and-loop fastener is one of the most famous examples. Other examples are dirt-repellent surfaces modelled on the lotus leaf or aircraft wings based on birds. Over millions of years, nature has developed many clever solutions.

A hook-and-loop fastener consists of two strips. One has lots of small, stiff **hooks**; the other has soft **loops**. When you press the two together, thousands of hooks catch in the loops. When you pull them apart, they come loose again with the typical ripping sound.

De Mestral experimented for years until he found a suitable material, namely nylon. At the beginning of the 1950s he patented his invention and founded a company called **Velcro**. The name combines the French words “velours” for velvet and “crochet” for hook. The fastener also became famous through space travel, where astronauts used it to fix objects in place in weightlessness.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant whose fruits are covered with tiny hooks.
Inventions that copy ideas from nature.
A legal right that reserves an invention for its inventor for a certain time.
A tough plastic used to make fibres.

gewusst: It took about ten years for George de Mestral to finish developing his material.
Children's shoes with hook-and-loop fasteners are popular because you do not have to tie any laces.
In English the fastener is often simply called “Velcro”, after the company name.

teile.einleitung: A directory structure is the arrangement in which a computer stores its files in folders and subfolders. It branches out like a tree, starting from the top folder, the root directory. If you organise your folders well, you can find files again quickly.
wichtigste: Files are stored in folders, which are also called directories.
A folder inside another folder is called a subfolder.
The top folder of a drive is called the root directory.
A file path gives the exact storage location of a file.
Windows separates folders in the path with the backslash, macOS and Linux with the forward slash.
A shortcut points to a file in another place.
Dates such as 2025-03-14 in the file name make sure files are sorted in the right order in time.

abschnitte.text: A directory structure branches out like an upside-down **tree**. At the very top is the **root directory**; below it are folders, inside them more subfolders and finally files. A school folder can, for example, contain subfolders for maths, German and French. This keeps things in order even with thousands of files.

A **file path** describes the route from the root directory to a file. In Windows it looks something like this: C:\School\Maths\Task.docx, separated with the backslash. In macOS and Linux the forward slash separates, for example /Users/lea/School/Task.docx. The path is like an address with which the computer finds the file straight away.

A **shortcut** is a pointer to a file or folder in another place. On the desktop you can use it to start a program quickly, even though it is stored somewhere else completely. If you delete the shortcut, the real file stays. In macOS such a thing is called an alias, and in Linux a symbolic link.

In Windows some characters are not allowed in file names, for example the question mark, the asterisk and the colon. The best way to write a date is as year, month, day, for example 2025-03-14. Then the computer sorts the files alphabetically and at the same time in the right order in time. Clear names such as “Bear-talk-2025-03-14” are much more helpful than “New Document 7”.

Early computers stored all their files in one single long list. In the 1960s the operating system **Multics** introduced a hierarchical file system with subfolders. The operating system Unix took over the idea, with the forward slash as the separator. Today all common operating systems and also cloud storage use such tree structures.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a folder on the computer.
The top folder of a drive, in which everything else is stored.
The exact address of a file in the folder tree.
A pointer to a file that is stored somewhere else.

gewusst: In Windows the first hard drive is usually called C, because A and B used to be reserved for floppy disks.
The backslash was chosen in Windows because the normal forward slash was already being used there for command options.
The symbol for a folder on the computer looks like a paper file folder.

teile.einleitung: Virtual memory management is a technique with which an operating system cleverly divides up a computer's main memory. Every running program gets its own, apparently huge memory area, even though the real memory is much smaller and is shared with other programs. Almost all of today's computers and mobile phones work like this.
wichtigste: Every process gets its own virtual address space.
The memory management unit translates virtual addresses into physical addresses.
Memory is divided into pages, which are 4 KiB in size by default on x86 processors.
The page table shows which virtual page is in which physical frame.
If a page that is needed is missing from main memory, a page fault occurs.
Rarely used pages are moved to a swap area on the storage drive.
If the system is doing almost nothing but swapping pages in and out, this is called thrashing.

abschnitte.text: Every program that runs is called a **process** and gets its own **virtual address space**. To the process, it looks as if it had the whole memory to itself. In reality, the operating system spreads the data across the real main memory and the hard drive or SSD. Because no process can see the memory of another, programs do not disturb each other and are better protected.

Virtual memory is divided into pieces of equal size, the **pages**. On x86 processors a page is 4 KiB in size by default, that is 4,096 bytes. The matching pieces in the real main memory are called frames. With 4 KiB pages, the lowest 12 bits of an address form the offset within the page, because 2 to the power of 12 is 4,096.

The **memory management unit**, MMU for short, is a component in the processor that translates every virtual address into a physical address. To do this it looks in the **page table**, which the operating system keeps for each process. So that this happens quickly, the translation lookaside buffer, TLB for short, remembers the most recently used translations. Without this cache, the processor would first have to search the table with every access.

When main memory runs short, the operating system moves rarely used pages to a **swap area** on the storage drive. In Windows this is called the page file, in Linux often swap. If a program needs a page that has been swapped out, this triggers a **page fault**, and the operating system fetches the page back. If this happens all the time, it is called thrashing, and the computer becomes extremely slow.

Virtual memory management was developed around 1960 at the University of Manchester for the **Atlas** mainframe computer. At that time main memory was very expensive and scarce. In the 1970s the technique spread to mainframes, and later it came to personal computers. Today Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS all use virtual memory.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fast memory in which running programs store their data.
A piece of virtual memory of equal size.
A list that shows where each virtual page really is.
A signal that a page that is needed is not in main memory at the moment.

gewusst: Despite its name, a page fault is not an error in the program but a completely normal process.
Accessing the hard drive is many thousands of times slower than accessing main memory.
Many systems support, as well as 4 KiB pages, much larger pages of several megabytes.

teile.einleitung: A container ship is a huge cargo ship that carries goods across the seas in large metal boxes called containers. Almost everything we buy, from clothes to toys and mobile phones, has travelled in one of these containers at some point. The largest of these ships are among the largest moving structures in the world.
wichtigste: Container ships carry goods in large standardised metal boxes.
A standard container is about 6 metres long; cargo is measured in TEU.
The largest container ships are about 400 metres long and carry more than 20,000 containers.
The world's largest container shipping company, MSC, is based in Geneva.
Containers can be moved from ship to lorry or train without repacking.
A large part of world trade is carried by container ships.
In large ports, huge cranes lift the containers off the ship.

abschnitte.text: A **container** is a large steel box with doors at one end. All containers come in standard sizes so that they fit everywhere. A 20-foot container is about 6 metres long and 2.4 metres wide. A ship's capacity is given in **TEU**, meaning how many of these 20-foot containers it can carry.

In the past, sacks, crates and barrels were loaded one by one by dock workers, which often took days. In 1956 the American **Malcom McLean** had a ship loaded with standardised containers for the first time. This saved an enormous amount of time and money. Since then the container has been the most important means of transport in **world trade**.

The largest container ships are almost 400 metres long and more than 60 metres wide. They can load more than 20,000 TEU, so many containers that placed end to end they would stretch over more than 100 kilometres. Despite their size they often have a crew of only about 20 to 30 people. They run on huge **diesel engines** that are as big as a house.

In **container ports** such as Shanghai, Singapore, Rotterdam or Hamburg, giant container cranes lift the boxes off the ship. The containers are then moved onto lorries, trains or smaller ships without having to be opened. This is called **combined transport**. Containers for Switzerland often come by Rhine barge to Basel or by rail into the country.

Although Switzerland has no access to the sea, the world's largest container shipping company, the Mediterranean Shipping Company, **MSC** for short, is based in **Geneva**. It was founded in 1970 by Gianluigi Aponte. The Rhine ports in **Basel** are Switzerland's gateway to the sea. From there, ships carry containers down the Rhine to the North Sea.

Container ships carry a great deal of goods using comparatively little energy per container. Even so, because of their size they emit a lot of exhaust fumes, often from heavy marine diesel. Sometimes containers go overboard in storms. In 2021 the container ship **Ever Given** blocked the Suez Canal for days, disrupting world trade.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large standardised steel box for transporting goods.
A unit that shows how many 20-foot containers a ship can carry.
A company that owns ships and uses them to transport goods or people.
A huge crane in the port that lifts containers onto and off ships.

gewusst: A container ship can carry as many goods as thousands of lorries.
Because containers are standardised, they fit on ships, trains and lorries all over the world.
Switzerland has its own small ocean-going fleet, even though it has no sea.

teile.einleitung: Electricity is a form of energy produced by tiny electrically charged particles. It makes lamps light up, charges mobile phones and drives trains. Without electricity, our modern life would almost come to a standstill.
wichtigste: Electricity comes from electric charges, above all from tiny particles called electrons.
Electric current is the flow of electrons through a conductor such as a copper wire.
Voltage is measured in volts, named after Alessandro Volta, who built the first usable battery around 1800.
In 1831 Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction, the basis of all generators.
For more than a hundred years, most of Switzerland's electricity has come from hydropower.
You must never put metal into a plug socket, because electricity can kill.
The first electric light in Switzerland shone in 1879 in a hotel in St Moritz.

abschnitte.text: All things are made of atoms, and inside them are positively charged **protons** and negatively charged **electrons**. Like charges push each other away; unlike charges attract each other. If you rub a balloon on your jumper, electrons move onto the balloon. If you then hold it against the wall, it sticks there. This is called **static electricity**, and lightning is also produced in a similar way.

Electric **current** is the flow of charges, much as water flows in a pipe. The **voltage** in volts is like the pressure that drives the water; the strength of the current is measured in amperes. Metals such as copper conduct electricity well, whereas rubber and plastic hardly do; they are called **insulators**. That is why cables are made of copper inside and covered with plastic outside. In Switzerland, plug sockets supply a voltage of 230 volts.

Around 1800 the Italian **Alessandro Volta** built the voltaic pile, the first usable battery. In 1831 the Englishman **Michael Faraday** discovered that a moving magnet in a coil of wire produces a current. In 1866 and 1867 Werner von Siemens described the dynamo-electric principle, which made it possible to produce electricity in large amounts. In 1880 Thomas Edison received a patent for his light bulb and put it into mass production. For especially long-lasting filaments he soon used carbonised bamboo fibres.

The first electric light in Switzerland shone in 1879 in a hotel in **St Moritz**. Soon afterwards, power stations were built on rivers and mountain lakes all over the country. Because Switzerland has hardly any coal, **hydropower** was also called “white coal”. It still supplies most of Switzerland's electricity today, and another large share comes from **nuclear power stations**. More and more electricity also comes from solar panels on roofs.

Electricity from a plug socket can seriously injure or even kill a person. That is why you must never put metal, such as scissors or a fork, into a **plug socket**. Electrical appliances do not belong near water, for example next to the bath. You should show damaged cables to an adult straight away. In a thunderstorm you protect yourself from **lightning** by going into a building or a car.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny negatively charged particle in every atom that carries the current.
The unit of electrical voltage, named after Alessandro Volta.
A machine that turns movement into electric current.
A material such as rubber or plastic that hardly conducts electricity.

gewusst: For a brief moment, a bolt of lightning can be many times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Your body uses electricity too, because your nerves send tiny electrical signals to your muscles and brain.
Electric eels can give electric shocks of several hundred volts.

teile.einleitung: Malware is software that has been built on purpose to harm computers, mobile phones or their users. In English all its kinds are grouped together under the word “malware”. They include viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware and many others.
wichtigste: In German malware is called “Schadprogramm”; in English all kinds are grouped together as malware.
A worm spreads by itself through networks without attaching itself to a file.
Spyware secretly spies on data and behaviour.
A keylogger records what is typed on the keyboard.
A botnet is a network of many infected computers that an attacker controls remotely.
Adware mainly shows unwanted advertising.
A rootkit hides deep in the system to cover its tracks.
On smartphones, malware often gets in through apps from unsafe sources.

abschnitte.text: **Malware** is a program with bad intentions. It can steal, delete or encrypt data, spy on devices or misuse them for attacks. The English word **malware** is made up of “malicious” and “software”. Often the victims notice nothing at first. Behind malware there are usually criminals who want to make money.

A **computer virus** attaches itself to other files or programs and spreads when they are opened. A **worm** needs no host file and spreads by itself through networks. A **Trojan** disguises itself as a useful program, for example a game, and secretly opens a back door. The name is a reminder of the Trojan Horse from the Greek legend. Ransomware is a kind of malware that encrypts data and demands a ransom.

**Spyware** secretly spies on what you do on the device and sends the data to strangers. A **keylogger** records every key you press and can steal passwords in this way. **Adware** mainly shows unwanted advertising, often in annoying windows. A **rootkit** hides deep in the operating system so that it is hardly ever discovered. Some malware combines several of these features.

Many infected computers can be linked together into a **botnet**. An attacker then controls them remotely without the owners noticing. Botnets are used, for example, to send out masses of spam emails. They can also bring down websites by having thousands of devices send requests at the same time. Poorly protected devices such as webcams or routers are also misused for botnets.

As early as 1971 there was a harmless, self-copying test program called Creeper. In 1986 one of the first viruses for PCs, Brain, appeared; it spread via floppy disks. In 1988 the **Morris worm** paralysed a large part of the internet of the time. In 2000 the worm **ILOVEYOU** sent itself out as a love letter by email and infected millions of computers. Today huge numbers of new variants of malware are discovered every day.

Always keep your operating system and apps up to date, because **updates** close security holes. Only download apps from the official app stores. Don't open unknown attachments and don't click on strange links. An **antivirus program** recognises a lot of known malware. In Switzerland the Federal Office for Cybersecurity NCSC provides information about current dangers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The English umbrella term for harmful programs.
A harmful program that disguises itself as a useful program.
A program that secretly records keyboard input.
Many remote-controlled, infected computers.
Software that searches for and removes malware.

gewusst: The Morris worm was written by a student who actually only wanted to measure the size of the internet.
The worm ILOVEYOU spread in an email with the subject “ILOVEYOU” and a supposed love letter as an attachment.
Smartphones and smart televisions can also be infected by malware.

teile.einleitung: A glider is an aeroplane without an engine. It glides silently through the air and uses rising air to gain height. Good pilots can fly them for hours and cover hundreds of kilometres.
wichtigste: A glider has no engine.
Warm rising air that glider pilots use is called a thermal.
Gliders have very long, narrow wings.
They are launched with a winch or towed behind a powered aeroplane.
Without rising air, a glider sinks slowly but steadily.
From 1891, Otto Lilienthal made the first successful gliding flights.

abschnitte.text: A glider glides slowly downwards like a paper aeroplane. As it does, air flows over the **wings** and creates lift, which holds it up. To stay up longer, the pilot looks for **updraughts**, that is, air that is rising. There the pilot circles and so gains height again.

When the sun warms the ground, warm air rises in bubbles; this is a **thermal**. Fluffy cumulus clouds often show where a thermal is. When the wind blows against a mountain, the air is pushed upwards; this is called **ridge lift**. In the Alps and the Jura, Swiss glider pilots use both.

Because it has no engine, a glider needs help to take off. In a **winch launch**, a winch pulls it up into the air on a long cable. In an aerotow, a powered aeroplane pulls it up and then the glider releases the rope. It lands at an airfield or, in an emergency, in a field.

Modern gliders are made of light **plastic** reinforced with glass or carbon fibres. Their wings are usually 15 to more than 25 metres long. They are built so that from a height of one kilometre they can glide 40 to more than 60 kilometres. Important instruments are the altimeter and the variometer, which shows climbing and sinking.

From 1891, the German aviation pioneer **Otto Lilienthal** made thousands of gliding flights with wings he built himself. In the 1920s, gliding developed into a sport on the Wasserkuppe mountain in Germany. Today there are competitions and championships all over the world. The longest glider flight covered more than 3000 kilometres.

begriffe.erklaerung: Warm air rising from the ground.
How many metres an aircraft glides forward for every metre of height it loses.
An instrument that shows whether the aircraft is climbing or sinking.
A take-off in which a winch pulls the aircraft up.

gewusst: Birds such as storks and eagles also circle in thermals to gain height without flapping their wings.
Glider pilots can sometimes stay in the air for several hours without using a single drop of fuel.

teile.einleitung: A helicopter, also called Hubschrauber in German, is a flying machine that has a large rotor on its roof instead of fixed wings. It can take off and land vertically, stand still in the air and even fly backwards. That is why it is irreplaceable for rescues in the mountains.
wichtigste: A helicopter has a large rotor on top instead of fixed wings.
It can take off and land vertically and hover in the air.
A small tail rotor stops the body from turning round as well.
In 1939 Igor Sikorsky developed one of the first practical helicopters.
The Swiss air rescue service Rega can be reached on the emergency number 1414.
Helicopters also carry materials to building sites and mountain huts.
In 2021 the small helicopter Ingenuity reached Mars with the rover Perseverance.

abschnitte.text: The rotor blades of a helicopter are shaped like narrow, spinning wings. When the **rotor** turns quickly, the blades produce lift and raise the machine up. The pilot can change the angle of the blades and so make the helicopter climb, descend or fly in any direction. Because it does not need to roll forwards, it needs no runway. It can also stay still in one place in the air; this is called **hovering**.

When the big rotor turns in one direction, the body wants to turn in the other direction. The small **tail rotor** at the end of the tail boom prevents this. It pushes sideways against the turning and keeps the helicopter straight. Some helicopters instead have two large rotors that turn in opposite directions. The tail rotor is almost invisible when it is running, so on the ground you must always keep your distance.

The artist and inventor Leonardo da Vinci drew a screw-shaped flying machine around 1490. But helicopters could only really fly in the 20th century. In 1939 the engineer **Igor Sikorsky** built the VS-300 in the USA, one of the first practical helicopters with a tail rotor. The word helicopter comes from Greek and roughly means spiral wing.

In Switzerland, **Rega** flies injured and ill people to hospital by helicopter. It was founded in 1952 and can be reached on the emergency number **1414**. Its helicopters are based all over Switzerland and can be in the air within a few minutes. In the mountains they also lift people who have had accidents out of steep terrain with a winch. Air Zermatt and Air Glaciers also rescue people in the Alps.

Helicopters carry heavy loads on a long cable under the body. In this way they take materials to **mountain huts**, building sites and ski lifts where no road leads. The Swiss Air Force also uses Super Puma helicopters to fight forest fires, scooping water from lakes. Helicopters are also used to check power lines and to bring trees out of steep forests.

In February 2021 NASA's rover **Perseverance** landed on Mars. It brought with it the small helicopter Ingenuity, which weighed only about 1.8 kilograms. In April 2021 Ingenuity took off; it was the first powered flight on another planet. Because the air on Mars is very thin, its rotors turned extremely fast.

begriffe.erklaerung: The spinning blades on the roof that carry the helicopter.
A small rotor at the back that stops the helicopter from spinning round in a circle.
When the helicopter stays still in one place in the air.
A device with a cable that rescuers use to pull people up or lower them down.

gewusst: A helicopter can even fly backwards and sideways.
Rega is a non-profit foundation supported by millions of patrons.
The Mars helicopter Ingenuity was planned for five flights but managed more than 70.

teile.einleitung: A laser is a device that produces an especially concentrated, powerful beam of light. Unlike a torch, it hardly scatters its light and often has only a single colour. The first working laser was built in 1960; today the technology is found in supermarket checkouts, printers and operating theatres.
wichtigste: A laser produces a narrow, concentrated beam of light.
The first working laser was built in 1960.
The word laser is an abbreviation from English.
Laser light usually has only a single colour.
At the supermarket checkout, a laser reads the barcode.
Lasers are also used in medicine and industry.
Laser beams can seriously injure your eyes.

abschnitte.text: **Laser** stands for “Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation”. Normal light, for example from a light bulb, shines in all directions and is made up of many colours. Laser light, on the other hand, is tightly concentrated and usually **of one colour**. That is why a laser beam stays almost equally narrow even over long distances.

Inside a laser there is a special material, for example a crystal, a gas or a semiconductor. Energy is supplied to it, for instance with electricity or bright light. The excited atoms then give off particles of light, which cause other atoms to send out exactly the same light. Two **mirrors** at the ends bounce the light back and forth again and again and strengthen it until a beam comes out.

**Albert Einstein** described the basic idea of stimulated emission of light as early as 1917. The American **Theodore Maiman** built the first working laser in 1960 using a ruby crystal. At first the laser was called “a solution looking for a problem”, because nobody knew what it should be used for. Today science and technology would be unthinkable without it.

At the **supermarket checkout**, a laser scans the barcode on the products. Laser printers, fibre-optic cables for the internet and, in the past, CD and DVD players also work with lasers. Eye doctors correct sight problems with lasers, and in factories powerful lasers cut metal. On building sites, lasers help to measure distances and heights precisely.

Laser beams must never be pointed at anyone's eyes, not even small **laser pointers**. Even a short time can damage the retina permanently. In research, lasers even measure the distance to the Moon by being reflected off mirrors that astronauts set up there. With LISA, ESA is planning an observatory in space in which laser beams between satellites are to detect gravitational waves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that produces a concentrated beam of light, usually of one colour.
A pattern of lines on products that a scanner can read.
A thin glass thread through which light can transmit data.
The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.

gewusst: Using laser beams reflected on the Moon, the distance to the Moon is measured to within a few centimetres.
This shows that the Moon moves measurably about 3.8 centimetres further away from the Earth each year.
You can only see laser beams in the air when dust, smoke or fog scatters the light.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Army knife, officially the Swiss officer's knife, is a folding knife with many tools in a small red handle. It was originally developed for the Swiss Army and is now a symbol of Switzerland all over the world. Besides the blade, it contains a screwdriver, tin opener, scissors and much more.
wichtigste: The Swiss Army knife was originally developed for the Swiss Army.
The classic knife has a red handle with a Swiss cross.
From 1891, Karl Elsener from Ibach in the canton of Schwyz supplied soldiers' knives to the army.
His company became the brand Victorinox.
A second well-known maker was Wenger in Delémont.
Pocket knives combine many tools in a single handle.
The knife is a world-famous Swiss souvenir.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss officer's knife** is a pocket knife whose blades and tools fold into the handle. There are models with just a few parts and ones with more than thirty functions. Typical parts are a blade, a tin opener, a screwdriver, a corkscrew and an awl. The classic handle is **red** and bears a Swiss cross.

At the end of the 19th century, the **Swiss Army** was looking for a practical knife for its soldiers. They needed to be able to open tins and take their rifles apart with it. From 1891, the cutler **Karl Elsener** from Ibach near Schwyz supplied such soldiers' knives. In 1897 he registered a lighter, more elegant model, which became known as the officer's knife.

After his mother Victoria died, Elsener named his company after her. When stainless steel came along, “inox” was added, and so the name **Victorinox** was born. A second maker, the company **Wenger** in Delémont in the Jura, also supplied army knives. In 2005 Victorinox took over Wenger, and today all Swiss officer's knives come from Ibach.

The red knife became famous when American soldiers took it home as a souvenir after the Second World War. Because they found the German word “Offiziersmesser” hard to pronounce, they simply called it the “Swiss Army Knife”. It has also travelled into space with astronauts and is today one of the best-known **souvenirs** of Switzerland. At the Museum of Modern Art in New York it is regarded as an example of good design.

A pocket knife is a tool, not a toy. Always cut away from your body and fold the blade back in straight after using it. Children should first practise using it with an adult, for example when **whittling** in the woods. Knives are banned on aircraft and in some places such as schools or stadiums.

begriffe.erklaerung: The official name of the Swiss pocket knife.
A pointed tool for piercing holes.
Short for stainless steel, from French.
A knife whose blade folds into the handle.

gewusst: Victorinox makes tens of thousands of pocket knives a day in Ibach.
English speakers call it the “Swiss Army Knife” because they found the German word too difficult.
A record-breaking model by Wenger had more than 80 tools and could hardly be held in one hand.

teile.einleitung: Wi-Fi is a wireless network that lets devices such as mobile phones, laptops and games consoles connect to the internet by radio. In German it is called WLAN, short for Wireless Local Area Network. At home, a router usually makes the Wi-Fi work.
wichtigste: WLAN, the German term, stands for Wireless Local Area Network.
In English-speaking countries it is usually called Wi-Fi.
The name of a Wi-Fi network is called the SSID.
Home routers usually transmit in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.
The 5 GHz band is faster but has a shorter range.
WPA3 is the newest of the widely used security standards.
Thick walls made of reinforced concrete weaken the signal particularly strongly.

abschnitte.text: **Wi-Fi** connects devices using **radio waves** instead of cables. At its heart is usually a **router**, which is connected to the internet connection and sends the data on to the devices by radio. A Wi-Fi network normally reaches through a flat or a house, which is why it is called a local network. In German-speaking countries it is called WLAN.

Home Wi-Fi routers usually transmit in two ranges, at 2.4 GHz and at 5 GHz. The 2.4 GHz band has a longer range but is often crowded, because many neighbours and even microwave ovens use it too. The 5 GHz band is faster but does not reach as far and goes through walls less well. Newer devices can also use the 6 GHz band.

Every Wi-Fi network has a name, the **SSID**, which appears in the list of available networks. To stop strangers from using it, the network is protected with a password and encryption. The old WEP standard is considered insecure; today WPA2 or the newest standard **WPA3** is used. A good Wi-Fi password is long and hard to guess.

The signal is weakened by obstacles, particularly strongly by thick walls made of **reinforced concrete**. Water, metal and underfloor heating can also interfere. The router is best placed high up and as close to the middle of the flat as possible. In large houses, repeaters or mesh systems that pass the signal on can help.

A public Wi-Fi access point is called a **hotspot**. You can find one at railway stations, in cafés, libraries or hotels, for example. On public networks other people may be able to read along, so you should not do online banking there. Many smartphones can become a hotspot themselves and share their mobile network with other devices.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that connects the home network to the internet.
The name of a Wi-Fi network.
How often a radio wave vibrates per second, measured in hertz.
Making data unreadable for people who are not allowed to see it.
A public Wi-Fi access point, for example at a railway station.

gewusst: The technical standard behind Wi-Fi is called IEEE 802.11 and was first published in 1997.
A microwave oven also works at about 2.4 GHz and can disturb the Wi-Fi while it is heating food.
New Wi-Fi generations have simple names such as Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 7.

teile.einleitung: A web server is a computer with a special program that provides web pages on the internet. When you enter an address in the browser, a web server sends you the matching page. Without web servers there would be no websites.
wichtigste: A web server delivers web pages to browsers.
Browser and server work according to the client-server model: the client asks, the server answers.
HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
The S in HTTPS stands for secure.
The status code 404 means that a page was not found.
The status code 200 means that the request was successful.
Apache HTTP Server is a well-known piece of web server software.

abschnitte.text: The word **server** comes from the English “to serve”. A **web server** is a program that runs on a computer and keeps web pages, pictures and videos ready. Often the computer itself is also called a web server. Many web servers are in large data centres and run day and night.

Your browser is the **client**; it makes a request, for example “Give me the home page”. The web server looks for the page and sends it back; this is called the **client-server model**. So that both understand each other, they speak the same language, the **HTTP** protocol. With HTTPS the connection is also encrypted.

With every answer, the server sends a number, the **status code**. 200 means “everything is fine”, and the page is displayed. 404 means “not found”, for example if you have made a typing mistake in the address. A 500, on the other hand, shows that an error has happened on the server itself.

Every server on the internet has a number, the **IP address**. Because numbers are hard to remember, there are names such as “admin.ch”, the so-called domains. A service called DNS translates the name into the right number, much like a telephone directory. Only then does the browser know which server to ask.

The very first web server ran at **CERN** in Geneva. There, around 1990, the British researcher Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web. His server was a NeXT computer with a note stuck on it saying that it must not be switched off. Today well-known web server programs are, for example, **Apache HTTP Server** and nginx.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer or program that provides data for others.
The device or program that makes a request, for example the browser.
Fixed rules for how computers communicate with each other.
A number that shows whether a request worked.
A building full of servers that are cooled and constantly supplied with electricity.

gewusst: Many websites design their 404 error page in a funny way, for example with a lost animal.
Large websites spread their content across thousands of servers around the world so that they load quickly.
Tim Berners-Lee's very first web server is now on display as a museum exhibit.

teile.einleitung: A queue is a data structure in which elements are dealt with in order. Whoever comes first is served first, just like in a queue at the checkout. Computers use queues wherever tasks have to be done one after another in an orderly way.
wichtigste: A queue works on the FIFO principle: first in, first out.
With enqueue you add an element at the back.
With dequeue you take out the element at the front.
If A, B and C are added, the first dequeue gives the A.
A ring buffer implements a queue of fixed size efficiently.
Breadth-first search in graphs uses a queue.
Print jobs are typically dealt with using a queue.

abschnitte.text: A **queue** works on the **FIFO** principle, which stands for first in, first out. Whatever goes in first also comes out first. The counterpart is the **stack**, in which the element added last is the first to be taken out, as with a pile of plates. Both structures are among the basic building blocks of computer science.

With **enqueue**, a new element is added at the back of the queue. With **dequeue**, the element at the front is taken out. If you add A, B and C one after another, the first dequeue gives the A, then B and finally C. There is often also an operation with which you only look at the front element without removing it.

A queue of fixed size can be built well as a **ring buffer** in an array. You remember where the start and where the end of the queue are. When the end reaches the last place, it jumps back to the beginning, as if the places were arranged in a circle. This means you do not have to move all the elements forward when taking one out.

A **deque**, pronounced like deck, allows inserting and removing at both ends. In a **priority queue**, it is not the oldest but the most important element that comes first, similar to the accident and emergency department of a hospital. It is usually implemented with a binary heap. Breadth-first search uses a normal queue to visit the nodes of a graph level by level.

If several people send documents to a printer at the same time, the **print jobs** end up in a queue. Keyboard input is also stored briefly so that no letter gets lost. When streaming videos, data packets are lined up in a buffer. And Python even has a ready-made tool for this called deque.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particular way of organising and storing data in the computer.
First in, first out: whoever comes first is served first.
A data structure in which what was added last comes out first.
A store with fixed places that are used as if they were in a circle.
The importance that decides who gets a turn first.

gewusst: The English word queue is pronounced the same as the letter Q.
Online shops also use virtual queues when there is a big rush, for example when concert tickets go on sale.
The mathematics of queues is called queueing theory and helps, for example, to plan the checkouts in a supermarket.

teile.einleitung: A software test checks whether a computer program does what it is supposed to do. Testers try out the program in a targeted way to find errors before the users come across them. Good testing is an art in its own right with many methods and levels.
wichtigste: A black-box test checks a program only through inputs and outputs, without knowing the code.
A regression test checks whether parts that worked before still work correctly after a change.
Edsger W. Dijkstra said, more or less, that testing can show the presence of errors but never their absence.
Boundary value analysis specifically tests values at the edges of valid ranges.
The integration test checks how several components work together.
With the acceptance test, the customer formally accepts the software.
Test coverage measures what proportion of the source code is run by tests.

abschnitte.text: Almost every larger program contains errors, which are called **bugs**. An error in a games app is annoying; an error in the controls of an aircraft or a bank can be dangerous and expensive. That is why developers check their programs with **software tests**. The earlier an error is found, the cheaper it is to fix.

Testing is done at several levels. In a **unit test**, you check individual small building blocks, for example a single function. In an **integration test**, you look at whether several building blocks work together correctly. The system test checks the whole program, and at the end the customer usually carries out the **acceptance test** to formally accept the software.

In a **black-box test**, you do not know the code and only check whether the right output comes out for an input. In a **white-box test**, you look into the code and make sure that as many parts of the program as possible are run. How much of the source code is run by tests is measured by the **test coverage**. High coverage is good, but it does not yet guarantee an error-free program.

You cannot try out every possible input; there are far too many. With **equivalence partitioning**, you divide inputs into groups that probably behave in the same way and test one representative of each. With **boundary value analysis**, you test the edges: if an age from 6 to 20 is allowed, you test, for example, 5, 6, 20 and 21. It is precisely at such boundaries that errors happen especially often.

When a program is changed, something that worked before can break without anyone noticing. A **regression test** therefore checks after every change whether old functions still work correctly. Today such tests usually run **automatically**, often hundreds or thousands of times a day. But the computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra reminded people that testing can only show that errors are there, never that there are none left.

begriffe.erklaerung: English for a small insect; this is what an error in a program is called.
A precisely described check with an input and an expected result.
The proportion of the code that is actually run during testing.
A repeated test of whether everything still works after a change.
A final test with which the customer accepts the software.

gewusst: Some companies pay rewards to people who find and report errors in their software.
In test-driven development, you even write the test first and only afterwards the program.
Edsger W. Dijkstra came from the Netherlands and is considered one of the most important computer scientists.

teile.einleitung: A vector graphic is a computer picture that does not consist of individual dots but of geometric shapes such as lines, circles and curves. Because the computer only remembers the shapes and their measurements, you can enlarge a vector graphic as much as you like. It always stays perfectly sharp.
