Because it was filled with flammable **hydrogen**, it burned out within seconds, and 36 people died. After that, the era of the great passenger Zeppelins came to an end.

Since the 1990s there has been the **Zeppelin NT**, a modern design using helium, which does not burn. It flies tourists over Lake Constance and can easily be seen from the Swiss shore. Zeppelins are also used for advertising, research and filming for television. In Friedrichshafen, a Zeppelin Museum shows the history of airships.

begriffe.erklaerung: An aircraft that floats thanks to a gas lighter than air and has engines.
A very light gas that burns easily.
A light gas that does not burn.
A cabin under an airship or balloon.

gewusst: The Hindenburg was almost as long as three football pitches end to end.
Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin was already over 60 years old when his first airship took off.

teile.einleitung: Artificial intelligence, AI for short, is a branch of computer science in which computers solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking. AI can recognise pictures, translate languages, write texts or win games. Since chatbots such as ChatGPT appeared, it has become part of everyday life for many people.
wichtigste: AI stands for artificial intelligence.
In 1950 Alan Turing suggested a test to check whether a machine can think in a human-like way.
AI began as a field of research in 1956 at the Dartmouth Conference in the USA.
In machine learning, a program finds patterns by itself from many examples.
In 1997 the IBM computer Deep Blue beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov.
On 30 November 2022, OpenAI released the chatbot ChatGPT.
Since 2024 the EU has classified AI systems according to their risk to people.

abschnitte.text: **Artificial intelligence** means that computers do things that look like thinking, such as recognising, planning or speaking. But an AI does not think like a person and has no feelings. Using data and statistics, it calculates which answer fits best. That is why it can make mistakes and sometimes state wrong things with great confidence.

Most AIs today use **machine learning**. Instead of programming in every rule, you show the program lots of examples, for instance thousands of pictures of cats and dogs. From these it finds patterns by itself and can then sort new pictures. Especially powerful are **neural networks**, which are loosely modelled on the structure of the brain. John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024 for laying their foundations.

In 1950 the British mathematician **Alan Turing** suggested the Turing test: a person chats by text and has to find out whether they are talking to a human or a machine. In 1956 the term “Artificial Intelligence” was established as a field of research at the Dartmouth Conference. In 1997 the IBM computer Deep Blue beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov. In March 2016 AlphaGo by DeepMind won 4 to 1 against the Go professional Lee Sedol.

Since 30 November 2022 anyone has been able to try out the chatbot **ChatGPT**, and many similar programs followed. AI is also found in voice assistants, translation programs, navigation apps and the suggestions of video platforms. In medicine it helps to detect illnesses on X-rays. Swiss universities such as ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne also do a great deal of research on AI.

AI can make work easier, but it can also spread false information or create fake pictures that look deceptively real. That is why you should always check an AI's answers critically. The EU's **AI Act** has been in force since 1 August 2024 and classifies AI systems according to their risk to people and fundamental rights. Especially dangerous uses are banned, and strict rules apply to risky ones.

begriffe.erklaerung: A precise step-by-step set of instructions for a computer.
A program learns to recognise patterns by itself from many examples.
A computing model that is linked up roughly like nerve cells in the brain.
A program you can have a conversation with by text.
A test of whether a machine seems like a human in conversation.

gewusst: The Go professional Lee Sedol managed to win one of the five games against AlphaGo.
Just two months after its launch, ChatGPT already had about 100 million users.
The game of Go has more possible positions than there are atoms in the visible universe.

teile.einleitung: Overfitting is a typical problem in machine learning: a model learns the training data so exactly by heart that it does badly with new data. It is like someone who, for an exam, only learns the answers to old exams by heart. When a new question comes up, they don't know what to do.
wichtigste: With overfitting, a model adapts too closely to the training data.
An overfitted model also learns random errors and noise.
Typical sign: the training error keeps falling while the validation error rises again.
The opposite is called underfitting; then the model is too simple.
More varied training data is usually the most reliable help against overfitting.
Early stopping and regularisation are other remedies.
The trade-off between too simple and too complex is called the bias-variance dilemma.

abschnitte.titel: Learned by heart instead of understood
abschnitte.text: A model in **machine learning** is meant to learn general rules from examples. With **overfitting**, however, it remembers every little detail of the training data, including coincidences and measurement errors. On the known data it is then almost perfect. But with new data it makes lots of mistakes, because the coincidences it learned by heart no longer apply there.

Imagine ten measurement points that lie roughly on a straight line. A **polynomial** of degree 9 can hit all ten points exactly. But to do so, the curve swings wildly up and down between the points. That is why it predicts nonsense for new values, whereas a simple straight line would be much better.

You divide the data into **training data** and **validation data**. The model only learns with the training data; the rest serves as a check. If the training error keeps falling while the validation error rises again, overfitting is beginning. With a decision tree, you can recognise it by the tree being very deep and having leaves with only a single example.

The most reliable help is to collect more and more varied training data. With **early stopping**, you stop the training as soon as the validation error no longer falls. **Regularisation**, such as L2 regularisation or weight decay, penalises large weights and makes the model smoother. Simpler models or decision trees that are pruned shorter also reduce the problem.

If a model is too simple, it explains even the training data badly; this is called **underfitting**. If it is too complex, it adapts too much. This trade-off is called the **bias-variance dilemma**. That is why good experts look for a model that is exactly as complicated as necessary, but no more complicated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that has learned from examples and makes predictions.
The examples from which a model learns.
Examples held back to check how good the model really is.
A trick that penalises models that are too complicated during learning.
When a model is too simple and does not even explain the training data well.

gewusst: An overfitted model can be 100 percent right on the training data and still fail with new data.
People sometimes overfit too, for example when they draw a general rule from a single experience.
In the regularisation method called dropout, parts of a neural network are switched off at random during training.

teile.einleitung: A spreadsheet is a computer program with which you can arrange numbers in a large table and have them calculated automatically. Well-known examples are Microsoft Excel, LibreOffice Calc and Google Sheets. If you change a number, the program recalculates all the results immediately.
wichtigste: A spreadsheet consists of rows, columns and cells.
Columns have letters and rows have numbers, so B3 is column B, row 3.
A formula always begins with an equals sign.
Functions such as SUM, AVERAGE and MAX calculate whole ranges.
Dollar signs as in $A$1 keep a reference fixed when copying.
You can make charts from the numbers, for example a pie chart for proportions.
The first spreadsheet for personal computers was called VisiCalc and appeared in 1979.

abschnitte.text: A spreadsheet looks like a huge sheet of squared paper. The columns are named with letters, the rows with numbers. Each box is called a **cell** and has its own **cell address**, for example B3 for column B, row 3. The range A1:C2 covers 3 columns and 2 rows, that is 6 cells.

A **formula** always begins with the sign =. If A1 contains the number 7 and B1 the number 6, =A1*B1 gives the result 42. The asterisk stands for times, the slash for divided by. The useful thing is: if you change the 7 to an 8, 48 appears in the result box straight away.

A **function** is a ready-made calculation rule. =SUM(A1:A3) adds up all the numbers from A1 to A3; with 4, 5 and 6 that gives 15. =AVERAGE calculates the mean; with 2, 4, 6 and 8 that is 5. MAX finds the largest value, MIN the smallest.

If you copy a formula into another cell, the cell addresses normally adjust automatically. This is called a relative reference. But if you write $A$1, the reference stays the same when copying; this is an **absolute reference**. You need this, for example, if all prices are to be calculated with the same discount from a single cell.

With a few clicks, the program turns numbers into **charts**. A pie chart shows proportions of a whole, a bar chart compares quantities, and a line chart shows changes over time. The first spreadsheet for small computers, VisiCalc, appeared in 1979 and made personal computers popular in offices. Microsoft Excel came on the market in 1985 and is now used all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single box in the table.
A calculation instruction that begins with =.
A ready-made calculation rule such as SUM or MAX.
A cell address with dollar signs that does not change when copied.

gewusst: Companies, schools and clubs use spreadsheets to manage budgets, marks and membership lists.
An Excel sheet can have over a million rows.
Some people even paint pictures in spreadsheets by colouring in cells.

teile.einleitung: A website is something offered on the internet that usually consists of several web pages that belong together. You open it with a browser by entering its address or following a link. The very first website was created in 1991 at CERN in Geneva.
wichtigste: A website usually consists of several pages.
The first page that you usually see first is called the home page.
Through a menu, often right at the top, you get to the other pages.
Websites show texts, pictures and videos.
Websites are made by people and need to be looked after.
A magnifying glass symbol often stands for search.
Before buying something on a website, you ask your parents first.

abschnitte.text: A **website** is a collection of web pages that belong together, for example the pages of a zoo or a school. Every website has an address, the **URL**, for example with the ending .ch for Switzerland. You open it with a **browser** such as Firefox, Chrome or Safari. Through links you jump from one page to the next.

abschnitte.titel: How a website is laid out
abschnitte.text: The **home page** is the first page that you usually get to see. Right at the top there is often a menu with which you can get to the different sections. A magnifying glass symbol leads to the search, a house symbol back to the home page. If a page is longer than the screen, you scroll down.

Websites are made by people, for example by web designers and programmers. The content is written in the language **HTML**, and the appearance is designed with CSS. The files are on a server, a computer that is connected to the internet around the clock. If nobody looks after a website any more, the information becomes out of date.

In 1989 the British physicist **Tim Berners-Lee** invented the World Wide Web at the CERN research centre in Geneva. He wanted researchers to be able to share their information easily. In 1991 the first website went online; it explained what the web is. Today there are about a billion websites worldwide (as of 2025), but only some of them are looked after regularly.

Not everything that is on a website is true, so you compare information with other sources. A padlock symbol next to the address shows an encrypted connection, but it does not guarantee that the page is trustworthy. If a website asks you to buy something or enter personal details, you ask your parents first. You can recognise good children's sites by the fact that they have no advertising and say clearly who makes them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program with which you look at websites.
The address of a website, for example with the ending .ch.
The language in which the content of a web page is written.
A computer on which the files of a website are stored.

gewusst: You can still look at the very first website today at its old address at CERN.
The first web server was a computer with a note stuck on it saying it must not be switched off.
The ending .ch stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Scrum is a method that teams use to carry out complicated projects step by step, especially in software development. Instead of planning everything in advance, the team works in short sections, the sprints, and keeps improving the result. Scrum is one of the best-known agile methods in the world.
wichtigste: In Scrum a sprint lasts at most one month.
The product owner is responsible for the product backlog and the value of the product.
The Scrum master supports the team and removes obstacles.
The daily scrum lasts at most 15 minutes.
The sprint retrospective concludes a sprint and improves teamwork.
The definition of done sets out when a result counts as finished.
Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland presented Scrum in 1995 at the OOPSLA conference.

abschnitte.text: The word **scrum** comes from rugby and means the huddle in which both teams bind tightly together. In 1986 the Japanese researchers Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka compared successful product teams to a rugby team. Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland developed a method from this and presented it in 1995 at the OOPSLA conference. Since 2010 they have described Scrum in the freely available **Scrum Guide**.

A Scrum team is small, usually ten people or fewer. The **product owner** decides what is built and looks after the list of tasks for this. The **Scrum master** helps the team to use Scrum well and clears obstacles out of the way. The developers carry out the tasks and organise themselves while doing so.

Work takes place in **sprints**, which last at most a month, often two weeks. At the start, the team plans in the sprint planning what it wants to achieve. Every day it meets for the **daily scrum**, which lasts at most 15 minutes. At the end it shows the result in the sprint review and discusses in the sprint retrospective how it can work together better.

The **product backlog** contains all the wishes and tasks for the product, ordered by importance. For a sprint, the team chooses some tasks from it; this is the sprint backlog. At the end of each sprint there should be a usable result, the **increment**. When something is really finished is decided by the shared **definition of done**.

In big projects, the requirements often change while the work is going on. Scrum makes it possible to get feedback regularly and adjust the plan. In 2001, 17 software developers, including Schwaber and Sutherland, wrote the **Agile Manifesto** with the core values of this way of working. Today companies outside computing, schools and authorities in Switzerland also use agile methods such as Scrum.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed period of work of at most one month.
The person who decides what is built next.
The person who helps the team and removes obstacles.
An ordered list of all open tasks.
The usable result of the work in a sprint.

gewusst: The daily scrum is often held standing up so that it stays short.
The Scrum Guide is only a few pages long and is available free of charge in many languages.

teile.einleitung: Training data is the examples from which an artificial intelligence learns. A program that is meant to recognise cats in photos, for example, needs thousands of pictures with and without cats. How well an AI works later depends a great deal on how good this data is.
wichtigste: A picture in the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits consists of 784 pixels.
The researcher Fei-Fei Li started the image database ImageNet with over 14 million labelled pictures.
Annotation means giving data the correct labels.
In data augmentation, pictures are artificially rotated, mirrored or brightened to get more variety.
A data leak occurs when information from the test data gets into training unnoticed.
A validation dataset is used to set hyperparameters without using up the test data.
The principle garbage in, garbage out says: faulty data leads to faulty results.
Common Crawl is a freely available collection of gathered web pages and a basis for many language models.

abschnitte.text: In **machine learning**, nobody writes exact rules such as a cat has pointed ears. Instead you show the computer a huge number of examples, the **training data**. From them it finds patterns by itself, just as a child learns what a dog is through many encounters. After training, the model should also classify new examples it has never seen correctly.

For an AI to learn, it often needs the correct answer for each example, a so-called **label**. A photo is given the label cat or dog, for example. Labelling is called **annotation** and is often done by many people in painstaking manual work. Well-known datasets are MNIST with handwritten digits of 28 by 28, that is 784 pixels, and **ImageNet**, which the researcher Fei-Fei Li started and which contains over 14 million labelled pictures.

The data is usually divided into three parts. With the **training data** the model learns; with the validation data you set settings such as the learning speed, which are called hyperparameters. The **test data** is kept back until the end so that you can check honestly how good the model is. If test data gets into training unnoticed, this is called a **data leak**, and the result looks better than it really is.

Faulty data leads to faulty results; in English this is called **garbage in, garbage out**. If the data shows almost only light-skinned faces, for example, the AI recognises other faces less well. This is then called a **bias**. If there are too few examples, pictures can be artificially rotated, mirrored or brightened; this is called data augmentation.

Large **language models** such as those behind chatbots learn from huge amounts of text. An important basis is **Common Crawl**, a freely available collection of regularly gathered web pages. This raises questions about copyright and data protection, because the texts come from many people. In 2025 ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne presented Apertus, an open Swiss language model for which it has been disclosed which data it was trained on.

begriffe.erklaerung: Examples from which an AI learns.
The correct answer or label for an example.
Data held back, with which the AI is checked at the end.
A distortion when data is one-sided and the AI becomes unfair as a result.
Artificially changing data to get more examples.

gewusst: When you have to click on pictures of traffic lights or zebra crossings on the internet, you are often helping to label training data at the same time.
The MNIST dataset contains 70,000 handwritten digits and has been used for practice for decades.
A competition using ImageNet sparked a big boom in artificial intelligence in 2012.

teile.einleitung: A bridge is a structure that leads over an obstacle such as a river, a valley or a road. Even in the Stone Age, people laid tree trunks across streams. Today there are bridges made of wood, stone, steel and concrete, and some are many kilometres long.
wichtigste: Bridges carry paths, roads or railway lines over obstacles.
On a suspension bridge, the roadway hangs from strong cables.
The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is a famous wooden bridge.
A legend involving the Devil surrounds the Devil's Bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge.
Castles had drawbridges that could be pulled up.
The longest bridge in the world is a railway viaduct in China about 165 kilometres long (as of 2026).
Important types of bridge are beam, arch, suspension and cable-stayed bridges.

abschnitte.text: A bridge spans an obstacle so that people, vehicles or trains can get across. The supports it stands on are called **piers**. The distance between two supports is the **span**. A bridge must carry its own weight, the traffic, the wind and sometimes snow. That is why engineers calculate every bridge precisely.

The simplest form is the **beam bridge**, in which a girder lies on supports. An **arch bridge** carries the weight through an arch into the ground; this is how the Romans built bridges and aqueducts of stone. On a **suspension bridge**, the roadway hangs from strong cables stretched over tall towers. A famous example is the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco. On cable-stayed bridges, the cables run diagonally straight from the tower to the roadway.

In the Middle Ages, castles protected themselves with a moat and a **drawbridge** that could be pulled up when there was danger. Bridges were important trade routes, so a bridge toll was often charged. In wartime, bridges were often destroyed so that enemies could not cross. With the railway in the 19th century, many new bridges of iron and steel were built.

The **Chapel Bridge** in Lucerne crosses the River Reuss and dates from the 14th century. It is thought to be one of the oldest surviving covered wooden bridges in Europe and is decorated with painted panels. In 1993 a large part of it burned down; afterwards it was rebuilt. Next to it stands the eight-sided Water Tower. Also well known are the Landwasser Viaduct of the Rhaetian Railway near Filisur and the many railway bridges on the Gotthard.

The **Devil's Bridge** in the canton of Uri leads through the wild Schöllenen Gorge on the way to the Gotthard. According to legend, the Devil helped the people of Uri build it and in return demanded the first soul to cross the bridge. The clever people of Uri sent a billy goat across first. Very close by, a monument commemorates the Russian general **Suvorov**, who marched through the Alps with his army in 1799.

The longest bridge in the world is in China; it is a railway viaduct about 165 kilometres long (as of 2026). That is about as far as from Zurich to Bern and some of the way back again. The highest bridge, the Duge Bridge in China, is more than 500 metres above a valley. Such record-breaking structures show how advanced **construction technology** is today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A strong support that a bridge stands on.
The distance between two supports of a bridge.
A long bridge with many arches or piers across a valley.
A bridge at a castle that could be pulled up.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge is one of the most photographed structures in Switzerland.
There are also bridges that turn or open up so that ships can pass through.
Some bridges are built only for animals, so that wild animals can cross motorways safely.

teile.einleitung: A sorting algorithm is exact instructions for putting things into an order, such as numbers by size or words in alphabetical order. Computers sort all the time, for example contacts, rankings or search results. Computer scientists have invented many different sorting algorithms, some simple, some very fast.
wichtigste: Sorting means putting things into an order according to a fixed rule.
You sort things so that you can find them more quickly.
Words in a dictionary are sorted alphabetically.
Bubble sort always compares two neighbouring numbers and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
Selection sort always looks for the smallest element and puts it at the front.
Insertion sort works like sorting playing cards in your hand.
Quicksort divides the list into smaller and larger values using a pivot element.

abschnitte.text: When sorting, you put things into an order according to a **rule**, for example ascending from small to large. The numbers 1, 3, 5, 7 are sorted in ascending order. If you sort 4, 1, 3, 2 in **descending** order from large to small, the 4 comes first. Words are sorted **alphabetically**, which is why “apple” comes before “zebra”.

Sorted things are much quicker to find. In a dictionary you do not have to read every page but can look things up directly. The contacts on your phone, the results list of a ski race or the books in a library are also sorted. In a sorted list, a computer can search in a flash with **binary search** by always looking in the middle.

In **bubble sort** you go through the list from front to back and always compare two neighbours. If they are in the wrong order, they are swapped. After the first complete pass, the largest number is certainly at the end; it has risen like a bubble. You repeat the passes until nothing more needs to be swapped.

In **selection sort** you look for the smallest element in the unsorted part and put it at the front. Then you look for the second smallest, and so on. **Insertion sort** works the way many people arrange playing cards in their hand. You take one card after another and slide it into the right place among the cards already sorted.

**Quicksort** was invented around 1960 by the Briton Tony Hoare. You choose a **pivot element** and divide the list into values that are smaller and values that are larger. Then you sort both parts further in the same way. **Merge sort** divides the list into halves, sorts them and then cleverly puts them back together. Such methods are much faster than bubble sort with long lists.

With simple methods such as bubble sort, the work grows very strongly when the list gets longer. With twice as many numbers, bubble sort needs about **four times as many** comparisons. For 1,000 numbers that is roughly half a million comparisons, whereas quicksort needs only about 14,000 on average. That is why computer programs usually use fast methods or mixtures of them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
Ordered from small to large.
A comparison value at which quicksort splits a list into two parts.
A search method that rules out half of a sorted list each time.

gewusst: There is even a deliberately bad method in which the numbers are shuffled at random until they happen to be in the right order.
You can act out sorting algorithms well with a school class, with everyone lining up by height and only neighbours allowed to swap.

teile.einleitung: A fridge is a device that keeps food cool so that it stays fresh for longer. It takes in the heat from its inside and gives it off to the outside. Today there is one in almost every kitchen, but a good hundred years ago it was still a rare luxury.
wichtigste: In the fridge, food stays fresh for longer.
In the cold, bacteria and moulds multiply more slowly.
A fridge carries heat from the inside to the outside.
That is why its back is warm.
Inside, it is usually about 4 to 7 degrees Celsius.
In the past, food was cooled with ice from lakes and glaciers.
Old fridges must be recycled because they contain refrigerants.

abschnitte.text: Food goes off because **bacteria** and moulds multiply in it. In the cold this happens much more slowly, which is why milk, meat, cheese and vegetables last longer in the fridge. The ideal temperature is about 5 degrees Celsius. In the **freezer compartment**, at about minus 18 degrees, it is much colder still, and food keeps there for months.

A special substance, the **refrigerant**, flows through pipes in the fridge. Inside, it evaporates and takes in heat as it does so, just as sweat cools your skin when it evaporates. A **compressor** then squeezes the vapour together, which makes it hot. In the grilles at the back it gives off its heat to the kitchen and turns liquid again; then the cycle starts all over.

Before there were fridges, food was cooled in cold cellars, in streams or with **natural ice**. In winter, blocks of ice were sawn from frozen lakes and stored in ice houses. In Switzerland, too, ice was fetched from lakes and even glaciers and taken to towns and hotels. Other methods were salting, smoking and drying.

In the 19th century the first refrigerating machines were invented, for example by the German engineer **Carl von Linde**. Electric fridges for homes appeared in the 1920s but were expensive. In Switzerland they spread to many households in the 1950s and 1960s. Today almost every family owns a fridge.

You should not leave the fridge door open for long, so that no warm air gets in. Let warm food cool down before you put it away. Modern appliances with a good **energy label** use much less electricity than old ones. Old fridges are disposed of properly because their refrigerants can harm the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance in the fridge that takes in heat and gives it off again.
A pump that squeezes gas together.
Ice from frozen lakes or glaciers that was once used for cooling.
A sticker that shows how economical an appliance is.

gewusst: A fridge does not really make cold; it pumps heat from its inside to the outside.
If you open the fridge door in summer to cool the kitchen, the room actually gets warmer overall.
Fridge magnets are a popular souvenir and hold notes on the fridge door.

teile.einleitung: A while loop is a building block in programming that repeats commands for as long as a condition is true. The English word while means “as long as”. It is especially useful when you do not know in advance how many times something needs to be repeated.
wichtigste: A while loop repeats commands as long as its condition is true.
It stops as soon as the condition becomes false.
If the condition is already false at the start, the loop does not run even once.
It is ideal when the number of repetitions is unknown in advance.
In Python, break ends a loop immediately.
With continue you jump straight to the next round.
If the condition never changes, you get an infinite loop.

abschnitte.text: First the computer checks the **condition**, for example x < 20. If it is true, it carries out the indented commands in the **loop body** and then checks again. If it is false, the program carries on after the loop. With while 5 < 3 the condition is false from the very start, so the contents run 0 times.

If you start with x = 1 and calculate while x < 20: x = x * 2, you get 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. At 32 the condition is false, so 32 is printed. With n = 10 and while n > 0: n = n-3 you get 7, 4, 1 and finally minus 2. The loop i = 0, while i < 5: i = i + 2 runs exactly 3 times.

If the condition never becomes false, the loop runs for ever: this is an **infinite loop**. It often happens by accident when you forget to change the variable. Sometimes people write while True on purpose, for example in a game that should keep running until it is closed. Then you need a **break** command inside so that the loop ends at some point.

A while loop is especially suitable when the number of repetitions is unknown in advance. A guessing game, for example, keeps asking for a number until it is right. A program can keep rolling a dice until a six comes up. If, on the other hand, you know exactly how often something is repeated, you usually use a **counting loop** with for.

With **break** you leave the loop immediately, whatever the condition says. With continue you skip the rest of the current round and jump straight to the next check. Some languages also have the do-while loop, which runs at least once because it only checks the condition at the end. Python does not have this form, so you build it with while True and break.

begriffe.erklaerung: A question that can be true or false, such as x < 20.
The indented commands that are repeated.
A loop that never stops because the condition always stays true.
A command that ends a loop immediately.

gewusst: Almost every computer game has a big loop inside that redraws the picture many times per second.
If a program is stuck in an infinite loop, you can stop it in Python with Ctrl and C.
An alarm clock that keeps ringing until you switch it off also works like a while loop.

teile.einleitung: A web address is the exact address of a page on the internet, just as a postal address identifies a house. You type it into the address bar at the top of the browser, for example www.sbb.ch. The technical term for it is URL.
wichtigste: A web address shows exactly where a page can be found on the internet.
Many web addresses begin with www.
The parts of a web address are separated by dots.
Each web address exists only once on the whole internet.
A web address must not contain any spaces.
Addresses with a secure connection begin with https.
Many federal offices have addresses ending in .ch, such as admin.ch.

abschnitte.text: Every website needs a unique **web address** so that the browser can find it. Each address exists only once on the whole internet. The technical term is **URL**, which stands for Uniform Resource Locator. Behind the name there is really a number, the IP address that a computer has on the internet.

A complete address such as https://www.sbb.ch/fahrplan has several parts. Right at the front is the **protocol**, that is https. Then comes the host name www and the **domain name** sbb. The ending .ch is the **top-level domain**, and after the slash comes the path to a particular page.

The ending often shows where a website comes from or what it is for. .ch stands for Switzerland, .de for Germany and .at for Austria. The ending .com was originally meant for companies, .org for organisations. Many federal offices use the address admin.ch, and since 2015 there has also been the ending .swiss.

If an address begins with **https**, the connection is encrypted, which you can often recognise by a little padlock. This means others cannot read what you enter. Be careful with typing mistakes, because then you usually end up on the wrong page. Fraudsters even deliberately register similar addresses such as sbb-tickets.com to deceive people.

The World Wide Web was invented around 1990 at **CERN** near Geneva by Tim Berners-Lee, and with it today's web addresses. A web address must not contain any spaces; hyphens are used instead. It makes no difference whether you type capital or small letters in the domain name. The Swiss ending .ch is managed by the SWITCH foundation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical term for a web address.
The name of a website, for example sbb.ch.
The ending of an address, such as .ch or .com.
The rules by which computers exchange data, such as https.
A program for displaying websites.

gewusst: The very first website in the world ran on a computer at CERN and can be seen online again today.
You can usually leave out the www in many addresses, and the page still opens.
The ending .ch comes from Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A light bulb, more precisely an incandescent lamp, is a lamp in which a thin wire gets so hot that it shines brightly. For more than a hundred years it lit up homes all over the world. Because it wastes a lot of electricity, it has now been replaced almost everywhere by LED lamps.
wichtigste: In a light bulb, a thin glowing wire gives off light.
A light bulb needs electric current to shine.
From 1879, Thomas Edison made the light bulb practical for everyday use.
The German name “Glühbirne” comes from the fact that the lamp looks like a pear (“Birne”).
A light bulb gets hot when it is on.
It turns most of the electricity into heat instead of light.
That is why it was replaced by more economical LED lamps.

abschnitte.text: When electric current flows through a very thin wire, the **filament**, it gets very hot. At about 2500 degrees Celsius it glows bright white and gives off light. Today the wire is usually made of **tungsten**, a metal that only melts at very high temperatures. So that the wire does not burn up, the glass bulb does not contain normal air but a protective gas or a vacuum.

Even before 1879, various researchers built glowing lamps, for example the Englishman **Joseph Swan**. But their lamps only lasted a short time. From 1879, **Thomas Edison** from the USA made the light bulb practical for everyday use by finding a long-lasting filament made of carbonised fibres. He also built electricity networks and power stations so that the lamps could shine in homes at all.

A classic light bulb turns only about five per cent of the electricity into light. The rest becomes heat, which is why it gets very hot after a short time. The power of a lamp is given in **watts**, named after James Watt. An old 60-watt light bulb is about as bright as an LED lamp of only around 8 watts.

To save energy, the European Union and Switzerland gradually banned the sale of most light bulbs from 2009. They were replaced first by energy-saving lamps and then by **LED** lamps. LEDs last much longer, hardly get warm and need only a fraction of the electricity. The familiar bulb shape still exists, but now with LED technology inside.

A torch needs a battery as its power source so that its little bulb can shine. In the past, torches, bicycle lights and car headlights also had small light bulbs in them. Today you find LEDs almost everywhere. Even so, the light bulb is still a symbol of a good idea, which is why comics often show a glowing bulb above a character who has an idea.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thin wire in a light bulb that shines when it glows.
A metal that does not melt until it is above 3400 degrees.
A light-emitting diode, a very economical electric light source.
The unit that shows how much electricity a device uses per second.

gewusst: In a fire station in Livermore, California, a light bulb has been burning almost without a break since 1901.
Edison and his team tested thousands of materials before they found a good filament.
A light bulb can get so hot that you can burn your fingers on it.

teile.einleitung: In computer science, a loop is a part of a program that repeats commands several times in a row. Instead of writing “move forward” ten times, you simply say “repeat 10 times: move forward”. Loops make programs shorter, clearer and less prone to errors.
wichtigste: A loop repeats one or more commands.
A counting loop is used when the number of repetitions is fixed beforehand.
A conditional loop runs until, or as long as, a condition is met.
A loop that never ends by itself is called an endless loop.
Loops can be nested inside each other.
In Scratch there are the blocks “repeat”, “repeat until” and “forever”.
In Python you write, for example, “for i in range(5):”, and the command is then carried out 5 times.

abschnitte.text: Programs consist of many commands that the computer carries out in order. Often the same thing has to happen several times. Instead of “forward, forward, forward” you say more briefly “3 times forward”. This is exactly what a **loop** does, which is also called a **repetition**. If you repeat “2 steps forward” 3 times, you take 6 steps altogether.

With a **counting loop**, it is fixed from the start how often something is repeated. In Scratch the block is called “repeat 10”. In Python you write “for i in range(5):”, and the indented command below it runs 5 times. If you set x to 0 and repeat “change x by 3” 5 times, x has the value 15 at the end. If you repeat “paint red, paint yellow” 3 times, the last colour you paint is yellow.

With loops you can easily draw shapes. “Repeat 4 times: move 100 steps, turn 90 degrees” gives a **square**. For an equilateral triangle you repeat 3 times and turn 120 degrees each time. In general, for a regular polygon you turn 360 degrees divided by the number of corners. This idea comes from the programming language Logo, in which a turtle drew lines on the screen.

Sometimes you don't know in advance how often something has to be repeated. Then you use a **conditional loop**. The Scratch block “repeat until” stops as soon as the condition becomes true, for example until the sprite touches the edge. In Python there is the while loop for this, which runs as long as a condition is true. An **endless loop** never ends by itself; in games this is often intended, but if there is a mistake, a program can hang because of it.

A loop can be inside another loop; this is called **nested**. If “repeat 3” is inside “repeat 4” and inside it says “play sound Meow”, the sprite miaows 4 times 3, that is 12 times. With nested loops you draw, for example, patterns made of many squares or go through all the squares of a game board. Computers manage millions of repetitions per second. That is why loops are one of the most important tools in programming.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of a program that repeats commands.
A loop with a fixed number of repetitions.
A loop that carries on or stops depending on a condition.
A loop that never stops by itself.
One loop is inside another loop.

gewusst: A washing machine works with loops when it turns the drum back and forth again and again.
The programming language Scratch was developed at MIT in the USA and is also used in many Swiss schools.
With just one loop and a small turning angle you can draw an almost perfect circle.

teile.einleitung: SQL is a language with which you query, enter, change and delete data in databases. The name stands for Structured Query Language. Almost every large app, every online shop and every bank works with SQL in the background.
wichtigste: In 1970 Edgar F. Codd described the relational database model, the basis of SQL.
With the command SELECT you read data from a table.
A primary key uniquely identifies each row of a table.
A foreign key refers to the primary key of another table.
With WHERE you filter rows according to a condition.
The A in ACID stands for atomicity.
Normalisation breaks tables down so that duplicate data is avoided.
In an SQL injection, harmful code gets into a query through input fields.

abschnitte.text: In a **relational database**, data is stored in tables, similar to a spreadsheet. Each row is a record, for example a pupil, and each column is a feature such as name or class. This idea was described by the British computer scientist **Edgar F. Codd** in 1970, when he was working at IBM. SQL is the language with which you talk to such databases.

With **SELECT** you read data, for example SELECT name FROM pupils. With INSERT you add new rows, with UPDATE you change them and with DELETE you delete them. The clause **WHERE** filters rows according to a condition, for example only children from class 5b. With ORDER BY you sort the results, and with GROUP BY you group identical values together.

Every row needs a unique identifier, the **primary key**, for example a pupil number. A **foreign key** refers to the primary key of another table. In this way a table of marks can point to the table of pupils without storing the name again each time. With the JOIN command you connect such tables in a query. Breaking data down into sensible tables without duplicate data is called **normalisation**.

At the beginning of the 1970s, Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce developed a query language called SEQUEL at IBM, which later became SQL. At the end of the 1970s, the first commercial SQL databases came on the market, including Oracle. In 1986 SQL became an official **standard**. Today there are many database systems, for example MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server and SQLite, which is found in almost every smartphone.

In a bank transfer, money has to be taken from one account and paid into another, and either both must happen or nothing at all. For this there are **transactions**, which follow the ACID rules: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. A dangerous attack is **SQL injection**, in which attackers sneak their own SQL code in through input fields. That is why good programs keep commands and user input strictly apart.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organised collection of data managed by a computer.
A question to the database, for example with SELECT.
A unique identifier for each row of a table.
A reference to the primary key of another table.
A group of changes that is carried out completely or not at all.

gewusst: Some people pronounce SQL like the English word sequel, others spell it out as S-Q-L.
SQLite is probably the most widely used database in the world, because it is in countless phones and browsers.
The name SEQUEL had to be changed because another company owned the rights to that name.

teile.einleitung: Crude oil is a thick, usually dark liquid from deep inside the Earth. It is used to make petrol, diesel, heating oil and many plastics. Because crude oil is so versatile, it is sometimes called “black gold”.
wichtigste: Crude oil formed from tiny sea creatures that were deposited millions of years ago.
Petrol, diesel, heating oil, kerosene and plastics are made from crude oil.
Crude oil is a fossil energy source and not renewable.
Burning it produces carbon dioxide, the greenhouse gas that humans release in the largest amounts.
Switzerland has to import all its crude oil, that is, bring it in from abroad.
From the 1950s, the use of cheap crude oil shot up.
Unlike crude oil, the wind never runs out.

abschnitte.text: Crude oil is a mixture of many **hydrocarbons**, that is, substances made of carbon and hydrogen. It can be pale yellow, brown or almost black and has a strong smell. Crude oil is lighter than water and therefore floats on top. Crude oil is often measured in **barrels**, a barrel holding about 159 litres. Together with natural gas and coal, it is one of the fossil energy sources.

Crude oil formed from tiny sea creatures such as **plankton**. When they died, they sank to the sea floor and were covered by mud. Over millions of years, pressure and heat slowly turned them into crude oil. The oil moved through porous rock until it was trapped in **deposits** beneath dense layers. Because this takes so long, crude oil is not renewable.

In 1859, Edwin Drake drilled one of the first oil wells in Pennsylvania in the USA. Today crude oil is extracted on land with pumps and at sea from **oil platforms**. Among the biggest producing countries are the USA, Saudi Arabia and Russia. In a **refinery**, the crude oil is heated and separated into petrol, diesel, heating oil, kerosene and other products. Switzerland's only refinery still in operation is in Cressier in the canton of Neuchâtel.

Switzerland has no oil wells of its own and has to **import** all its crude oil. For a long time many Swiss households were heated with heating oil; today fewer and fewer are. The environmental historian Christian Pfister coined the term **1950s syndrome** for the sharp rise in the use of cheap fossil energy from that time. When the oil crisis broke out in 1973, oil suddenly became scarce and expensive. At that time Switzerland had three **car-free Sundays**, on which the roads stayed empty.

Burning petrol, diesel and heating oil produces **carbon dioxide**, the most important greenhouse gas released by humans. It makes **climate change** worse. In accidents involving tankers or oil platforms, oil can get into the sea and pollute birds, fish and coasts. That is why people are looking for alternatives such as electric cars and renewable energy. Renewable sources such as sun, wind and water never run out.

begriffe.erklaerung: A factory in which crude oil is split into petrol, diesel and other products.
A unit of measurement for crude oil, a barrel of about 159 litres.
Bringing goods in from abroad.
Tiny living things that float in water and from which crude oil formed.

gewusst: Many plastic things, such as toys, toothbrushes or raincoats, are made from crude oil.
Chewing gum, paints and some medicines also contain substances made from crude oil.
Even in ancient times, people used crude oil that came to the surface by itself to seal boats.

teile.einleitung: A submarine is a ship that can travel under water. The German name “U-Boot” is short for “Unterseeboot”, meaning undersea boat. Submarines can dive, travel long distances under water and surface again.
wichtigste: A submarine travels under water.
To dive, a submarine fills its ballast tanks with water.
To surface, the water is pushed out again with compressed air.
With a periscope you can look above the surface from under water.
In both world wars submarines sank many ships.
In 1960 the Swiss Jacques Piccard reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
Captain Nemo's Nautilus from a novel by Jules Verne is famous.

abschnitte.text: A submarine has large **ballast tanks**. When they are filled with air, the boat floats on the surface. When water is let in, it becomes heavier and dives. To surface, **compressed air** pushes the water out again.

Under water it is dark, and most submarines have no windows. Just below the surface, the crew looks through a **periscope**, a tube with mirrors. In the depths, submarines find their way with **sonar**, which sends out sound waves and measures the echo. Dolphins find their way in a similar way.

As early as 1775, the American David Bushnell built a small diving boat called the Turtle. In 1870, **Jules Verne**'s novel “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea” was published, featuring Captain Nemo's submarine Nautilus. In the First World War, in 1915, a German submarine sank the British passenger ship **Lusitania**, killing many Americans too. From 1 February 1917, Germany waged unrestricted submarine warfare, in which even neutral merchant ships were sunk without warning.

Today many navies have large **nuclear submarines** that can stay under water for months. The first of these was the American USS Nautilus in 1954. Smaller submarines run on diesel and batteries. There are also research submarines and even submarines for tourists.

The Swiss scientist **Auguste Piccard** developed a deep-sea diving vessel, the bathyscaphe. On 23 January 1960, his son **Jacques Piccard** and Don Walsh dived almost 11,000 metres in the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of the **Mariana Trench**. This is the deepest point of all the oceans. For the 1964 Swiss National Exhibition, Jacques Piccard built the tourist submarine “Auguste Piccard”, which took tens of thousands of visitors through Lake Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tank in a submarine that is filled with water to dive.
A viewing tube used to look above the surface from under water.
Locating things under water using sound waves.
A special diving vessel for very great depths.

gewusst: At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the water presses more than a thousand times harder than at the surface.
The Nautilus in the novel is named after the nautilus, a relative of the squid with a shell.

teile.einleitung: A video consists of moving pictures, often together with sound. Really it is many single pictures shown one after another so quickly that our eye sees a smooth movement. Today we watch videos on mobile phones, computers or televisions.
wichtigste: A video shows moving pictures, usually with sound.
It consists of many single pictures, about 25 to 30 per second.
A triangle on a button means play, and two vertical lines mean pause.
A square usually means stop.
In video editing, you cut out parts and put them together in a new way.
For a wide video, you hold the phone sideways.
Subtitles show as text what is being said in the video.

abschnitte.text: A video is a sequence of **single pictures**, which are also called frames. In Europe a video usually shows 25 pictures per second, in the USA often 30. Because the eye can no longer see the pictures one by one, we see a flowing movement. The Latin word video means “I see”.

Almost everywhere the buttons look the same. A **triangle** starts the video, two vertical lines mean pause, and a square usually means stop. Two triangles one after another wind forwards or backwards. These symbols come from old cassette recorders and video recorders.

Today anyone can shoot videos with a mobile phone. If you hold the phone **sideways**, the picture is wide, like on a television. You should hold it steady and make sure there is good light, ideally with the light behind the camera. If you film other people, you must ask them first, because everyone has a right to their own image.

In **video editing**, you cut out unnecessary parts and put the scenes together in a new way. You can add music, titles and **subtitles**. Subtitles help people who cannot hear well, and everyone who watches a video without sound. Editing programs are now available free of charge for tablets and phones.

In the past, videos were stored on magnetic tape in **video cassettes**, later on DVDs. Today videos are mostly digital files, for example in the MP4 format. The resolution tells you how many pixels a picture has; Full HD has 1,920 by 1,080 points. Since YouTube was founded in 2005, watching videos on the internet has become completely normal.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single picture of a video.
How many pixels a video picture has.
Trimming video scenes and putting them together in a new way.
Text in the video that shows what is being said.

gewusst: Videos need a lot of storage space, so they are strongly compressed when saved, without you noticing much.
Slow-motion shots are made when a camera records a great many pictures per second and plays them back more slowly.
In the 1980s and 1990s, video cassettes were found in almost every household.

teile.einleitung: Supervised learning is an important method of machine learning in which a computer learns from examples whose correct answer is known. It is given, for example, thousands of photos labelled “cat” or “dog” and finds the rules by itself to sort new photos correctly. This is how spam filters, image recognition and many other applications of artificial intelligence work.
wichtigste: In supervised learning, a model learns from examples whose correct answer is known.
If a category is predicted, this is called classification.
If a numerical value such as the price of a flat is predicted, this is called regression.
Well-known methods are linear regression, k-nearest neighbours, support vector machines and neural networks.
A model is checked with test data that it did not see while learning.
The confusion matrix shows which predictions were right and which were wrong.
With unevenly distributed data, accuracy on its own is a misleading measure.

abschnitte.text: The model is given **training data** in which the correct answer, the so-called label, is given for each example. From this it looks for patterns that connect input and answer. After that it should also find the right answer for new examples. The name comes from the fact that the labels “supervise” the learning like a teacher.

In **classification**, the model assigns something to a group, for example an email as spam or not spam. In **regression**, it predicts a continuous numerical value, for example the price of a flat from its size and location. Linear regression does this by putting a straight line through the data and minimising the mean squared deviation. At the end, classification networks turn their raw values into probabilities that add up to 1 with the softmax function.

The **k-nearest neighbours** method looks at the k most similar training points and chooses the class that is in the majority there. A **support vector machine** looks for the dividing plane with the greatest possible distance to both classes. Decision trees ask simple yes-no questions one after another. Especially powerful today are artificial neural networks, which recognise pictures and speech, for example.

A model is checked with **test data** that it never saw while learning. In k-fold cross-validation, the data is divided into k parts, and each part serves once as the test part. The **confusion matrix** counts true and false positive as well as true and false negative predictions. If a model recognises 60 out of 80 sick people, its sensitivity is 75 percent. If 99 percent of people are healthy, a model that always says “healthy” already reaches 99 percent accuracy, even though it is useless.

If a model learns the training data by heart instead of finding general rules, this is called **overfitting**. It is then bad with new data. A model also takes on errors and prejudices that are in the training data. That is why good, varied and carefully labelled data is just as important as the method itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: The correct answer that belongs to a training example.
Assignment to a group, for example spam or not spam.
Prediction of a numerical value such as a price.
The model learns the examples by heart and fails with new data.
A table of a model's right and wrong predictions.

gewusst: When you have to click on pictures of traffic lights or bicycles on a website, you are sometimes helping to label training data.
Millions of labelled photos are used for large image recognition models.
The idea of linear regression is over 200 years old, much older than any computer.

teile.einleitung: A motorbike is a vehicle with two wheels and an engine. You sit on it as on a bicycle, but you do not have to pedal, because the engine drives the back wheel. Motorbikes are nimble, fast and very popular with many people in their free time.
wichtigste: A motorbike normally has two wheels.
The first motorbike with a petrol engine was the Reitwagen built by Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach in 1885.
In Switzerland, anyone riding a motorbike must wear a helmet.
For a motorbike you need a category A or A1 driving licence.
In bends, the rider leans into the curve together with the motorbike.
The Swiss rider Thomas Lüthi became motorcycle world champion in the 125cc class in 2005.

abschnitte.text: A motorbike has a **frame**, two wheels, an engine, a tank and handlebars. You accelerate with the right-hand grip, and you brake and change gear with levers worked by hand and foot. The engine's power usually reaches the back wheel through a chain. Electric motorbikes without a petrol engine are becoming more and more common.

In 1885 **Gottlieb Daimler** and Wilhelm Maybach built the Reitwagen, a wooden frame with a petrol engine. It is regarded as the first motorbike. Soon companies such as Harley-Davidson in the USA, BMW in Germany and Honda in Japan appeared. Over time, motorbikes became lighter, more powerful and safer.

There are many types: **scooters** with small wheels for town, touring bikes for long journeys and sports bikes for high speeds. Off-road motorbikes, known as motocross bikes, ride over sand, mud and jumps. A motorbike with a sidecar has three wheels and offers room for a second person alongside.

The best known racing series is **MotoGP**, in which riders reach more than 350 km/h. **Thomas Lüthi** from Bern became world champion in the class up to 125 cubic centimetres in 2005. Dominique Aegerter from the canton of Bern has also had great success in motorcycle racing. Because circuit racing was banned in Switzerland for a long time after 1955, Swiss riders compete abroad.

Motorcyclists have hardly any protection in accidents, which is why a **helmet** is compulsory. Protective clothing with body armour, gloves and boots is very important. In Switzerland you may ride small motorbikes of up to 125 cubic centimetres from the age of 16 with category A1. For bigger machines you need category A.

begriffe.erklaerung: The size of the engine, measured in cubic centimetres.
When rider and motorbike tilt to one side in a bend.
Hard padding in clothing that protects you in a fall.
A carriage at the side with a third wheel for a passenger.

gewusst: The first Reitwagen of 1885 had a wooden frame.
Racing riders lean so far into bends that their knee almost touches the ground.
Good motorcyclists always look where they want to go when riding through a bend.

teile.einleitung: Turtle graphics is a way of drawing pictures with simple commands: a little turtle walks across the screen and drags a line behind it. The idea comes from the programming language Logo, which was developed for children. Today many pupils learn programming with the turtle.
wichtigste: In turtle graphics you move a turtle that draws a trail as it walks.
The idea comes from the programming language Logo for children.
In Python, forward(100) moves the turtle 100 steps forward.
The command left(90) turns the turtle 90 degrees to the left.
With penup() the turtle moves without drawing.
With loops you can quickly make polygons, stars and patterns.
Turtle graphics combines programming with geometry.

abschnitte.text: In **turtle graphics** you control an imaginary turtle. It always has a position and a direction it is facing. You give it commands such as “go forward” or “turn”. As it moves, it drags a **pen** behind it and so draws lines. Because it is easy to put yourself in the turtle's place, you understand the commands very quickly.

The idea comes from the programming language **Logo**, which was developed in the USA from 1967. A well-known inventor was the mathematician and educator **Seymour Papert**. At first there were even small robots that moved about on the floor as turtles and drew on paper with a real pen. Later the turtle moved onto the screen.

Python has a built-in module called turtle. With forward(100) the turtle walks 100 steps forward, and with right(90) and left(90) it turns 90 degrees. With penup() it lifts the pen and walks without drawing; with pendown() it lowers it again. The command pencolor('red') colours the lines red, and circle(50) draws a circle with a radius of 50. With goto(0, 0) the turtle jumps to the middle of the window, because that is where the **origin** of the coordinates is.

With a **loop**, commands can be repeated. Going forward and turning 90 degrees four times gives a square. The loop for i in range(5): forward(100); right(144) draws a five-pointed star. If you gradually increase the length in a loop, you get a spiral.

Turtle graphics is well suited to getting started with programming, because you see every result straight away. Along the way you learn a lot about **angles**, polygons and coordinates. In Swiss schools, programs such as XLogo or TigerJython are used for this, for example. Scratch also has a pen extension that draws on the same principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The drawing figure on the screen, a turtle.
A programming language that was developed for children.
A part of a program that is repeated several times.
Numbers that say exactly where a point is.

gewusst: The first turtles were real small robots that moved across large sheets of paper with a pen.
For a regular polygon, the turtle always has to turn exactly 360 degrees in total.
For the star, the turtle turns 144 degrees five times, so twice all the way round in total.

teile.einleitung: Web hosting means that a provider makes storage space and servers available so that a website can be reached on the internet. Without hosting, a website would only be on your own computer, and nobody else could see it. The servers are usually in large data centres and run day and night.
wichtigste: A web hosting provider makes storage space and servers available for websites.
With shared hosting, several websites share one server.
If you rent a whole server on your own, you have a dedicated server.
Traditionally, files are uploaded to the web space with the FTP protocol.
The servers are usually in data centres.
A backup is a safety copy of the website data.
For some Swiss companies the location matters because of Swiss data protection.

abschnitte.text: A website consists of files such as texts, pictures and programs. So that others can call them up at any time, these files have to be on a **server** that is always switched on and connected to the internet. A **web host** rents out such space. You can think of it like a flat that you rent for your website.

With **shared hosting**, many websites share one server; this is cheap and enough for small sites. With a virtual server, you get a separate part of a server with more freedom. If you rent a whole computer on your own, it is called a **dedicated server**. With cloud hosting, the computing power is spread flexibly across many servers.

A hosting offer usually states the **storage space**, that is, how much data you may store on the server. Email addresses, a database and a security certificate for https are often included. Many providers regularly make a **backup**, a safety copy of the website data. Traditionally, files are uploaded with the **FTP** protocol, or more securely today with SFTP.

The servers of web hosts are in **data centres**. These are large buildings with thousands of computers in cabinets, powerful cooling and emergency power. They are monitored around the clock and protected against fire and break-ins. In Switzerland there are several large data centres, some of them even in former military facilities in the Alps.

For some companies, hospitals and authorities, it is important that the data stays in Switzerland. Then the Swiss **Data Protection Act** applies, which has been in force in a new version since 2023. That is why Swiss hosts often advertise with data centres in the country. Anyone who makes a small website can also use free offers, but then often has to accept advertising or restrictions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer that provides data on the internet around the clock.
The rented storage space for a website.
A building full of servers with cooling and emergency power.
A protocol for uploading files to a server.
A safety copy of data.

gewusst: Data centres need so much electricity that some pass on their waste heat to heat homes or swimming pools.
Today you can host a simple website for just a few francs a month.
Many large websites are on servers in several countries at the same time so that they load quickly everywhere.

teile.einleitung: Version control is a system that stores all the changes to files, above all to program code. You can look at any time to see who changed what and when, and go back to earlier versions. For teams who work on software together, it is indispensable today.
wichtigste: Version control stores the whole history of files.
A saved state of changes with a description is called a commit.
A parallel line of development is called a branch.
The storage place with all the files and their history is called a repository.
Subversion is an example of a central version control system, Git of a distributed one.
If two people change the same line differently, a merge conflict arises when combining them.
An early system was SCCS, which was created at Bell Labs in 1972.

abschnitte.text: If you just save a file, you overwrite the old version. **Version control**, on the other hand, remembers every intermediate state. This lets you undo a mistake, even if it was made weeks ago. You can also see who wrote which line and why.

A **commit** is a saved state of changes with a short description, such as “Fixed login bug”. All the commits together are kept in a **repository**. With a **branch** you can create a parallel line of development and try out a new feature without disturbing the main program. A tag marks a fixed state, for example version 1.0.

When the work on a branch is finished, it is combined with the main branch; this is called a **merge**. Usually this works automatically. But if two people have changed the same line differently, a **merge conflict** arises. Then a person has to decide which version is right.

With a **central version control system** such as Subversion, the history is kept on a single server. With a **distributed version control system** such as Git, every person has a complete copy with the whole history. A big advantage is that you can work and make commits even without a connection to the server. Today Git is by far the most widely used system.

One of the first systems was **SCCS**, which was developed at Bell Labs in the USA in 1972. Later came RCS, CVS and, in 2000, Subversion. In 2005 **Linus Torvalds**, the inventor of Linux, wrote the Git system to manage work on the Linux kernel. Platforms such as GitHub and GitLab, on which millions of people share their code, are built on Git.

begriffe.erklaerung: A saved state of changes with a description.
The storage place for all the files and their history.
A parallel line of development; the word means a branch of a tree.
Combining two lines of development.
A fixed marker for a particular state.

gewusst: Linus Torvalds wrote the first version of Git in just a few days.
Books, websites and even legal texts are sometimes managed with Git.
Every commit in Git has a long identifier made of digits and letters that makes it unique.
